News.title: Two children, 11 & 13, rushed to hospital after ‘malfunction’ on fairground ride as woman, 21, also injured
News.content:
FAIRGROUND RUSH Two children, 11 & 13, rushed to hospital after ‘malfunction’ on fairground ride as woman, 21, also injured

TWO children have been rushed to hospital after a fairground ride “malfunctioned” with a woman also injured.

Emergency services were called to Blyth Road fields in Maltby, near Rotherham, South Yorkshire, at around 7.30pm on Friday night after reports of injuries at the Maltby Crags Fair.



Police have now confirmed two children, aged 11 and 13, and a 21-year-old woman were taken to hospital.

A South Yorkshire Police spokesman said: “Emergency services are currently in attendance at an incident at Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham after two young people, aged 11 and 13, and a 21-year-old woman were injured while on a ride.



“They have been taken to hospital for treatment and the fairground has now closed for the evening (11 September).

“Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground but has since been reopened.”

Posting on social media, one local has said the “malfunction” involved a car coming off the track of the ride before crashing into another.

She wrote: “A car came off the track, and another one crashed into it.”



She said a number of people had fallen from the ride and at least two boys had been injured.

Maltby Crags Funfair, presented by J Holmes & Sons, has been running in Maltby since September 9.

It is due to operate all weekend between 5pm and 9pm, but it is not known whether it will still be operating.

It is not yet known what ride has malfunctioned.

There was a huge emergency services response to the incident this evening with pictures circulating on social media showing at least six police cars in attendance.



It is understood the Air Ambulance was also called to the scene.

News.title: ‘Strong indications’ Osama bin Laden was plotting terror attack on Britain before 9/11, bombshell new CIA docs reveal
News.content:
TERROR boss Osama bin Laden wanted to attack Britain on its own soil years before 9/11, new bombshell CIA memos reveal.

US spies claimed to have had “strong indications” that the UK was on an Al-Qaeda hit list with the reports unearthed in top secret documents released by the CIA to mark the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks.



The huge trove of documents released by the spy agency included one from August 28, 1998, which said Bin Laden was looking to target the UK.

It was among 69 newly declassified briefing notes released – marking the largest release of information related to 9/11 ever.



The UK had been directly mentioned in a document titled “Bin Ladin Terrorist Network Still a Threat”.

The CIA appeared to purposely misspell the terror boss’ name throughout the docs.



Compiled after American cruise missile strikes on Al-Qaeda bases in Sudan, the memo said Bin Laden was seeking to target the UK.

The memo said: “Hours before the US missile strikes, Bin Laden was looking at options for further attacks against the US as well as the UK.”



“Bin Ladin did not indicate precise targets or timing.”

The memo also warned that a US Embassy in a redacted country was “a possible target” and said a man had been authorized by bin Laden to “explore attacks in the US.”

Another memo written at the end of that year, was marked “Significant Near-Term Threat of Bin Ladin Attacks”.

It warned: “We have strong indications that he would like to attack the US and allies such as the UK and Israel on their own soil.

“If Bin Ladin judges these venues are too well defended, however, he will target US and allied interests in other areas of the world accessible to his network.”



A file from August 1999 highlighted Bin Laden’s anger that two of his London-based henchmen had been detained by British police.

The memo revealed: “His organisation’s capabilities have suffered from the arrest of key operatives.

“Bin Ladin in interviews last year expressed anger over the arrests of his senior procurement officer and the chief of his organisation in the UK.”



The docs warn of Bin Laden’s plotting “despite sparse, vague, and imperfect information”.

They included intel about plans by Bin Laden to hijack planes, noting the possibility that a group “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.

The CIA said the huge document release “aimed to give Americans a glimpse into our most sensitive intelligence from the years before and day after one of our nation’s darkest moments”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It said the 71 partially-redacted briefing notes “trace the story of CIA analysts’ evolving understanding” of Al-Qaeda.

Two of the memos had been released before.

News.title: Nigel Farage secures record £36m donation from crypto billionaire to help give Reform ‘fair fight’ at the polls
News.content:
NIGEL Farage has secured a record £36million donation from a crypto billionaire in order to help give Reform a “fair fight” in the polls.

The whopping sum is the largest single donation to a British political party in history.



Brit Ben Delo, co-founder of trading platform BitMEX, insisted only a huge cash injection would allow the party to battle against the “entrenched advantages” enjoyed by its political rivals.

Mr Delo, who was already Reform UK’s second largest donor, wrote in the Daily Telegraph: “My conclusion from Reform’s recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government.”



The significant sum dwarfs the previous donation record of £10million, left to the Conservatives as a bequest.

Mr Farage, who faces an ongoing police probe into party financing, said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo has shown such confidence in Reform.

“Ben knows that we are the only party that can turn the country around and reverse Britain’s decline.”

Mr Delo is now Reform’s largest donor having previously been second behind billionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave £9million to the party last year.

Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.

Mr Delo continued: “Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of ‘our democracy’ while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field.



“My conclusion from Reform’s recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government.”

The Telegraph reported the £36million figure represents £1million a month between now and the latest possible date of the next general election in 2029, but Mr Delo has made the payment up front to avoid attempts to block it.

MPs last week backed measures including a cap on overseas donations at £100,000 and a suspension of funding through cryptocurrency, but the draft legislation still needs to be passed by the House of Lords to become law.

Ministers have argued the changes will prevent foreign money influencing elections, but Reform has said it is a bid to choke its funding.

Reform has faced ongoing questions about its finances which overshadowed its annual conference last week following an undercover investigation broadcast on Channel 4 News.



Detectives from the Metropolitan Police are investigating after the report showed senior party figures appearing to discuss how to disguise donations from foreign sources.

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and has said it will co-operate fully with the probe.

Mr Farage’s long-time aide Dan Jukes, who denies wrongdoing, and head of policy James Orr have been suspended pending an internal investigation into the allegations.

The party leader also faces an investigation by Parliament’s standards watchdog over a £5 million gift he received from Mr Harborne.

Mr Farage has said he has done nothing wrong and the gift was not political.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Labour spokesperson said: “Nigel Farage is still up to his neck in scandal over his secret £5million ‘gift’ from his other crypto-billionaire backer and the criminal investigation into potentially illegal donations.

“The questions he faces aren’t going away – in fact they’re piling up.”

News.title: Two women, 27 & 41, brutally attack man, 70, during dog walk by kicking and stamping on OAP as pair jailed
News.content:
'TERRIFYING ORDEAL' Two women, 27 & 41, brutally attack man, 70, during dog walk by kicking and stamping on OAP as pair jailed

TWO women who brutally attacked a 70-year-old man by kicking and stamping on him while he was on a dog walk have been jailed.

Leanne Yates, 41, and Chloe Thompson, 27, subjected the victim to a “terrifying ordeal” in a Middlesbrough park.



The pair broke away from the group they were with and approached the pensioner on the evening of March 9 to ask him for money.

He said he had none and took his dog home, Teeside Crown Court heard.



When he returned to Ayresome Gardens to walk his other dog he came across the group again.

The victim moved out of the way to let them pass but CCTV shows the man in the group “strike the pensioner to his face” Cainan Lonsdale, prosecuting, said.



The pensioner punched back only for the man to “make another blow to his face” knocking him to the ground.

Thompson is then seen dragging the victim onto the pavement from the grass verge while Yates “is stamping and kicking him” as the group gathered around, the barrister said.

The victim’s pockets were rifled through and his satchel was taken, but later discarded when the gang found it only held a dog lead, bags, a hat and gloves.

The pensioner went home and his partner took him to hospital after seeing his injuries.



He said his “vision was affected” and photos showed bruising, swelling and a large cut on his cheek.

The women were both found with drugs when they were arrested.

Yates, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty to attempted robbery; assault occasioning actual bodily harm; and the possession of a class A drug.

Thompson, of New Street in Thornaby, admitted attempted robbery; assault occasioning actual bodily harm; two counts of the possession of a class C drug; and failing to surrender.

Judge Richard Wright acknowledged the difficult backgrounds of the two women and considered their upbringings mitigating circumstances.



He told the pair at the sentencing hearing: “Yates – you took the lead in kicking and stamping on him.

“Thompson – you dragged him about. This was a terrifying ordeal for him.”

“When you attack a 70 year old man, in the dark, who was doing no more than walking his dog.

“When you put him to the ground and kick and stamp on him – you go to prison” he said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Thompson and Yates were jailed for three years and three years and nine months respectively.

News.title: Woman suffered seizure after being repeatedly raped in secluded park by man, 25, she met in nightclub
News.content:
'RUINED MY LIFE' Woman suffered seizure after being repeatedly raped in secluded park by man, 25, she met in nightclub

A WOMAN suffered a seizure after being repeatedly raped in a secluded park by a man she had met in a nightclub.

The victim had been out with pals in South Shields and ended up in Industry nightclub before being separated from friends and meeting Aiden Johnson, 25.

They kissed and swapped details before leaving the club together at around 5am when the woman said she needed to get a taxi home.

Johnson offered to help get her one as he led her through a housing estate, which prosecutors said was “on the pretext of finding a taxi”.





He then attempted to lift her dress up but she told him she wasn’t interested in having sex with him.

Newcastle Crown Court was told he then led her to a park where she stumbled to the floor.

Prosecutor Ben Sayers said Johnson then “seized the opportunity” to carry out the first part of the sex attack.

Mr Sayers told the court: “Ignoring her resistance, he continued to subject her to further sexual acts. She repeatedly told him to stop.”



He raped her three times in total as well as sexually assaulting her.

Mr Sayers said: “She told him throughout she did not want to do anything. He ignored her protests and her efforts to push and kick him off. He tried to reassure her it was all fine.”

During the brutal attack, the woman suffered a seizure and when she came round she told Johnson she had been sexually abused once and didn’t need it again.

Johnson told her, he “wasn’t like that”.



He left in a taxi and asked her to go with him but she refused.

She called her family and later reported the attack.

When he was arrested, Johnson claimed he went to the park hoping for sex but said none occurred.

However, his DNA was found on her underwear.

The woman said in a victim impact statement: “What happened to me has completely ruined my life.



“I haven’t been the same person since and don’t think I ever will be.

“The trauma got so bad I took myself to a bridge to end my life.

“I’ve been diagnosed with PTSD.

“I think about what happened from the minute I wake up until I go to sleep. I can’t switch off. I have constant nightmares.

“I’ve tried all the support there is but still feel broken. I most likely will be on medication for the rest of my life so I can feel somewhat human and have some control of my body.



“I’m scared to be alone in public in case something like this happens again.

“I didn’t do anything wrong. I trusted someone to help me get home and they used that trust to hurt me, so I don’t trust anyone.

“This has taken everything from me, my confidence, my mental health, sense of safety and my trust.

“It’s hard to put into words how much this has destroyed me.”

Johnson, who has a caution for sexual assault when he was a youth, was found guilty of three counts of rape, attempted rape and assault by penetration.



He was imprisoned for eight years and has been put on the sex offenders register for life and was also given a restraining order.

Judge Sarah Mallett told him: “Your conduct that night has devastated her life as it has your own.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Defending Johnson, Jane Foley said Johnson continues to maintain the sexual activity was consensual and has a supportive family.

The court was told he had led a “productive life”.

News.title: Why the fate of Trump’s final two years in office hangs in the balance – as JD and Lil’ Marco battle to succeed him
News.content:
DONALD TRUMP used to say he was “tired of winning” but has finally admitted: “I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.”

After a near two-hour turn on Wednesday evening, the ageing President was back in front of 10,000 true believers on Thursday night.



Half an hour into his planned ten-minute closing remarks of the Republican Party’s jazzy gathering in Dallas, Texas, The Don was in pensive mode.

He had just seen what we all witnessed in the giant arena: Life after him.



Mocked by the Mad Mullahs of Iran, battered in the opinion polls back home and facing the prospect of being a lame duck come November, this impromptu convention to launch his party’s midterm election campaign felt a little like a last hurrah.

“Just pretend I’m on the ballot”, Trump begged two nights in a row, as he sought to breathe life into his party’s tricky prospects for crucial Senate and Congressional elections eight weeks away.

The fate of his final two years in office hangs in the balance. If he retains his grip on Washington, he has promised the world — in the form of a $5,000 bung to every US citizen.

Should he lose, it will be a long 24 months cornered in the West Wing as his Democrat enemies use every tool in the shed to push and probe his legacy, family and businesses.

Six months into his “four to six week” war in the Middle East, Trump still insists his party must stick with him for a similar bounce to 2016 and 2024, when scores of down ticket nobodies were elected on his coat tails.

Plenty of candidates who steered well clear of the jamboree clearly disagree.



Obviously still loved in the convention hall, tanking approval ratings and a fading star quality are getting to our ratings-obsessed chum as he demanded a sworn pledge of loyalty from the crowd.

But they had just gone absolutely wild . . . for another man.

Vice President JD Vance, just 42, put in the performance of his admittedly short career.

His pacey primetime speech hit all the right buttons for the politicos and dispelled some — well deserved — pundit views that he is just, well, a bit weird.



Having shed a few pounds and grown a few greys over the past year, Vance was relaxed, funny and fired up.

Dealing with a heckler so effortlessly some suggested it must have been a scripted plant, JD — as the room chanted — stepped up to the plate and, frankly, knocked it out the park as they say here.

Having endlessly let it be known he was against the war in Iran all along,

Vance’s speech went hard on disgruntled MAGA fans, mis-sold an America First isolationist dream, urging them not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater”.



Trump’s mealy mouthed midterm campaign riff, that the Republicans are mainstream compared to the now extremist woke left Democrats, was distilled far more clearly by Vance: “It’s common sense or the crazies.”

Though he chickened out of mentioning Iran by name, “don’t hand over the country to a bunch of crazy people just because you disagree with a policy decision”, landed exactly where JD aimed it.

While he got a thumbs-up from Trump at the end of the speech, the speed at which the No2 was rushed from the stage, not even to return for the sing-along and balloon-laden end-of-convention ceremonies, said it all.

I would not have wanted to be any other leading Republican eyeing a tilt at 2028, judging by the roar of that crowd.



For the first time there’s a real buzz around JD, which might explain why increasingly respected Secretary of State Marco Rubio has briefed that he has “no plans” to run against his close buddy.

While Texas Senator Ted Cruz is clearly eyeing another doomed bid, other floated candidates such as the berk-ish Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and loony tunes ex-intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard need to give their heads a wobble before getting into the race.

The consensus from behind the scenes in Texas is only the man Trump once derided as Lil’ Marco could upset the JD juggernaut.

At 55, Rubio is a spring chicken compared to recent Presidents but he still carries the scars from his 2016 bid.



It would be highly unusual for a sitting VP to seek the nomination for the top job and not get it, so there’s a pecking order to contend with and plenty of MAGA powerbrokers are already locked in for Vance.

While establishment Republicans and plenty of big donors are urging the smoother and more traditionally conservative Rubio to change his mind, some wise hands say he would have a stronger bid in 2032 should Vance shoot and miss in two years’ time. Which could well happen.

Barely a Senator before he was thrust into the White House, it’s going to take more than one decent speech and a powerful back story to prove Vance is ready for the big seat.

A few years ago he was calling Trump “Hitler”, now he acts like his boss is the second coming. One minute he’s the true isolationist, the next he is meddling in European politics.

Hyper-online, White House insiders are quick to warn of his occasional hotheadness.



Truth be told, the Republicans may have the making of a winner here but they don’t know for sure. Which is why anointing him Trump’s successor without a proper contest may spell disaster.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The big guy’s endorsement will certainly end the primary hopes of any other candidate but even Trump seems hesitant, publicly stating he is not sure who would be the best candidate between his VP and top diplomat.

Despite the cheers of the crowd, Trump was far from alone as the Republicans headed off from Texas for the stump . . .

News.title: National security must ALWAYS trump welfare because without it, the entire country is reduced to a heap of cinders
News.content:
Benefits state

BRITAIN’S Armed Forces are running out of ammo and manpower — but there’s cash coming out of our ears for the workshy.

Andy Burnham admitted as much when he told MPs he would not cut the bloated benefits bill to boost military spending. He insisted he would never be forced to choose between the two.



But it’s clear he already has — and that welfare is the hands-down winner.

At a time when our defence capabilities urgently need bolstering amid the mounting threat posed by Russia, Iran and others, we face the jaw-dropping reality that the number of people who claim state handouts for ADHD has almost doubled in the past three years to 100,000 — while the number of full-time soldiers has shrunk to just 82,000.



In addition, the 70,000 people claiming benefits for anxiety now outstrips the combined full-time personnel of the Royal Navy and the RAF.

Since Labour grabbed power, the total welfare bill has shot up by a staggering £20billion a year. It’s not so much Benefits Street as Benefits State.

Those who are unable to work because of genuine disability deserve support.

But it’s right to ask why these numbers are suddenly rocketing at a time when shameless “sickfluencers” are teaching millions how to game the system.

If the PM is as keen as we think on turning the clock back six decades, he should heed the words of a Labour big beast from that period.

Denis Healey, who served as Defence Secretary and Chancellor, warned that national security must ALWAYS trump welfare, education and housing.



Because without it, the entire country is reduced to a heap of cinders.

Ship has sailed

LABOUR’S much trumpeted “one in, one out” deal to return illegal migrants was exposed as a failing gimmick months ago.

About 1,400 have been swapped so far — that’s a drop in the Channel when 20,000 have made the crossing already this year, and 50 of those kicked out simply returned on the next boat.

Now France wants us to take asylum-seekers from across Europe in a replacement for the agreement, which expires next month. Ministers should accept this stunt is dead.

It’s time to sink it and launch a serious deterrent to stop asylum cheats coming here in the first place.



PM’s drill rap

IN his first words to the Commons as PM, Andy Burnham promised a “place first rather than party first” approach.

So why is he set to delay giving the go-ahead for gas drilling in the North Sea until after a crunch by-election next month?

Simple. He’s scared it will help Green Party leader Zack Polanski to storm to victory in Sir Keir Starmer’s old seat.

His bold new politics have been shelved so he can cynically drill for votes instead.

News.content:

Writing in the Daily Telegraph, external, Ben Delo said he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".

The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK.

Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.

Delo said he was donating Â£1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

But Labour previously introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.

Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated Â£4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong in order to continue his backing for the party.

Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.

News.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
News.content:
"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" â Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

News.title: Masked men, lorries and road blocks: How anti-migrant activists are changing tactics
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

News.title: Trump to arrive in Ireland for two-day visit
News.content:
An avid golf fan, in July Trump said he hoped to travel to Doonbeg to watch the Irish Open.

In a special video message, he told the US Embassy's Fourth of July celebration event that he wants to see "Rory [McIlroy] and all the great players".

"There's nothing better than Irish-American friendship and I have a beautiful place over there - it's one of the best, most beautiful golf courses anywhere in the world," said Trump in his message, which was broadcast on a large screen.

"We have a place that's so top and we have the Irish Open going to be there.

"They call it Trump National, we sometimes use the name of the location, but it's Trump National Golf Club, and we're looking forward to it.

"We're going to have a tremendous celebration. I think I'm going to come over and I'm going to see it and watch. It'll be something very, very special."

President Connolly, an outspoken Gaza activist who has been critical of the US and said Trump is acting "like a bully" over tariffs, has come under pressure to raise issues in the Middle East during her brief meeting with the US president.

Sinn FÃ©in and a series of other parties in the Republic who backed her in the Irish presidency campaign last year have called on her to raise Gaza during her meeting with Trump.

News.title: Is a September heatwave forecast for the UK?
News.content:
Temperatures are set to climb across the UK this weekend, reaching summerlike levels in some places.

It will feel warm and muggy - especially where there are sunny spells - although heavy rain also features in the forecast.

The warmth will persist into Monday in many areas but nowhere is expected to reach heatwave criteria and cooler conditions are due to return by midweek.

Computer weather models paint a very mixed picture for the second half of September but, while there are likely to be some warm spells, there are currently no definitive signs of a heatwave.

News.title: American Shelton to face Zverev in US Open final
News.content:
Ben Shelton powered his way into the US Open final with an impressive four-set win over Frances Tiafoe in an epic all-American semi-final.

Both players were bidding to reach their first Grand Slam final and put on a show for a raucous crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium, with eighth seed Shelton coming from a set down to win 4-6 6-3 6-3 7-5.

Neither American was overawed by the occasion and they lived up to their reputations as dazzling shot-makers but, after three hours and 17 minutes, it was Shelton who won through.

The 23-year-old will face Alexander Zverev in Sunday's showpiece after the top seed beat unseeded Russian Karen Khachanov 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6) to reach a third Grand Slam final in a row and continue his bid for a second major of the year.

"Frances is like a big brother to me, every time that we get to take to this court together and play each other is super special," said Shelton, who also paid tribute to his late grandmother and those affected by the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago in his on-court interview.

"This is both of our favourite tournament, our favourite court in the world and to be able to light it up in front of you guys [the crowd] is the best feeling there is."

After losing his previous two major semi-finals, Shelton can now look forward to his maiden final and will aim to end a 23-year wait for an American winner in the men's singles of a Grand Slam.

Since Andy Roddick's triumph at Flushing Meadows in 2003 - 11 months after Shelton was born - an American man has only reached a Grand Slam final on six previous occasions, most recently Taylor Fritz two years ago in New York.

To end the drought and emulate Roddick will require another first of Shelton as he has lost all five previous meetings with Zverev, but with the confidence gained from this run and the backing of a partisan crowd, there is a chance to make history.

"I'm going to need you guys on Sunday to bring the energy," Shelton added.

"I'm going to leave it all on the court and I hope you guys come and back me. Let's do this for the USA."

News.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
News.content:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Two beams of light illuminated the Manhattan sky for a Tribute in Light on Friday evening, as other landmarks in the state lit up in blue in commemoration.

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they were not required to vote along party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: Children and woman injured on fairground ride
News.content:
Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said.

Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening, which closed early after the incident.

South Yorkshire Police said three people, aged 11, 13 and 21, had been taken to hospital for treatment. The extent of their injuries is not yet clear.

Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground, the force added, with the road since reopening.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service confirmed the two injured children were taken to Sheffield Children's Hospital after it attended the fair at about 18:50 BST.

Two ambulances and three rapid response vehicles were sent to the scene, the service said.

News.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
News.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

News.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
News.content:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

News.title: Families of British victims mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Families of British victims of 9/11 were among those who gathered in London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks in the US.

The event, hosted by UK charity Since 9/11, was held near a memorial sculpture made from steel recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

In a video address played to attendees, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11."

There were 67 British citizens among the 2,977 people murdered on 9/11.

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, with the US ambassador to the UK, have separately attended a special Changing of the Guard ceremony while a number of vigils are taking place in the US.

A memorial has been held at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, with relatives of the victims reading out their names.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, in Virginia, President Donald Trump said the US would "never, ever forget", adding "on days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of".

News.title: Police to crack down on face coverings at protests
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
News.content:
The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

News.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

Dunkley's barrister Balbir Singh told Judge Michael Chambers KC that Lashley's body had never been found, and had decomposed after initially being put in the cellar.

"When he was moving about nine months to a year later, the skeleton was disposed of into the bins," Singh added.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

He was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

News.title: Unearthing the Bayeux tapestry’s 1,000 year journey to the British Museum
News.content:
Crowds queued outside the British Museum this week, some dressed in medieval attire, for a first look at the Bayeux Tapestry, on display in England for the first time since it was made almost 1,000 years ago.

The 70-metre embroidery tells the story of the Norman Conquest of 1066 in astonishing detail. But its own story is almost as remarkable: a revolution it narrowly survived, a dictator who took an interest in it, and a war that nearly saw it disappear again.

So how exactly did this centuries-old artefact end up back on English soil, on loan from France?

The Bayeux Tapestry exhibition at the British Museum is sponsored by WorldQuant, founded by Igor Tulchinsky.

News.title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles after calling US-South Korea-Japan military drills ‘provocative’
News.content:

North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea on Saturday, its neighbours said, a day after the US, South Korea and Japan ended their trilateral military exercise that Pyongyang viewed as a provocation.

The short-range ballistic missile launches, the first in three weeks, came as North Korea continued its weapons displays after rebuffing US president Donald Trump’s decision to scale back a major military drill with South Korea in a goodwill gesture.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles from North Korea’s eastern coastal Wonsan area. It said the missiles flew about 250km each in a direction towards North Korea’s eastern waters.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff added it had boosted its surveillance posture and was closely exchanging information on the launches with the US and Japan.

South Korea’s presidential national security council issued a statement urging North Korea to halt ballistic missile firings in violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

The US Pacific Command said the latest missile launches didn’t pose an immediate threat to American territory or to its allies.

On Friday, the US, South Korea and Japan ended their five-day Freedom Edge exercise as scheduled. The US Pacific Command said the militaries of the three countries “trained side by side across air, sea and cyber domains, sharpening the interoperability that keeps the region secure”. It cited maritime manoeuvres, air refuelling, cyber coordination, and medical drills.

South Korea’s military said earlier that the exercise was defensive in nature and meant to enhance a joint response capability against North Korean nuclear threats.

But hours after the exercise began on Monday, North Korean defence minister Kim Song Gi slammed it as “provocative” and threatened to take “strong and reflective countermeasures from the standpoint of power”.

open image in gallery Supporters of the Korean Peace Solidarity for Sovereignty and Reunification protest against the South Korea, US and Japan trilateral military exercise Freedom Edge in front of the American embassy in Seoul on 7 September 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

On Sunday, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for building a more reliable nuclear deterrent in a ceremony to commission the country’s second naval destroyer.

North Korea says its two destroyers can carry nuclear-capable missiles.

The second destroyer was damaged during a botched launch last year but was relaunched after repairs.

Mr Kim has focused on expanding North Korea’s nuclear arsenal after his high-stakes diplomacy with Mr Trump collapsed in 2019.

Mr Trump last month ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea. He cited what he called a good relationship with Mr Kim, who had called the drill an invasion rehearsal.

But Mr Kim’s sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, rebuffed Mr Trump’s move, saying just shortening the drill would not change its “provocative, aggressive nature”.

The North Korean military later launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea, apparently following through with its previous threat to respond to the US-South Korean drill.

Now, apparently emboldened by his advancing nuclear programme and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts said Kim would likely aim to win greater concessions in potential diplomacy with the US.

Mr Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the US dropped its “hostile policy” against his country and respected what he called North Korea’s status as a nuclear state.

News.title: ‘It’s like failing your driving test every week’: SNL UK stars on returning to one of the most brutal jobs in comedy
News.content:

When Sky announced that it was bringing the legendary US sketch show Saturday Night Live to the UK, the public had questions. Would it be British enough? Edgy enough? Cooler than its American cousin?

The answer was emphatically delivered in week one when the cast performed a Hamnet parody, in which William Shakespeare returned to his family from London on a Lime scooter with a mild ketamine addiction and a “c***y little earring”. It was deeply British, a touch provocative, and extremely funny.

To get the sketch into the show, the cast had to talk to Sky and “have almost like a board meeting in the hallway about getting ‘c***y’ in, and the meaning of that”, says Jack Shep, who played a Brat-ified version of the bard. He had to explain how the word had become positive slang in Gen Z culture. “It was awesome. We were like, ‘It’s different now!’ That was week one, so that tells you everything you need to know.”

open image in gallery Jack Shep as a Brat-ified William Shakespeare in one of the show's first sketches ( Sky UK )

Since then, the sketch show has continued to venture near the knuckle when searching for the nation’s funny bone – from skewering former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor over his Jeffrey Epstein links to the Muppet-esque portrayal of Keir Starmer – and it’s worked. SNL UK received a warm – and relieved – reception from viewers and critics alike after its first run, while its sketches have been watched over 54 million times on YouTube since it premiered in March. National treasures Louis Theroux and Martin Lewis even made cameos as themselves in various skits.

Tonight, the show is back for more, just four months after the first series came to an end. No one is more surprised than its cast of rising stars – many of whom had been warned that attempting to bring the live sketch show to a hard-to-please, ever sceptical Britain would be a disaster. “We have been spoken to by pretty much everyone in the industry who told us why it was gonna be bad,” says Paddy Young, who co-hosts the Weekend Update segment. “A poisoned chalice, that’s what I got told. But it makes me feel very patriotic. How else would this country respond to something that’s high risk like this? Of course, we’re just going to say it’s going to be bad.”

open image in gallery Emma Sidi, Ania Magliano and Paddy Young during the Weekend Update segment ( Sky UK )

“People were like, ‘I think it was… good?’” Shep says of SNL UK’s first show. “It’s like we were waiting to hear a gunshot but we haven’t heard one. It’s been really nice. We obviously had supporters from early on, but I think everyone was very sceptical.”

Sitting across from the cast in a London hotel while they’re in junket mode, it’s clear to see that the doubters never needed to worry. Watching them fire jokes back and forth between one another feels like securing front-row tickets to the Wimbledon of comedy, with their electric rapport leaving me with mild whiplash (or rather, quiplash).

Surely those comedy sceptics must be eating their words? “A lot of them are dead,” Shep jokes, with Young quickly adding: “Yeah. Coincidence?”

Even fellow cast member Emma Sidi wasn’t sure the format would work in the UK until the first show aired. “I couldn’t see the laughter working in the room as well as it does,” she admits. “I think that’s only because we haven’t had a big comedy show with a live studio audience be successful in the UK for such a long time. I had a disconnect of even imagining a room full of British people laughing. In my head, it was either a dated thing or an American thing – but then we were like, it can work.”

open image in gallery Larry Dean as King Charles, George Fouracres as Keir Starmer, Celeste Dring as Angela Rayner, Emma Sidi as Queen Camilla and Jack Shep as a flight attendant in a sketch ( Sky UK )

After 16 weeks off – during which the show’s stars and its extensive team of writers have been performing at the Edinburgh Fringe, cramming in holidays and rearranging tour dates – they’re all ready to return. Although given sketches are pitched on a week-by-week basis for each Saturday’s particular celebrity host, there’s not much they could do to prepare over the summer.

“It’s hard to prep material in advance,” says star Celeste Dring, who spent the time off hiring an accountant and moving flats. “You need to be around everyone and you need some feedback on what’s working, what’s not working.”

Young, who teases that he may or may not be reprising the role of now-prime minister Andy Burnham (although he may have to shave that impressive ’tache), admits that “a smart person” would have brushed up his impressions ahead of series two, but he didn’t. Instead, he’s been recovering after slicing open his finger with a samurai sword – which actually sounds like a great idea for a sketch.

“I’m in physio and I can only do that,” he says, while trying to bend the injured finger. “It builds character. The thing with hands is they’re overrated. Once you lose one, you think, ‘God, I don’t need that for anything. I don’t want to open a bottle of Pepsi…or Coke or Dr Pepper.” Briefly dropping into an eerily accurate impersonation of US president Donald Trump, he adds: “‘We love the lilt!’ I have been practising a few impressions, I guess. That’s Angela Rayner by the way.”

open image in gallery Louis Theroux made a cameo in the final episode of SNL UK's first series ( Sky UK )

Meanwhile, Sidi spent the time off getting to know her baby son, who she welcomed last year with husband and SNL UK writer Al Roberts. “I wasn’t really able to do that during the last series,” she says. “I saw him learn to walk and I was a bit nervous that I’d be busy doing the show while he did that, but he did it in front of me so that’s great.”

The comedy couple will be doing the “crazy juggle” between work and parenting once again when they return to what Sidi describes as “Hogwarts for comedy”, but it does mean that they get to spend some quality time together. “This is a really weird way of dating,” she giggles. “We’re at work together, talking about comedy, without a baby.”

A typical week at SNL UK isn’t for the faint of heart; the cast and writers pitch sketches on a Monday, then plan sets, costumes and scripts all week before performing what can often be a completely different version of the skit on Saturday night. They get the Sunday off before starting all over again with new ideas for another celebrity host on Monday.

The cast are still getting used to watching their jokes, some of which they’ve been developing and working on all week, be savagely cut after Saturday afternoon’s dress rehearsal. “The second a sketch gets cut, you go, ‘I’m devastated.’ But then you go, ‘I know why – it wasn’t good enough’,” Sidi says. “It’s like doing your driving test every week and failing every week and rebooking every week. That’s what it feels like doing SNL. It is really fun, but it is brutal. There’s no two ways about it. But you just need to rebook that driving test – don’t give up. You will learn to drive.”

It’s the same for the show’s Weekend Update segment, where Young and co-anchor Ania Magliano deliver quickfire jokes about the week’s biggest news stories. “When you’re churning out ideas and most of them just by their very nature don’t work, that is such a weird thing,” Young says. “A show might go well on Saturday and then you have one day off and on Monday, you’re back to being crap all over again. It’s really humbling.”

While the likes of Tina Fey, Jamie Dornan, Hannah Waddingham and Ncuti Gatwa were the first celebrity hosts to take a chance on SNL’s British cousin, Jurassic Park star Jeff Goldblum is kicking off series two tonight with CMAT as his musical guest. Despite just how physically and mentally tiring making the show can be, its cast – which recently welcomed comedian and Such Brave Girls star Freddie Meredith into their ranks – can’t wait to return for their sophomore year and the sketch madness that’ll come with it.

For Young, it’s all worth it for the curtain call at the end of each live show, where the celebrity host and full cast take to the stage as the credits start to roll. “When we’re all waiting to go on for the bow and normally we’re all wearing whatever the last costume is, that’s always pretty sweet,” he says. “It’s just surreal to see Louis Theroux standing next to some Beefeaters. You see that and you think, ‘That’s why I got into this game’.”

‘Saturday Night Live UK’ returns tonight at 10pm on Sky One

News.title: I’m 69. Please stop saying that I’m in midlife or middle-aged
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Last week I turned 69. And I don’t think I’m middle-aged.

I understand why people use the term. We are living longer, many of us are healthier for longer, and people in their sixties and seventies often feel very different from previous generations at the same age. But extending midlife further and further doesn’t seem to me to be the answer.

The long-running MIDUS study asked people when they thought midlife ended. The average answer was 59. That feels much closer to my own sense of it.

open image in gallery That time between midlife and old age is full of opportunities – we just don’t know how to correctly engage with it ( Getty Images )

When I turned 60, nothing happened. Nobody treated me differently. I didn’t feel a shift in my body. If anything, I was the healthiest I had ever been. There has been research done in the past that suggests most of us feel younger than our years past 40, so perhaps this isn’t unusual.

But I’m less interested in feeling younger than in simply being 60, or 69, and having that be enough of an answer on its own.

So I was fascinated to read research from Stanford suggesting that ageing may not happen at a slow, steady pace. The researchers found dramatic molecular changes at two particular points in adulthood, around the ages of 44 and 60, involving everything from immune function and cardiovascular health to the way we metabolise carbohydrates and alcohol.

Yet I didn’t recognise myself in the idea of some great physical shift at 60 at all.

And that interested me. Because perhaps part of the problem is that we still don’t have very good ways of talking about this stage of life. We seem to move from midlife to old age without much language for what comes between. And I don’t want to pretend that 60 is really 40, or that 70 is really 50. I’d rather acknowledge that these years are different.

What would it actually mean to name this stage properly?

Perhaps part of the problem is that we still don’t have very good ways of talking about this stage of life

The phase from 60 to 80 feels to me like a distinct period of life. It isn’t simply an extension of midlife, and it isn’t necessarily old age as most people imagine it either. It has its own possibilities, limitations, changes and questions.

My own life since 60 certainly hasn't looked like winding down. I divorced, completed a doctorate, bought four acres of woodland, wrote more books and eventually stepped back from much of the work that had defined me for decades. In many respects my life has expanded. But I am also more aware of my body, of people around me becoming ill or dying, and of the simple mathematical fact that there is more life behind me than ahead. Both things are true.

Work can look different here, not necessarily less of it, but differently motivated. The question shifts from: what am I climbing toward? to: what is actually worth my remaining time? Relationships can become more selective too, while creativity may intensify once there is less need to build a career or prove something to anyone.

None of this requires the dramatic “reinvention” we’re so often told later life should involve. Simply continuing, doing work you value and ageing without a headline-worthy transformation attached, is good enough.

There is loss in these years too, and pretending otherwise is its own erasure. Parents die, friends die, capacities narrow in places even when health holds up in others. A stage of life that can't hold both the loss and the freedom honestly isn't being named. It’s being marketed.

I've been trying to find a name for it. The one I keep coming back to is: olderhood, roughly the years from 60 to 80.

Not because everyone between those ages is the same, or because something magical happens on a particular birthday, but because it gives us a way to acknowledge that this is a life stage of its own.

open image in gallery If the image of being older is being frail – we need to keep proving we are the exception ( Getty )

For me, olderhood is less about a number than a shift in orientation. Your career stops being the organising principle of identity, and something else moves into that space: a clearer sense of who you actually are, alongside an honest reckoning with the fact that time is now finite in a way it wasn’t at 40.

That’s not decline. It’s focus.

This didn’t happen to me because some biological alarm went off at 60. It happened because I stopped organising my life around who I was supposed to become and started paying attention to who I already was.

I notice how rarely that’s the picture we're given of ageing.

Too often, age itself is treated as something to be afraid of, something to be managed out of sight rather than lived through. Look at photographs of older celebrities, women in particular. Nicole Kidman is a good example, styled and retouched in the photos for her recent Vogue shoot until it's genuinely hard to tell how much of what you're seeing is her face and how much is the work done to it. The message underneath is simple: you are allowed to be this age, as long as no one can actually see it.

open image in gallery It’s time we stopped airbrushing women’s real age out of existence and started to celebrate everything that we can do in olderhood ( Venetia Scott/Vogue )

And the flip side is just as damaging.

If the only publicly visible image of being old is frailty, then everyone who is older but not frail has to keep proving they’re the exception.

I’m 70, but I can still do this.

I’m 65, but I can still...

That “but” is doing a lot of work, and it's exhausting, because it means the only way to be seen as vital at this age is to distance yourself from your own age group. And if we keep doing that, younger people only see frailty when they picture old age. They also need to see that being 70 or 75 can mean being active, curious and engaged with life. That is part of what living longer actually looks like.

I’d rather say it plainly. Old and active. Old and curious. Old and, some days, tired.

Olderhood shouldn’t need a disclaimer. It should just be visible, ordinary, and allowed to look like what it actually is.

Dr Denise Taylor is a chartered psychologist and author of ‘ThriveSpan: Walking Gently Into What Matters Now’. She writes about ageing and later life at denisetaylor.co.uk

At least 35 people died after a fast-spreading fire destroyed a passenger ferry in the Philippines, with a survivor describing how panicked crowds trampled him as he attempted to secure a life jacket.

At least 54 people were still unaccounted for following the inferno that swept through the vessel on Wednesday night off southwestern Palawan province. There were 43 survivors. Coastguard images captured the ship's blackened interior, revealing ashes, warped metal, a destroyed car, and suspected human remains.

"The fire quickly spread. That’s when I dropped to the ground and my back was burned," Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva recounted in a video broadcast by News5. He said that he jumped from a window. "I wanted to get a life jacket but failed to get one because people were stepping on me. People were in panic."

Intense heat and heavy smoke severely hindered rescue workers on Thursday, delaying search efforts for any trapped passengers inside the vessel.

By Friday, the death toll reached 35 following the recovery of additional bodies.

The vessel had departed from the capital, Manila, and was roughly 7.4km off Turda village, near its destination of Coron in Palawan province, when the blaze was reported. The cause of the outbreak remains unknown.

“It’s painful to think that your child was asking for help while she was burning alive," Lira Daco said as she waited at a rescue centre in Turda for word about her missing 20-year-old daughter Cyriel.

"I don’t know how we can find out which one is my child," she added regarding the remains found inside the ship. "It’s ok if she just drowned and we can recover her body and give her a proper burial. But now we can’t recognize or hug her."

Philippine coast guard personnel stand next to body bags of victims of the ferry fire in Coron, Palawan province, on 12 September 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Ship records indicated that 134 people were aboard—117 passengers and 17 crew—on the 53m vessel, which had a total carrying capacity of 306 passengers and 27 crew.

Two individuals listed on the manifest later informed authorities that they had failed to board, the coastguard reported.

Among those saved were two Chilean tourists, confirmed Rachel Conserman, a staff member at vessel owner Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc.

Both are currently receiving hospital treatment in Coron for their injuries.

Coron is a popular tourist destination, renowned for its clear blue waters, dramatic limestone cliffs and rock formations.

Ferries serve as a widespread means of transport across the Philippine archipelago. Maritime accidents are not uncommon due to severe storms, poorly maintained craft, overcrowding and weak enforcement of safety regulations, particularly in remote island provinces.

The region previously suffered the history's worst peacetime sea disaster in 1987, when the ferry Dona Paz collided with an oil tanker in the central Philippines, claiming over 4,300 lives.
