Top left caretakers in charge for those games, Leicester lost both and were relegated by two points. With decisive action then, much of this story might have been different.

In March, Jon Rudkin was made ‘chief football officer’ – a bigger job and better title even though Leicester were en route to a second straight relegation

Hamza Choudhury’s move to Sheffield United in January 2025 was a classic example of Rudkin's dithering

UNFORCED ERRORS

Leicester’s Premier League title winners are immortal in the eyes of fans – so why are the majority not involved today?

In an interview with Daily Mail Sport in March 2026, Marc Albrighton revealed: ‘We all say that if we could have a job at any of our former clubs, we’d choose Leicester.

‘I would have thought there must be some way we could pass on our experience and try to get that culture back. There has never been any contact with me from the club regarding this.’

Skipper Wes Morgan left to join Nottingham Forest as a scout and now works as an agent. Hugely popular former boss Nigel Pearson could offer valuable advice at a time like this. It is baffling that Leicester would not make these moves.

The 5000-1 fixture on May 30, which marked 10 years since the title win, should have been a key priority for months in advance. Perhaps it was, but if so, that was not how all of those involved saw it, with some not informed of plans until mid-April.

Even against the backdrop of relegation to League One, this should still have been a cause for celebration. Instead, it is understood that some of the key figures left the event feeling dissatisfied.

These are one-off mistakes but there are many others that were repeated again and again. Players’ contracts were allowed to run into the final year far too often. Managers were left scratching their heads when the role did not develop as had been advertised to them. Some senior staff have even wondered privately whether Top always knew their roles at the club.

Baffling decisions are being made to this day, like offering three, four and even five-year contracts to new players – a rarity across the EFL and certainly in League One. Will they ever learn?

Leicester’s Premier League title winners are immortal in the eyes of fans – so why are the majority not involved today?

WHAT NEXT?

Seagrave might have been kryptonite for the first team but it has helped the academy thrive. Jeremy Monga joined Manchester City this summer after breaking into the Leicester side aged 15, while Louis Page is wanted by Manchester United.

Academy products Bade Aluko, Will Alves and Sammy Braybrooke have all played along with Page this season, while Ben Nelson would have been central had he not sustained a serious knee injury.

It was alarming to hear Martin call out these youngsters after the Oxford debacle as it is crucial their confidence is not destroyed. They are vital to the club’s future, both on and off the pitch.

Since the 2018-19 accounting period, Leicester’s cumulative losses are about £323m. The income in League One is dwarfed by what the Premier League and even the Championship generate, and Seagrave is hugely expensive to run.

Leicester need to get back up to the second tier this term and to stay above water in the years to come, they will have to keep selling. They need Aluko, Alves, Braybrooke, Page and others to develop rapidly. Academy players have accounted for 43 per cent of all playing time this term, and 11 graduates have made first-team squads.

Academy products such as Sammy Braybrooke (left) and Jayden Joseph have played a part this season

Martin tries to galvanise his players but his possession-heavy style is already turning off many fans

Leicester are trying to restart. Fourteen players have arrived since the end of last season; 34 have left, and there has been a significant reduction in the wage bill.

Supporters do not want to hear that this team needs time, but it probably does – although Martin's possession-heavy style is already turning off many fans.

Is Top truly serious about selling the club, though? Or is it like the elderly relative who has little desire to move home but puts their property on the market to appease worried family members? We will soon see, but decisive action is needed. Supporters deserve it.

Sadly, we have been saying these things for far too long. It gives no pleasure to write it, but things may become worse before they improve. League Two does not bear thinking about.

Sports.title: 'Scoring in a derby, on my debut, was a tremendous source of joy': The incredible tale of MIKHEIL KAVELASHVILI, Man City star turned disputed president of Georgia - as he reveals why City fans will stay with him 'for the rest of my life'
Sports.content:
‘What a story! Mikheil Kavelashvili, on his debut, in a Manchester derby! It’s a long name to splash across a Manchester City shirt but it will be splashed across a few headlines if City go on from this.’ Martin Tyler, Sky Sports commentary, April 6, 1996

Our conversation was a little unexpected. If you know much about the guy with the long name, you will probably understand why.

It was a fortnight ago that Daily Mail Sport took a punt, which meant sending an email to a generic media address in the Georgian parliament. The gist: would Mikheil Kavelashvili fancy a chat?

Again, if you know, you know. If you don’t, then this one is rather interesting – Kavelashvili played 28 games for Manchester City in an earlier time in his life and for the past 21 months has operated in a different line of work. He is the disputed president of Georgia. Reaching him would likely be a non-starter.

But 18 hours later, a reply came back from the people who handle his affairs and they wanted to know our area of interest, so I explained: Maine Road, April 1996, Manchester City 2 Manchester United 3.

It was Kavelashvili’s debut and after Eric Cantona tucked away a penalty for 1-0, City’s new striker stepped on to a Niall Quinn knock-down and poked past Peter Schmeichel to level. City lost the game, before long they had lost their place in the Premier League, too, and Kavelashvili’s headlines didn’t materialise. Soon enough, he was on loan to Grasshoppers in Switzerland.

Mikheil Kavelashvili, the disputed president of Georgia, during his swearing-in ceremony in 2024

And Kavelashvili back in his footballing days when he had a spell with a struggling Manchester City in the late 1990s

A few more messages came and went on this theme and curiosity from the other end shaped into an indirect ‘yes’ – the president wouldn’t take a phone call but might answer our questions in writing.

After a week of silence, they arrived on Wednesday morning. On Sunday, United and City will contest the 199th Manchester derby at Old Trafford.

Somewhere in Georgia, a 55-year-old who played in the 135th will be aware of how that all goes. Today, he is depicted as an anti-West hardliner of the right and his election to the presidency in 2024 has been rejected by political opposition and the European Parliament.

It’s a serious debate in the real world. But it turns out he still follows the goings-on in his other life. And, surprisingly, he was open to discussing the way it was, meaning he still believes City deserved a draw three decades ago.

He still reckons he could have done more to save City from relegation. And he can also see a comparison between one of his many City managers, Frank Clark, and Margaret Thatcher.

Football. You never quite know where it’s going to lead.

The Manchester City of 1996 was somewhat different to the one of 2026. Kavelashvili arrived into the chaotic landscape of Alan Ball’s squad in the March, following a prolonged campaign of recommendations from the better-known Georgian at Maine Road, the great Georgi Kinkladze.

Aged 24, Kavelashvili signed for £1.4million from the Russian champions Spartak Vladikavkaz.

Kavelashvili celebrates his goal at Maine Road which briefly levelled the Manchester derby in April 1996

‘I remember him as a warm, nice fella,’ Quinn (right) says. ‘We called him Kav. There was a lot going on at the club, things were tense, but he was one of those forwards who worked hard'

‘My move to Manchester City was preceded by a match I played in Wales as part of the Georgian national team, which we won, and by winning the Russian championship, where I also became the team’s top scorer,’ Kavelashvili tells me.

‘Of course, Gio’s recommendation also played a very significant role. Before signing the contract, the club’s president, Francis Lee, told me that the idea behind my move was to build, in the future, a team around Giorgi Kinkladze that would play more creative football. This was a very interesting project for me.

‘In addition to all of this, I was deeply impressed by the fans’ attitude. I saw in them that special passion and emotion which, in my view, are eternal and unaffected by the passing of generations.

‘Gio had told me a great deal about all of this before, but what I witnessed with my own eyes exceeded all my expectations. I would like to thank the fans and the club itself for the emotions they gave me. I am certain (they) will stay with me for the rest of my life.’

All of that being said, City were in dire trouble. When Kavelashvili signed, they were three points above the relegation zone and their striker, the cult hero Uwe Rosler, had engaged in open rebellion against Ball. For the Manchester derby, the German was abruptly dropped and the new guy was thrown in for his debut alongside Quinn.

‘I remember him as a warm, nice fella,’ Quinn tells me this week. ‘We called him Kav. There was a lot going on at the club, things were tense, but he came in and was one of those forwards who worked hard.

‘He wouldn’t wait with hands on hips – he’d do his own running and he had his moment against United.’

Alan Ball's Manchester City was a very different animal to today's club

Kavelashvili was given his chance after Ball fell out with City's German striker Uwe Rosler (pictured)

How much did that goal change the path of Kavelashvili’s life? Given the profile of the Premier League and a Manchester derby, was it in some way tied to a political party utilising him years later as a recognisable face? It’s impossible to know and interesting to ponder.

Naturally, Kavelashvili remembers the game against United, who were a nose ahead of Newcastle United at the top of the table, with Sir Alex Ferguson three weeks shy of baiting Kevin Keegan into his ‘I will love it…’ speech.

‘In a match like this, the positions occupied by the teams in the league table are virtually irrelevant,’ Kavelashvili says. ‘The fans create an atmosphere that makes it feel as though you are playing in a tournament final. An unforgettable experience.

‘Manchester United at the time were one of the best teams in Europe. Nevertheless, we genuinely believed that we could do it.’

Martin Tyler’s commentary suggested Kavelashvili’s goal for 1-1 would make the headlines, but City were only level for one minute before Andy Cole got United’s second. Kavelashvili had another excellent chance, but Schmeichel blocked the drive with his face, and the Georgian was then substituted for Rosler.

The latter’s subsequent equaliser became iconic for the manner in which he celebrated – he ran towards Ball and wagged his finger.

Rosler, who had only learned he was on the bench when he saw Kavelashvili’s shirt hanging in the dressing room, then opened the chasm further when he told Match of the Day that there was a ‘massive problem’ with the manager. By then, Ryan Giggs had scored the winner and City were in the bottom three.

‘In my view, we should at least not have lost the match, as it was an evenly contested game overall and we had several opportunities to score, including a chance for me,’ Kavelashvili says. ‘We made several costly mistakes and were punished. Given the way the match unfolded, I believe a draw would have been a fairer result.

‘As for my goal, scoring in a derby of this magnitude, especially in my debut match, was, of course, a tremendous source of joy. Unfortunately, however, the result of the match somewhat overshadowed that joy.’

Kavelashvili takes on Steve Bruce in the Manchester Derby in 1996

Kavelashvili arrived at City following a prolonged campaign of recommendations from the better-known Georgian at Maine Road, the great Georgi Kinkladze (pictured)

The farce of City’s season was encapsulated by the final day, when they faced Liverpool. In the dying seconds, at 2-2, Ball mistakenly believed a draw would keep his side safe due to scores elsewhere, so there was a directive to get the ball to the corner.

It was only when the injured Quinn came sprinting out of the physio room and waving his arms for the team to attack that anyone realised they were dawdling towards their own demise.

His team-mate Keith Curle had another observation. ‘Kav missed a sitter in that game!’ he tells me.

Kavelashvili would go on to play 24 games for City in the second tier the next season, scoring two more goals, before being loaned out to Switzerland in 1997 and sold in 1999. He appears to hold some regrets.

‘As my contract was signed towards the end of the season, I joined the team only four or five matches before the end of the championship,’ he says. ‘By that point, the team’s main objective was already to avoid relegation.

‘This may also have influenced the coach to place greater trust in players he knew well and with whom he had previous experience of working. This is entirely understandable. However, I believe that, had I been given a little more confidence, I could have contributed more to the team. Incidentally, Gary Lineker expressed a similar view at the time.’

Quinn is succinct in describing his reaction to the events of December 2024, when he heard a former team-mate had become the head of state in Georgia after spending eight years as a member of the county’s parliament.

Having left England in 1999 and retired in 2006, Kavelashvili’s name had barely been uttered in our native footballing circles.

‘Jeez, that was a surprise!’ says Quinn. ‘Didn’t see that coming, if I’m honest.’ He likely spoke for the rest of the City dressing room.

Around the time of that 2024 election, Clark, who managed Kavelashvili during the 1996-97 season, told The Athletic: ‘Good luck to him, if he is going to be dealing with Putin, although he might find Putin is easier to deal with than I was. I am joking of course… I hope I am a nicer person than Putin.’

The former City player Keith Curle remembers 'Kav' well and particularly the final game of the season which saw City relegated. ‘Kav missed a sitter in that game!’ he says

I redirect that thought to Kavelashvili, who says: ‘As I understood it, Frank Clark’s joke was a reference to his own steadfastness and adherence to principle. However, in politics, the ability to find compromises is no less important.

‘If he wanted to compare himself specifically to a politician, I would have found it more natural for him to draw a comparison with a British politician, such as Winston Churchill or Margaret Thatcher.

'They had very clear principles, but they also had to make difficult decisions in the complex world of politics and, when necessary, find compromises.’

For those who follow Georgian politics, Clark’s comment about Putin might chime in ways the former manager did not intend. Kavelashvili’s stance on neighbouring Russia has been accused by critics of being sympathetic – a point he has previously denied – and that sits alongside furious, ongoing opposition to his ascension to power with the Georgian Dream party.

The European Parliament said in 2025 that it ‘refuses to recognise the self-proclaimed authorities of the ruling Georgian Dream party following the rigged parliamentary elections’.

As headlines they are heaven and earth removed from what Tyler had in mind when he reported on a football match. That fixture may or may not have been a sliding-door moment for Kavelashvili. And for Georgia, as a whole.

As for Kavelashvili, he traces his involvement in politics to an ‘injustice’ more than a decade ago, when he felt football in his country was being hijacked for ‘political objectives’. After speaking out, he says he found himself in the political arena.

That journey has followed a surreal and contentious direction. So have Manchester City, in their way.

‘As someone who once had a connection with the club, [City's recent success] makes me very happy,’ Kavelashvili says

For his part, Kavelashvili has kept an eye on a club whose subsequent success bears no resemblance to the one he represented. ‘As someone who once had a connection with the club, this makes me very happy,’ he says.

Returning to the theme of Ball and Francis Lee, he adds: ‘Their vision was based on developing a more creative style. It is worth noting that, at the time, relatively few teams had such a vision. It was during those years that Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool were beginning to develop a similar approach.

‘Unfortunately, at that point, Manchester City found itself in a situation that made it very difficult to fully implement these ideas. However, today, when I look at what City has become, I can see that Alan Ball and Francis Lee were the first to attempt to introduce this football philosophy at the club.’

It’s an interesting theory. Along with a few other things, it might also be vulnerable to dispute.

Sports.title: 'They spent £50m on Andrey Santos who didn't kick a ball at Chelsea. It's madness': PAUL INCE on United's midfield revamp, Michael Carrick's future, fighting Sir Alex Ferguson and his chastening derby day 'wake-up call'
Sports.content:
'They spent £50m on Andrey Santos who didn't kick a ball at Chelsea. It's madness': PAUL INCE on United's midfield revamp, Michael Carrick's future, fighting Sir Alex Ferguson and his chastening derby day 'wake-up call'

When Manchester United were embarrassed 5-1 in the Maine Road derby 37 years ago this month, Sir Alex Ferguson retreated to his home in Cheshire, went straight to bed and hid under a pillow.

‘We chose the worst possible day to reach rock bottom,’ Ferguson wrote later. ‘A sense of guilt had engulfed me.’

The new signings he brought to Old Trafford in the summer of 1989 who were staying at the Ramada Hotel in the city centre had no choice but to seek refuge in their rooms that night. Paul Ince, Neil Webb, Gary Pallister and Danny Wallace had planned to go out for dinner with their partners until security suggested it might be wiser to order room service instead.

‘There were fans outside the hotel shouting abuse, saying we were c**p and all this stuff,’ recalls Ince. ‘We never went out that night. We stayed in our rooms and didn’t move.

‘My debut was at home to Millwall a week earlier and we won 5-1. I said to my wife, “Claire, I like it here. This is easy”. But that was a wake-up call for us: what it meant for United fans and the people of Manchester.

‘That’s the rivalry they have. They expected us to beat Manchester City. I don't think we lost one after that, and I scored a couple of goals, so I’m quite pleased about that.’

Paul Ince lost his first derby as a Manchester United player 5-1, back in 1989. It was another 13 years before Manchester City would win another one

Ince (pictured dribbling past Peter Reid and Colin Hendry in 1990) has largely happy memories of the fixture

In fact, it was another 13 years and 17 games before Ferguson’s side lost to City as the gap between the two clubs widened in the 90s – including a 5-0 win at Old Trafford in Ince’s final season at the club that gave United fans a belated sense of revenge.

When they meet there again in the 199th derby on Sunday, the dramatic reversal of fortunes can perhaps be best demonstrated by the money spent on midfield reinforcements this summer.

The £326.6million City have paid for Enzo Fernandez, Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi is more than double United’s £155m outlay on Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Nearly half a billion pounds' worth of midfielders coming to Manchester.

There were fans outside the hotel shouting abuse, saying we were c**p and all this stuff. We never went out that night

Ince, part of a formidable unit alongside Bryan Robson and Roy Keane, shakes his head. ‘I remember when I joined United, Sir Alex said to me: “I watched you for two years before I decided to buy you.” Two years! These players are one-season wonders and go for £100m.

‘No disrespect to Elliot Anderson but he was in a team at Nottingham Forest that nearly went down. Enzo Fernandez cost £125m. What? I don't get it, I really don't. The money’s going really crazy.

‘United have spent £50m on Santos, who didn’t kick a ball at Chelsea more or less, and £70m on Baleba who was out for most of last season and can’t play until October. Tielemans was £35m.

‘When you think about Roy Keane, Stevie Gerrard and Frank Lampard compared to what these players actually do, it’s madness the amount of money they're paying. Keane and Gerrard would cost £200m these days.

‘The United midfield in our time was probably one of the best in Europe. Bryan Robson was my idol and Keane was a phenomenal player. You don't get those types now. If we sit down here in 30 years’ time and you ask me who were the greatest midfield players at United, we’ll still be saying Keane, Robson and Paul Scholes.’

'When I joined United, Sir Alex Ferguson said to me: “I watched you for two years before I decided to buy you.” Two years! These players are one-season wonders and go for £100m'

'United have spent £50m on Andrey Santos (right), who didn’t kick a ball at Chelsea more or less,' says Ince

It’s not the only unfavourable comparison Ince draws with the present after seeing the empire Ferguson built crumble over the last 13 years.

‘Since Fergie left in 2013, we've gone through about seven or eight managers. The recruitment has been poor. The people upstairs have been poor. The way they’ve run the club has been poor, so what do you expect?

INCE'S DEFIB MESSAGE AFTER HODDLE SCARE Glenn Hoddle’s collapse in the BT Sport studios eight years ago gave Paul Ince harrowing proof of the importance of defibrillators. Ince witnessed Hoddle, his former England and Wolves boss, suffer a heart attack after going off air on his 61st birthday in 2018, and the efforts of sound engineer Simon Daniels to save him. Now he has joined Neil Ruddock, Julian Dicks, Iain Dowie and Roy Keane to support Sky Bet and the British Heart Foundation’s mission to ease people’s fears over using a defibrillator. It marks the start of the third year of the Sky Bet Every Minute Matters campaign, which has inspired 500,000 fans to learn life-saving CPR. ‘It brought me back to when Glenn had his cardiac arrest. It was the worst experience of my life,’ says Ince. ‘Trying to keep him awake, talking about England and Wolves. Now when I see him on the golf course, I think, “He couldn't have been here”. ‘Sixty nine per cent of football fans are scared of using a defib. It's simple. You don't have to be a doctor. It's just a machine that tells you what to do and you press the buttons. There’s nothing to be scared of. Just take 15 minutes, go on the BHF website. It shows you how to do a CPR and use a defib machine. You can be the one saving someone’s life.’ Fans can learn lifesaving CPR and defibrillation skills in just 15 minutes: Search BHF RevivR and/or visit https://revivr.bhf.org.uk/ To check whether you are eligible for a free defibrillator go to bhf.org.uk/defibfunding

‘United have brought in different types of managers, and it just hasn’t worked. They gave Ole Gunnar Solskjaer a two-year contract and we saw what happened after that. I just hope it's not the same situation with Michael Carrick. Is he ready for that yet? I don't know.

‘It's funny how you can lose your job at Middlesbrough and get the biggest job in the world. It’s mad how football works, but we can’t keep changing managers. We've got to stick with one, and I think Carrick deserves that chance.’

A month short of his 59th birthday, Ince doesn’t shirk a challenge any more than he did after arriving at Old Trafford from West Ham as a brash 21-year-old in 1989.

He has turned up at a studio on the outskirts of Manchester with some other big characters from the dawn of the Premier League – Neil Ruddock, Iain Dowie and Julian Dicks – as part of a campaign by the British Heart Foundation and Sky Bet to change misconceptions among football fans who are afraid of using a defibrillator.

‘The characters are going out of the game,’ says Ince, who went on to play for Inter Milan and Liverpool and finish his career with 53 England caps. ‘Players are more concerned about themselves and what people think. Everyone feels so precious about what they've got to do and what they can't do.

‘If I were a player today, I’d never be on social media if I couldn’t take what people say about me. If you don’t like it, get off it.

‘We always had an opinion. If Fergie said something to me and I disagreed with it, I’d tell him. Same with Roy Keane. We disagreed with each other but let's just get on with it. We're good mates, go and play for each other. All that kind of stuff's gone now.’

Ince remembers having to be 'separated' from Ferguson after a 3-1 win over Norwich at Carrow Road in 1993 on the way to United ending their long wait for the title.

He won the Premier League twice at Old Trafford as well as the FA Cup, League Cup, European Cup Winners’ Cup and UEFA Super Cup.

Ferguson’s concerns over the player’s self-styled ‘Guvnor’ image, and desire to clear a pathway for a young Nicky Butt, led to him sanctioning Ince’s £7.5m move to Inter Milan against the wishes of the board in the summer of 1995 after United’s Double winners lost the title to Blackburn and FA Cup to Everton.

The manager drove the short distance to Mottram Hall, where Ince was on the golf course with Ryan Giggs, to tell him face to face.

‘I was one up on the 17th so I was devastated,’ smiles Ince, who still plays with Giggs on the Icons Series.

'We can’t keep changing managers,' Ince says of United. 'We've got to stick with one, and I think Carrick deserves that chance’

Ince won the Premier League, FA Cup and League Cup at United but Ferguson’s concerns over his self-styled ‘Guvnor’ image partly led to him sanctioning his 1995 move to Inter Milan

Ince was at home in Bramhall with his agent and a delegation from Inter led by chairman Massimo Moratti putting the final touches to the deal when Ferguson phoned from a summer holiday in Colorado asking him to call the move off.

‘The horse had bolted, to be fair,’ says Ince. ‘We were sat down in the kitchen. Moratti was there with his vice-president and a couple of henchmen, as they do.

‘Sir Alex said: “Listen, Paul, I want you to stay. You know, Nicky Butt's coming through so you might have to fight for your place."

‘No disrespect, Nicky Butt is a very good player and good friend of mine, but he wasn't a better player than me at that time. When he said that, I thought “no thanks” and off I went.’

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: I've drilled into the facts and figures and here's why Pochettino is right to say those Chelsea titles stink and Spurs should be handed a Premier League trophy. It's just a shame the powers-that-be aren't that brave
Sports.content:
RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: I've drilled into the facts and figures and here's why Pochettino is right to say those Chelsea titles stink and Spurs should be handed a Premier League trophy. It's just a shame the powers-that-be aren't that brave

Mauricio Pochettino was right about Chelsea with his little rant this week. Of course he was. When they won the Premier League ahead of his Tottenham side in 2017, it was a success built on cheating. Chelsea confessed.

By Pochettino’s logic, they should have been stripped of that title. But we know that didn’t happen – when Chelsea self-reported secret payments exceeding £47million to unregistered agents and third parties, they received the equivalent of a slapped wrist. A tickle, actually.

The Premier League and the FA settled on fines totalling around £20m earlier this year. That’s a fraction more than the club pocketed in compensation from Manchester City for a manager they had already sacked; as a penalty, it was softer and more misplaced than a bad Panenka.

We know why that was – the authorities saluted Chelsea’s co-operation after they came forward with some troubling discoveries in old accounts. The FA commission gushed about their honesty in the 63 pages of their written explanation, which I’ve read.

But there was no sporting sanction handed to the current regime for the sins of the father. By their reckoning, there was only so far they could go in penalising BlueCo for offences under Roman Abramovich, with the masses of rule breaches occurring between 2009 and 2022.

So not a single point was docked, much less the three Premier League titles won in that period. Pochettino finds that strange because it is. And strange can be upgraded to outrageous when we revisit the signings made outside the rules – Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.

Chelsea won the Premier League in 2017, a success built on cheating to which they subsequently confessed

The club made signings beyond the rules including that of the Belgian midfielder Eden Hazard

I wrote about this issue at length three years ago when Chelsea first came forward. The focus then, and in the past few days since Pochettino opened his spleen, has largely been on Hazard.

In the context of that title-winning season, 2016-17, he scored 16 league goals and those played a decisive role in the seven-point gap to Spurs come May.

In that campaign and so many others, the chicanery involved in swinging Hazard away from Manchester United in 2012 paid for itself many times over.

A report in The Times last year specifically alleged the move to Old Trafford from Lille broke down because United wouldn’t pay a backhander to an agent, thus bypassing the books and the rules; Hazard instead went to Stamford Bridge for £32m and history tells us a £20m fine isn’t remotely equal to what he brought.

But that’s Hazard. What about Willian? Just Willian.

Why? Well, that breach of the regulations was more relevant to Tottenham – they tried to sign him in August 2013 and got awfully close.

He was at their training ground for eight hours and even completed his medical. Then something happened – he got in a van and headed for Chelsea. Abramovich had got on the phone to the Anzhi Makhachkala owner, another oligarch named Suleyman Kerimov, and Willian was rerouted.

That deal was one of the dodgy ones. And it was mentioned in the FA’s documentation earlier this summer, citing a figure at Chelsea whose name was redacted. This individual felt that losing Willian was ‘not good’ and that the player going to Tottenham would add ‘insult to injury’.

Pochettino wasn’t at Spurs when that hijacking occurred but he was there in the 2016-17 season. And Willian, like Hazard, was exceptional for Antonio Conte that year. I’ve gone over a few of his notable contributions, meaning the sort that turned losses to draws or draws to wins – the kind you can measure.

Willian, who was signed by Chelsea from under the noses of Tottenham, was superb in the 2016-17 season as the Blues won the title

Antonio Conte celebrates winning the title as manager of Chelsea in May 2017

We can start with Hull in the October of 2016. Willian scored the first in a 2-0 win, a screamer from the edge of the area, and two months later he was set loose in a sprint against Nicolas Otamendi at 1-1 with Manchester City. Willian, as usual, got there first. The finish was handy too. Chelsea won.

At Sunderland, he turned a draw into a win with an assist, in the 4-2 victory against Stoke he got the goals for 2-1 and 3-2, and then he scored the first in the return fixture against Sunderland.

The latter was a rout and none of this is an exact science. Maybe a replacement would have done the same.

But those are the kind of equivocations that snare lawyers and commissions. The rest of us? We all saw Willian at his best – he turned games. It would have to be a damned good replacement.

And by our calculations, that replacement would need to be worth 13 points. Again, the margin to Tottenham was seven. Again, no sporting sanction was found to be suitable.

If Pochettino is furious, he has every right to be. Had he mentioned the FA Cup semi-final of that season, he would have even more fuel to rage on – Willian scored the first two in a 4-2 win and was named man of the match in Daily Mail Sport's player ratings. The other two goals? Matic and Hazard, both on the list of iffy signings. A clean sweep and a dirty win.

When Pochettino spoke this week, the following line was less dramatic than some: ‘Maybe with the same rules we could've signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals. It's not me complaining, it's the truth.’

That makes you think of Willian. And Willian makes you think of other seasons, like 2015-16, when he scored an equaliser in the 86th minute against Newcastle in the September. In May they were relegated by two points.

Pochettino was right to say it stinks. His error was to think that common sense might apply

Chelsea players Pedro, David Luiz, Willian, Nathan Ake and Cezar Azpilicueta celebrate going 1-0 up against Tottenham in the FA Cup semi-final in 2017

Correcting all of those little and large contributions after the fact would be perilously hard. But to rule that sporting sanctions are unnecessary? That seems like an affront to logic.

Maybe the authorities just didn’t want to pull any threads out of the jumper. Maybe they just don’t like an asterisk on old tables. And maybe there is nothing to be gleaned from all of the above while we wait to see how the Premier League untangle the vastly larger case against Manchester City.

But Pochettino was right to say it stinks. His error was to think that common sense might apply in his line of work.

Sports.title: US Open tickets plummet ahead of men's semi-final... to the price of LESS than a Honey Deuce cocktail!
Sports.content:
Tickets for the highly coveted men's semi-final afternoon session at this year's US Open plummeted on resale sites to as low as $19 ahead of the tournament's number one seed Alexander Zverev's meeting with Karen Khachanov.

In the build-up to the final Grand Slam of the year, most of the headlines surrounding tickets to the event centred on their sky-high resale prices, with grounds passes for the first week of the US Open - with a face value of $65 - being sold on the secondary market for upwards of $300.

While the USTA is powerless to stop tickets being sold for miles more than their initial value, the tournament's organisers do receive a 'legal share revenue' from seats sold on Ticketmaster, their official partner.

Weeks later however, the focus is on dropping prices, with the cost of a seat inside the Arthur Ashe nosediving on the eve of the first men's semi-final.

While many fans have eagerly taken advantage of the deals for a seat in the upper levels of the 23,000-plus stadium, the pricier lower bowl of the US Open's show court was visibly more sparse than organisers may have hoped for.

As per ticket resale site StubHub, via journalist Ben Rothenberg, the lowest prices for tickets for Friday afternoon were $19 and $21, with up to five sets of Grand Slam tennis available for the price of less than one of the US Open's trademark Honey Deuce cocktails ($23).

Tickets to the men's semi-final between Alexander Zverev and world No50 Karen Khachanov on the afternoon of Day 13 at the US Open dropped sharply

Tennis tournaments must contend with the absence in the latter stages of stars like last year's winner Carlos Alcaraz

Tickets costing less than one of the tournament's famous Honey Deuce cocktails were available hours before the first serve in the semi-final

Ticket prices on the secondary markets have dropped since last year across the board, with TicketData reporting that the average price of the cheapest ticket across both day and night sessions on Day 13 of the tournament has shifted from $319 in 2025, to $244 today.

Demand remains much higher for Day 13's night session this year, which will feature two Americans vying to become the first home favourite to win a Grand Slam in 23 years - Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe.

Shelton and Tiafoe have been scheduled second on men's semi-finals day despite Zverev having played his quarter-final on Wednesday rather than Tuesday with one eye on the demands of broadcasters' primetime slot

But the dip in prices throws into relief how important the game's biggest men's stars, Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, have become to contemporary tennis.

While last season featured the young rivalry played out over three of the four Grand Slam finals, this year form and fitness has kept Alcaraz and Sinner from meeting in the biggest matches on tour.

Last year, both Alcaraz and Sinner played on Day 13, with the Spaniard beating the world No1 in their eventual final on Sunday. On host broadcaster ABC, their clash averaged 3million viewers, 82 per cent up on 2024.

This year, viewing figures have been more modest. The French Open, contested by Zverev and Flavio Cobolli, saw a 20-year viewing low, with just 1.3m viewers tuning in on broadcasters TNT and truTV.

Wimbledon viewers were also less tempted than 2025's Alcaraz-Sinner meeting one year on, with BBC registering a peak at 5.95million for the Italian's defeat of Zverev in four sets.

This was down on the previous year's 8.3million and the 7.5million who watched Alcaraz's second Wimbledon final against Novak Djokovic in 2024.

This US Open saw Sinner withdraw on the eve of the tournament as he continued to suffer from inflammation in his knee.

Alcaraz returned to competitive action in New York after four months nursing a wrist injury, but was knocked out in a five-set classic by Shelton - a quarter-final clash that would have sent viewership soaring through the roof, but for its early-hours finish at 3.34am on Wednesday morning.

Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Debutant Razaullah hits sensational knock as Pakistan FINALLY show guts and heart to make England pay for their lack of variety for the first time in the series, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
Debutant Razaullah hits sensational knock as Pakistan FINALLY show guts and heart to make England pay for their lack of variety for the first time in the series, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

After a few weeks in which Pakistan's batsmen have headed lemming-like to their doom, they finally made England's bowlers look mortal, unexpectedly dragging this third and final Test into a fourth morning thanks to a raucous stand of 121 between tailenders Razaullah and Mohammad Abbas.

Barring more madness on Saturday, it will still not be enough to avoid the 3-0 whitewash that has looked almost inevitable from the opening day of the series. Pakistan's lead is just 130, and this pitch remains the best batting strip of the summer, though that isn't saying much.

But a total of 449 after five successive surrenders below 200 made a welcome change for their supporters and provided England's bowlers with a useful reality check ahead of stiffer challenges in South Africa this winter. Ollie Robinson's bowling average for the series even nudged above eight, for goodness sake.

When the dismissal of Razaullah for 81 off 63 balls, stumped as he tried to swing Dan Lawrence for what would have been a tenth six, triggered the close at 7pm, he walked off to a standing ovation from fans of both sides – relieved, regardless of affiliation, to have finally seen some kind of contest. The applause felt like the highlight of the series.

At none for two after two balls of their second innings on Thursday afternoon, no one could rule out another two-day finish in this era of fast-forward Tests. Instead, Pakistan found previously hidden reserves of guts and heart on an Edgbaston surface that was badly betrayed by their first-innings collapse of 133.

And the manner in which Razaullah counter-attacked, while Abbas carefully compiled a career-best 42, was a reminder that for all the excellence of England's seamers, their lack of a frontline spinner is a weakness opponents will seek to exploit.

Debutant Razaullah (left) ensured Pakistan finally showed some fight against England

There are concerns around England's lack of front-line spinner and how they may fare in less helpful conditions

Lawrence had struck earlier in the day with his loopy off-breaks when Azan Awais tickled his second ball down the leg side to end a third-wicket stand of 125 with Shan Masood. But as Razaullah used the pace of the quick bowlers to launch one six after another, it was clear, for the first time in this series, that England were paying for their lack of variety.

At first, it seemed like a bit of fun. He had walked out into a hopeless situation after Gus Atkinson had removed Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran in successive overs to reduce Pakistan to 318 for eight, still one run short of an innings defeat.

But he ensured England would bat again by pulling Josh Tongue for six, then pulled and drove Atkinson for three meaty sixes in four balls. A straight six off Jofra Archer brought up a 43-ball half-century, and another next ball Pakistan's 400.

Razaullah, one of four members of this team drafted in at the last minute following the Pakistan board's chaotic decimation of their touring party, swung Archer for another six, before even Abbas got in on the act, bringing up the 100 lead with a straight six off a startled Atkinson.

Perhaps the pick of Razaullah's strokes was a flat-batted thrash over extra cover off Atkinson, by which point England and Joe Root were looking worryingly devoid of ideas. It almost came as a surprise when Abbas cut Tongue to Atkinson at point to end the most entertaining passage of play of the Test summer.

Razaullah had time for one more blow, heaving Lawrence over midwicket towards the building site, before he was stumped by Jordan Cox, who enjoyed an excellent day with the gloves in the absence of the injured Jamie Smith. He walked off cursing his demise, though there was no need for self-reproach.

With the exception of Robinson, who went at 2.34 an over and will finish the series with a remarkable haul of 21 wickets at 8.76, England's other quicks went the distance. Between them, Archer, Atkinson and Tongue conceded 335 runs at nearly five an over while taking six wickets, and did little to quieten those who have wondered how they might fare in less helpful conditions.

They remain a quartet full of potential, able to pose different threats despite their mutual right-handedness. But the comparisons to England's 2005 Ashes-winning foursome of Steve Harmison, Matthew Hoggard, Andrew Flintoff and Simon Jones look, on this evidence anyway, to be premature.

Ollie Robinson will finish the series with a remarkable haul of 21 wickets at 8.76

Earlier, they had been held up by Masood, who seemed set to become the first centurion on either side in this series, only to be brilliantly caught low in the cordon by Lawrence off Atkinson on 95.

Babar Azam, having played nicely for 76, then got into a flap against the short stuff, eventually gloving an unconvincing pull off Tongue down the leg side off Cox. Archer then bounced out Saud Shakeel, Pakistan's best batsman on this trip, with a brute, and England seemed set for a three-day win when Atkinson had Ghori and Imran caught behind off inside edges.

But the 21-year-old Razaullah, who scored a hundred opening the batting for Peshawar against Islamabad in November, was determined not to go down without a fight.

He had already marked his debut with the wicket of Root in his first over, adding three more to finish with Pakistan's best figures. Now he batted with a freedom that suggested a new star may have emerged from the debris of a troubled tour.

He has already enjoyed a debut to remember. If he can make England fight for their runs, Pakistan may even fly home with a spring in their step.

Sports.title: San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan quietly inks new contract after team's scandalized offseason
Sports.content:
San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan quietly inks new contract after team's scandalized offseason

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Kyle Shanahan didn’t just pick up a win during the San Francisco 49ers’ recent road trip to Melbourne, Australia. The 10th-year head coach also got himself a contract extension at a particularly welcome moment for the team.

According to multiple reports, the 46-year-old son of two-time Super Bowl-winning head coach Mike Shanahan has received a multiyear extension with the Niners. Terms of the deal were not immediately released.

The Daily Mail has sought comment from team officials.

Shanahan has gone 83-67 over his decade by the Bay. Over that time, the 49ers have reached the playoffs six times, including two trips to the Super Bowl, both of which ended in defeat.

The 49ers picked up a surprisingly easy 27-7 Week 1 win over the rival Los Angeles Rams – a team considered by many to be a Super Bowl contender. The victory was a welcome change for a team that has been decimated by injuries, including Shanahan’s own absence from training camp after a serious offseason car crash.

The July 14 incident had been shrouded in mystery after Palo Alto police initially refused to release an accident report or bodycam footage while officers initially blamed the other driver only for Shanahan to ultimately take responsibility.

Kyle Shanahan has reportedly received a new contract extension with the 49ers

Niners fans had reason to celebrate on Thursday night as San Francisco tormented LA

Later it was revealed that Shanahan collided with a car driven by a 21-year-old woman, saying the crash occurred when he reached for his phone.

The incident left Shanahan with a concussion, broken ribs, a broken nose, a broken hand and more than 40 stitches to close a cut over his eye. A few symptoms from the concussion remain.

As he told reporters at training camp, Shanahan was driving at around 20mph with his Tesla in autopilot mode when the crash happened. In autopilot mode, Tesla 'matches the speed of your vehicle to that of the surrounding traffic' and 'assists in steering within a clearly marked lane, and uses traffic-aware cruise control.'

But Shanahan insisted he still should not have taken his eyes off the road when he reached behind his seat for his phone.

'I've had autopilot for nine years, so I'm pretty comfortable with it,' he said. 'Who knows what happened when I turned around, whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off. That's something that I don't know yet.

'But regardless, that is always your fault, whether you're in autopilot or not. You can't take your eyes off the road. It's a partnership driving.

The 49ers' offseason was marred by Jeff York's arrest and guilty plea for disorderly conduct

'You don't just turn it over to a computer. It's a good lesson, no matter how comfortable I am with that, that I believe someday could save my life or someone else's.'

Shanahan was the only person who needed to be hospitalized and police didn't issue him a ticket for the cell phone use.

And of course, the car crash was the least of the 49ers worries after top executive Jed York was arrested after allegedly trying to pay $140 for sex at an Ohio trailer park. The 46-year-old pleaded no contest to charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools. He was sentenced to one day in jail and fined $1,150.

For his part, Shanahan has tried to claim that York's arrest is 'irrelevant' to his players, while linebacker Fred Warner insisted it wasn't a topic of conversation in the locker room.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
