World.title: From roughing it to Arctic luxury: Two sisters and three countries in two weeks
World.content:
There are probably more glamourous ways to begin a luxurious Nordic adventure than boarding a crammed Ryanair flight at London Stansted, but that’s exactly how this adventure started – a once in a lifetime tour for two weeks.

 

My sister Nyeema and I were fairly certain they had squeezed a few more seats onto the aircraft since either of us last flew with them. But there we were, two British sisters embarking on a girls-only holiday that would take us through Greenland, Iceland and Norway – from the decidedly and deliberately non-luxurious to the seriously expensive, with an extraordinary amount packed in between.

Sisters Nadira Tudor and Nyeema Yasin in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

By the end, we decided we could describe each destination in just three words.

For Nyeema, Nuuk was “remote, dystopian and mesmerising”. Mine were “sci-fi, raw and out-of-this-world”.

Reykjavík? She chose “charming, colourful and vibrant”. I went for “fresh-fishy, stunning and commercial”.

And Norway?

“Picturesque, historic and rainy,” according to my sister.

For me: “Luxurious, fairytale and quality.”

Those words turned out to say rather more about our journey than we realised.

Greenland: Raw, beautiful and suddenly everyone is talking about it

After a quick stopover in Copenhagen, we headed for Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, arriving to a spectacular bright daytime sky after midnight and a landscape that immediately felt unlike anywhere else.

There is undoubtedly something almost otherworldly about Greenland.

Famous Gulfoss Waterfall in Blaskogabyggo, Iceland on the Hvita river Euronews Baku Bureau

The scale, silence, water and mountains, punctuated by tiny splashes of colourful buildings, can make you feel as though you have landed on a film set... or the moon.

Filmmakers have already discovered it. Borgen: Power & Glory, starring Sidse Babett Knudsen put Greenland at the heart of a story about resources, Denmark and competing global interests in the Arctic.

Watching the real Greenland, those themes suddenly don’t seem particularly fictional.

Because one man seemed to be everywhere we went.

Donald Trump.

We had travelled to Greenland expecting to talk about landscapes, ice, culture and Arctic tourism. Instead, the US President’s name followed us around Nuuk.

Restaurants. Shops. Museums. Conversations with people we met and everybody seemed to have an opinion.

Some people we spoke to believed Trump’s repeated interest in taking control of Greenland had inadvertently done the country a favour. Whatever they thought of his politics, they liked the attention he had brought – and some thought it could ultimately benefit tourism.

A few were surprisingly relaxed, even telling us they didn’t particularly care if America took over. Most of the people we encountered, however, hated the idea.

What fascinated me was that a US president thousands of kilometres away had somehow become part of the everyday experience or travelling through Greenland.

Nuuk Cathedral or Church of Our Saviour, a wooden Lutheran cathedral in Old Nuuk neighbourhood Euronews Baku Bureau

We met Alice Burton, a former Head of Press Section at the US Embassy in Vienna, in our shared accommodation, who would become our partial travel companion, who had been hearing similar things from the locals.

“Nuuk is the most quiet capital I’ve ever visited,” she told me.

There are for sure few cars, little honking, hardly any sirens and remarkably few people on the streets.

“A world in itself,” Alice reflected.

Tourist Alice Burton eating whale steak in Three Coats restaurant in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

Yet politically, Greenland now feels anything but isolated.

Official tourism research estimated that just over 149,000 international tourists visited Greenland in 2024, with almost two-thirds arriving by cruise ship. Nuuk’s international airport is meanwhile transforming access to the capital.

For a destination with a population of fewer than 60,000 people, those numbers really matter.

What tourists don’t necessarily see in Greenland

It was how strongly I sensed a “them and us” relationship between Greenlanders and the Danes.

Along with Donald Trump, the divide surfaced in conversations with people we met unprompted, and in the way some Greenlanders spoke about Denmark, language, history and identity.

These individuals are not a measure of wider public opinion, but the sense of separation was striking – especially in the museums we visited.

Rather than presenting visitors with a sanitised Arctic idyll, Nuuk’s cultural institutions openly explore Greenland’s complicated relationship with Denmark.

Alice, Nyeema and I were all particularly struck by Nuna, an exhibition at Nuuk Art Museum examining land, identity and Greenland’s relationship with outside powers. At its entrance was a message requiring little explanation.

'Greenland is not for sale'

Talk to people and another Greenland begins to emerge – a society having its own conversation about identity, autonomy and Denmark while simultaneously confronting extraordinary new interest from the outside world.

Climate change, military security, natural resources, Indigenous identity, tourism and the interests of global powers increasingly collide here.

And yet everyday life carries on around the geopolitical noise.

On the water, however, there are bright blue mini-icebergs, mountains rising directly from the waves, rocks, sky and sea stretching into the distance and an undeniable silence, exactly the Greenland one imagines.

Perhaps “out of this world” wasn’t such an exaggeration after all.

Iceland: When tourism becomes a well-oiled machine

Arriving in Reykjavík after Greenland felt like jumping several stages forward in the evolution of a tourism industry.

If Greenland feels like a destination being on the cusp of something, Iceland has had years to work out what international visitors want.

And it shows.

Grimnes-og Grafningshreppur, the Kerio Volcanic Crater Lake, filled with turquoise-blue water Euronews Baku Bureau

The statistics underline just how important tourism has become. Statistics Iceland recorded an estimated 10.16 million overnight stays in registered accommodation in 2025, up 9.1% in a year.

Tourism directly accounted for 8.8% of Iceland’s GDP in 2025, while tourism consumption by domestic and international visitors reached almost ISK 914 billion, which equates to over 6.5 billion euros.

Those are substantial numbers for a small island nation and as a traveller, you can see the sophisticated industry that has grown around them.

Reykjavik is charming and colourful but also extremely tourism-savvy.

Excursions are offered everywhere and so are restaurants, shops selling Icelandic designs, outdoor clothing galore, Viking paraphernalia and row upon row of traditional woollen jumpers.

The latter look as they are going to itch and after my sister and I tried on a very wide variety of designs, we realised that they didn’t.

They do, however, shed hair like a loveable dog.

Cod with a honey and mustard sauce, at Three Coats restaurant in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

And then there was the food.

Fish was a highlight: extraordinarily fresh cod, tasting unlike any cod that you will be served in the UK, despite it being renowned for fish and chips.

There’s also smoked salmon, shrimp and warming soup served inside a bread bowl.

For the more adventurous, menus can venture into horse, whale steak and slithers of smoked puffin.

Iceland has become extremely good at turning what makes it distinctive into an experience visitors can easily access, but there is, however, one unavoidable issue.

It is very expensive.

But again, as in Greenland, there is no ignoring the disappearing glaciers, pollution of the oceans and land and the doom of climate change and for a country so dependent on both tourism and fishing, these aspects are difficult to ignore.

And perhaps at that is the contradiction at the heart of Iceland’s success. It has become supremely good at selling the experience of Iceland. But the thing that everybody has fundamentally travelled there for is something nobody has created.

Nature.

Our own excursion beyond Reykjavik may have had us packed together liked sardines, but once the city disappeared behind us it became increasingly difficult for us to complain.

Iceland straddles the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Fissures cut through the landscape, geothermal activity bubbles beneath it and volcanoes, waterfalls and vast expanses of open land make it feel as though the planet is showing.

Hollywood clearly agrees.

Game of Thrones turned Icelandic landscapes into territory north of “the Wall”, while Christopher Nolan transformed parts of the country into another planet for Interstellar starring Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway. The Star Wars universe has also found a home within Iceland’s otherworldly scenery.

Norway: When expensive starts to feel worth it

Bergen greeted us with torrential rain, which cleared the following morning.

We wanted to travel from Bergen through Myrdal to Flam, but there was one problem, and that was the direct trains we wanted were all sold out, but we found an alternative router from Bergen towards Myrdal via Voss, before joining the famous Flam Railway.

Mountains stretched beyond what the eye – or an iPhone camera – could properly absorb.

Water cascading from waterfalls and wild rivers, tiny settlements beneath enormous peaks.

The Flam Railway runs for around 20 kilometres through spectacularly dramatic mountain scenery towards the fjord below and has become one of Norway’s best-known rail experiences.

Myrdal station where you can catch the Flam Railway to the Hardangerfjord Euronews Baku Bureau

Hollywood has also exploited this country with good reason. Tom Cruise has repeatedly returned with the Mission Impossible franchise. Mission Impossible: Fallout features the spectacular clifftop finale at Preikestolen with Cruise and Henry Caville and in Dead Reckoning, Cruise launched a motorcycle from Helsetkopen. Daniel Craig’s final James Bond film, No Time to Die, also used Norwegian locations, as did the hit series Succession, featuring Brian Cox and Jeremy Strong.

The price of luxury

Norway is also expensive, but tourist don't appear to be staying away.

Norwegian commercial accommodation recorded 40.6 million guest nights in 2025 up 5.2% in a year.

International visitors accounted for a record 14.2 million guest nights – an increase of 14% – and around three quarters of foreign guest nights came from European markets.

Germany was the largest overseas market, followed by Sweden, the Netherlands, the UK and Denmark.

Bergen itself is flourishing, with the wider region recording around three million commercial guest nights in 2024, 13.5% higher than in 2019.

Eirik Gjøvåg Berge, Chief Communications Officer at Visit Bergen, told Euronews that it is important to distinguish between Norway’s reputation for high prices and what visitors are actually doing.

He points out that the evidence, does not suggest high costs are driving international travellers away.

“In fact, favourable exchange rates for many international visitors, combined with Norway's strong appeal as a nature and experience destination, have helped drive continued growth,” he says.

Does quality justify the price?

Hilde Berentsen, General Manager of Home Hotel Havnekontoret, seems to think so. “If you pay for a service then you can have a higher quality,” she told me. “If you always go for the cheapest thing, then you don’t have quality around you.”

Berentsen has watched Bergen’s tourism industry develop since the hotel opened in 2006.

Hilde Berentsen in the lobby of the popular Home Hotel Havnekontoret located next to the harbour in Bergen, Norway Euronews Baku Bureau

One of its first celebrity guests was football legend Diego Maradona, who stayed with his team and the hotel has subsequently attracted considerable publicity for its luxury suite, which became known as Bergen’s most expensive hotel room. More famous guests have since followed suit.

“Everything cannot be for everybody,” she said, pointing to camping, caravans and cheaper accommodation as alternative ways of experiencing the country.

According to Visit Bergen, tourism supports around 13000 jobs and generates approximately more than 617 million euros (NOK 6.7 billion) in annual value creation.

Three countries, three very different versions of northern tourism.

Bird’s eye view of houses dotted around the mountains skirting Bergen Euronews Baku Bureau

By the time my sister and I had reached the end of our journey, that decidedly non-luxurious flight out of Stansted seemed a very long way away.

We had travelled through three countries united by extraordinary natural beauty but offering remarkably different experiences.

There were no Mediterranean beaches, no sun loungers and frankly, not a great deal of sun on this holiday.

Instead, there were fjords, mountains, volcanoes, waterfalls, tectonic plates, Viking jumpers, fresh fish, packed trains, unexpected friendships and Donald Trump.

Two sisters beginning this journey with no expectations, but the end allowing three words to describe each location, but probably, they were nearly not enough.

World.title: How the ECB rate hike will affect mortgage borrowers
World.content:
Mortgage rates have continued to climb across the eurozone’s four biggest economies since August, although the effect of the European Central Bank’s latest interest-rate increase varies significantly between countries.

 

Quoted fixed rates now range from around 2.2% in Spain to an average of 4.46% in Germany, although the figures cover different mortgage terms and are therefore not directly comparable.

The ECB’s latest increase was largely priced into mortgage offers before it was announced, brokers said. Banks in France, Italy and Spain had already anticipated the decision, while German mortgage rates continued to follow 10-year government bond yields more closely.

The increases follow a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields examined by Euronews Business in August. Higher government borrowing costs have already fed into mortgage offers in Germany and, indirectly, Italy, while French and Spanish rates remain more closely linked to ECB expectations.

French mortgage rates could approach 4%

French mortgage rates rose by 10 basis points in early September, taking the average rate on a new 20-year fixed mortgage from 3.44% in August to around 3.54%, according to Pierre Chapon, co-founder of mortgage broker Pretto.

Chapon said banks had already priced in the ECB’s decision but could raise rates again before the central bank’s next meeting.

“We expect the same range of increase next month as the inflation trend continues,” he said, referring to a possible rise of another 10–20 basis points.

France is an overwhelmingly fixed-rate mortgage market, with such products accounting for 99.6% of new housing loans in the latest available Banque de France data.

Pretto said the average rate on a 20-year fixed mortgage could reach 3.8%–4% by the end of the year if inflation does not ease.

A rise from the current 3.54% to 3.9% would add about €37 to the monthly repayment on a new €200,000 mortgage over 20 years. It would also increase the total interest bill by approximately €8,930.

French banks are not tightening their lending conditions, according to Pretto. It said strong balance sheets, relatively cheap deposits and fierce competition in a subdued mortgage market were helping to protect borrowers.

Italian variable-rate borrowers face a quicker impact

In Italy, the ECB increase is expected to have a more immediate effect on variable-rate mortgages.

“Following today’s decision, we expect the average nominal interest rate, or TAN, on new 20- and 30-year variable-rate mortgages to rise from approximately 2.80%, recorded during the first weeks of September, to around 3.05% over the coming weeks,” Nicoletta Papucci, marketing director at MutuiOnline.it, told Euronews Business.

A 25-basis-point increase would add approximately €25 to the monthly repayment on a €200,000 variable-rate mortgage with 20 years remaining, assuming it is passed through in full. That is equivalent to just under €6,000 in additional interest over the period.

Fixed-rate mortgages, which accounted for 92.2% of Italian mortgage applications in 2026, respond more closely to long-term euro interest-rate swaps than to individual ECB decisions.

Nevertheless, MutuiOnline expects the average rate on new 20- and 30-year fixed mortgages to rise from 3.46% in August to about 3.75% by the end of 2026. On a new €200,000 mortgage over 20 years, that would add around €30 to the monthly repayment and approximately €7,200 to the total interest bill.

Italian mortgage pricing had already been affected by rising government bond yields and, more directly, by higher long-term swap rates. Banks raised rates on different fixed-rate products by between 10 and 40 basis points during August and early September.

The increases also affected green mortgages, “which had previously been among the most competitively priced products”, Papucci said.

A significant part of the repricing had therefore taken place before the ECB’s decision. However, MutuiOnline has not observed widespread increases in deposit requirements or significant restrictions on credit.

Spanish mortgage rates could rise further

Fixed mortgage rates in Spain remain below 3%, but brokers expect some lenders to increase their offers following the ECB decision.

A significant part of the latest rise had already been priced into fixed-rate offers because Euribor, the benchmark used for many Spanish mortgages, had anticipated the ECB’s move several weeks earlier.

Since the previous ECB increase in June, rates on popular 30-year fixed mortgages have risen from around 2%–2.5% to approximately 2.2%–2.8%, according to Spanish mortgage broker iAhorro.

Initial rates on mixed mortgages — which are fixed for a certain period before becoming variable — have increased from around 1.85% to approximately 2%–2.1%.

Spokesperson Laura Martinez told Euronews Business that “several lenders will likely revise their mortgage products upward in the coming weeks”.

She expects increases of up to 0.5 percentage points at some banks, although others may raise rates by a more moderate 0.2 percentage points or hold them steady to attract customers and meet year-end sales targets.

For a €200,000 mortgage over 30 years, iAhorro calculated that the rise in Euribor from 2.172% in September 2025 to a provisional 3.101% in September 2026 would increase repayments by €98.92 a month, or €1,187.03 a year.

That calculation reflects the full year-on-year rise in Euribor, rather than the effect of the ECB’s latest 25-basis-point increase alone.

Borrowers with Euribor-linked mortgages due for review in September will feel the increase first. Those reviewed between October and December could follow, with repayments rising by around €100 a month if Euribor remains above 3.1%.

Competition between Spanish banks nevertheless remains strong. At iAhorro, mixed-rate products accounted for 52% of completed mortgages in August, with almost all the remainder on fixed rates and variable-rate products representing a negligible share.

German mortgages continue to follow Bund yields

German fixed mortgage rates continue to be driven more by government bond yields and other long-term market rates than by individual ECB decisions.

“The markets had already priced in the second rate hike this year, so it had no impact on government bond yields and, consequently, on mortgage rates,” Michael Neumann, chief executive of Dr Klein Privatkunden, told Euronews Business.

Dr Klein said its best available rate for a 20-year mortgage had risen from 3.99% to 4.24% over the previous month. For a €200,000 mortgage, this would add about €42 to the monthly repayment.

Neumann nevertheless expects mortgage rates to stabilise and move broadly sideways over the rest of the year.

Another brokerage in Germany, Interhyp, said its average rate for a 20-year fixed mortgage had risen from 4.32% in mid-August to 4.46%. “Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict at the end of February, rates for 20-year fixed-rate mortgages have increased by around 0.5 percentage points, from approximately 3.9% to around 4.4%."

Interhyp attributed the increase to inflation concerns, elevated energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty, which have pushed up long-term bond yields and lenders’ funding costs.

It said the outlook remained highly uncertain: its panel of experts was almost evenly divided between those expecting German mortgage rates to rise, remain stable or decline by the end of the year.

Despite the higher cost of borrowing, both German brokers said demand for home ownership remained strong. However, rising rates and high transaction costs were making purchases increasingly difficult to afford.

World.title: Houthis seize key Yemeni island in Bab el-Mandeb, taking control of the strait
World.content:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Friday, after capturing an island located in the middle of the crucial Red Sea waterway, a local government official and eyewitnesses said.

 

"Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday," the official said, referring to a rocky volcanic island also known as Perim that divides the narrowest part of the strait into two shipping lanes.

"The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking on condition of anonymity.

An eyewitness said gunmen were "deploying along the Bab el-Mandeb shore and are driving around in military vehicles."

Further reports emerged on Friday that the group also seized the town of Dhubab and the coastal village of Murad, meaning that all of Yemen's Red Sea coast was now under Houthi control in an 18-hour blitz.

Government military sources said that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands, following earlier reports that the Zuqar island — the largest of the three major islands in the Red Sea archipelago further north from Bab el-Mandeb — was already captured.

They said they were unsure about the status of their soldiers, who number more than 2,000, but believe the Houthis have ordered them to surrender.

A senior military official said that the besieged forces have appealed to authorities for "rescue, food and water, and the lifting of the siege, which would require air support".

On Thursday, Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from government forces in a blitz offensive that also saw them taking control of Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters," according to military sources.

By Thursday evening, multiple videos appeared online of Houthi fighters' apparent celebrations in Mokha and their seizure of considerable weapons and equipment left behind by government forces. Euronews could not verify the authenticity of the footage.

Another crisis on the horizon

The Houthis, who controlled about one-third of Yemen's territory prior to the offensive, have previously targeted shipping in the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb account for more than one quarter of seaborne crude oil and petroleum trade. Nearly one-third of the world's container traffic passes through the Red Sea alone.

The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.

Yemen's internationally recognised government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".

Yet a member of the Houthis' politburo on Friday sought to allay global fears for international shipping, stating the group posed "no danger" to Red Sea cargo routes.

"Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly," Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet. "There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side."

FILE: Yemeni fishermen pass by a commercial ship at the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, 5 April 2026 AP Photo

The Houthis corrected this statement to say Saudi Arabia remains an exception.

"Maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi ships, which have already been banned," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Friday evening.

According to Senior Director at the Soufan Center Caroline Rose, the Houthi takeover of Perim Island and Yemen's coastline creates in a chokehold which fill force shipping operators to reconsider costlier alternatives, while also impacting the key infrastructure the region relies on, such as the Suez Canal.

"Instead of going through the Red Sea, Suez, then Europe, they now have to explore a much more onerous path through Asia, the Cape of Good Hope, the Atlantic, then to Europe," Rose told Euronews.

"This adds weeks, greater insurance requirements given the proliferation of drones and overall risk, cost, and personnel needs to the journey, something that will undoubtedly increase prices."

Houthis marching on

Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.

The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, triggering the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.

FILE: A Yemeni fighter backed by the Saudi-led coalition fires his weapon during clashes with Houthi rebels on the Kassara frontline near Marib, 20 June 2021 AP Photo

The Houthis engaged in a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia, while also launching attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also said it has the right to defend itself.

Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.

A friend in need

Last month, Saudi Arabia signed a NATO-style mutual defence agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan in Mecca, but it seems unlikely either of the two would get involved.

On Tuesday, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan would "honour" the pact "in case there is a need".

Just one day later, the Pakistan foreign ministry said that the Mecca pact was a "defensive alliance focused on deterrence".

"There is no such thing under discussion right now. When the time comes, we will act under the agreement," spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told the press at the weekly media briefing.

In July, US President Donald Trump said Washington would respond against the Houthis if they attempted to block maritime traffic in the Red Sea, after weeks of US strikes from March 2025 — early in Trump's second term — hit a range of military and industrial targets.

However, Washington is reportedly reluctant to enter the fray at this time as it remains bogged down in its own war with Iran since February.

According to US outlets, Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for strikes on Houthi positions as they approached Mokha on Thursday. Riyadh and the White House are yet to comment on these reports.

FILE: US President Donald Trump welcomes Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the White House, 18 November 2025 AP Photo

Meanwhile in Brussels, the EU's External Action Service strongly condemned Houthi attacks earlier this week, calling for the group to "end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea" and respect UN resolutions.

Brussels had not publicly commented on the Houthis' seizure of Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb shoreline at the time of publication.

Operation Aspides, the 27-member bloc's defensive naval mission stationed in Djibouti has been tasked with protecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, but its current mandate does not cover offensive action against Houthi positions on land or on islands.

It is not clear at this time whether the group's lightning takeover of Bab el-Mandeb will expedite talks about expanding its mandate which EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Euronews in mid-July were already under way.

"What is tricky about the Houthis is that they have proven resilient with on-and-off-again maritime campaigns and coalitions directed at degrading their offensive capabilities," Rose said.

"Neither the US nor the EU have revived former efforts to consolidate a concerted campaign around the Houthis’ recent expansion, though it’s possible in the next few months as the US seeks leverage with Iran," she added.

Tehran salutes 'resounding victory'

Tehran chimed in on Friday, calling for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since the Houthi Red Sea offensive.

In a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Iran's foreign ministry said Yemen’s sovereignty must be respected, and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.

Meanwhile, reports have claimed that Iran's elite paramilitary IRGC has deployed dozens of advisors to aid the Houthis in their operations. Euronews could not independently verify the claims at this time.

Supporters celebrate at a rally to celebrate the group's capture of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, in Houthi-controlled Sana'a, 11 September 2026 AP Photo

A potential disruption to Bab el-Mandeb would work in Tehran's favour, as its blockade of Hormuz has put significant pressure on the world's energy markets, sparking a crisis that could worsen even further as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.

"The Houthi offensive to capture territory near the Bab al Mandeb advances Iranian objectives under the current regional campaign that Iran is waging against the United States and its allies," Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its latest analysis on Friday.

"Iran has recently pursued the following lines of effort under this regional campaign: targeting US naval forces, attacking US forces across the region, (and) disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," it added.

"The Houthis and Iran may currently share a common objective in Houthi control over the Red Sea coastline, but the nature of their relationship means that the Houthis will independently determine their level of involvement in supporting other Iranian objectives."

The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help it defend the country's coasts.

"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

World.title: French blockade looms over Commission’s plan to fast-track trade deals in English
World.content:
France will push back against a European Commission plan to fast-track ratification of trade agreements by circulating only English-language versions during talks with EU governments and lawmakers, skipping translation into the bloc’s 24 official languages, according to several sources.

 

The slow ratification of the contentious EU–Mercosur trade deal has frustrated the Commission, which wants to accelerate negotiations and bring deals into force more quickly as it seeks new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions.

Translating the agreements into every official EU language can take months due to the legal scrubbing required before the ratification process begins.

The EU executive has confirmed to Euronews that trade chief Maroš Šefčovič told EU trade ministers in February that the trade deal with India concluded on 27 January could serve as a test case for using English as the main language during ratification.

“We lost almost €300 billion by not having the Mercosur agreement in place since 2021, if it comes to the GDP, and more than €200 billion in export opportunities,” Šefčovič told journalists after meeting ministers on 20 February, adding that once negotiations end it can take up to 2.5 years before businesses can operate in partner countries.

“In today's world, we cannot simply lose the time,” he said.

Šefčovič said the Commission would ensure the agreements are translated into all 24 official EU languages once published in the Official Journal, i.e. after ratification. He added the proposal was backed by at least seven member states at the meeting, though not all countries had time to speak.

French sources who spoke to Euronews were insistent that Paris would vigorously oppose the move to English-only agreements if necessary.

“As a matter of principle, we defend the use of all the languages of the Union, and in particular French, which is one of the EU’s working languages,” one official told Euronews.

'Transparency, precision and understanding'

Language policy in the bloc’s institutions remains politically sensitive for countries such as France, whose language has declined sharply over the past decades as English massively dominates daily work in the European Union institutions – despite French, German and English being the three official working languages.

“Switching entirely to English raises a legal and democratic issue, and the Commission is well aware of it,” another French official told Euronews.

On its website, the European Commission says linguistic diversity is essential and that the EU promotes multilingualism in its institutional work.

The bloc once even had a commissioner dedicated to multilingualism, though the portfolio was gradually merged with others and eventually disappeared.

"I have the impression that in some cases the Commission seizes the opportunity to push the idea that English has a superior status, and that the other official languages are translation languages that can come later," Michele Gazzola, expert in language policy, said.

He added that relying only on English during ratification could pose problems for members of the European Parliament, and even more so if national parliaments are involved.

“It’s a matter of transparency, precision and understanding."

World.title: France joins Slovakia in asking to delist Russian oligarch Usmanov
World.content:
The French government has joined Slovakia in seeking the delisting of Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov, causing “huge frustration” among other EU countries, four EU diplomats told Euronews.

 

Slovakia has long pushed for Usmanov and another Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, to be removed from the EU's sanctions list targeting individuals close to Vladimir Putin's regime and the military-industrial complex sustaining the war in Ukraine.

But Bratislava is no longer alone. Paris has also called for Usmanov, who has been under EU sanctions since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, to be delisted.

Usmanov is an Uzbek-born Russian billionaire who built his fortune through investments in metals, mining, telecommunications and technology and is considered close to the Kremlin.

Usmanov denies this.

The French move has caused “huge frustration” among other member states, particularly against the backdrop of escalating hybrid threats in Europe, including the latest case of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany.

“It raised a lot of questions about the motivation — seems mostly economic reasons at play here. Not a lot of understanding on the side of other member states,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the talks.

The EU sanctions regime currently targets more than 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex and its contribution to the invasion of Ukraine. The regime is due for renewal on 15 September, with member states under pressure to reach an agreement by then.

Individual listings have so far been renewed every six months, but a 12-month renewal is now on the table. Sectoral sanctions already shifted from six-month to 12-month renewal cycles in July.

In several meetings of EU ambassadors, Slovakia has opposed the renewal, pushing for both oligarchs to be delisted and the six-month timeframe to remain in place.

The Slovak demands are not new. Bratislava has repeatedly called for the delisting of the two high-profile Russian oligarchs, including when the sanctions were last extended in March.

EU sanctions require unanimous approval for renewal, meaning a single country can veto an extension. Slovakia's opposition has already caused frustration among member states, but France's new position is likely to complicate the talks further.

Paris presented Usmanov's delisting as a political compromise, betting that Slovakia would not abandon its two delisting demands as it did last time.

EU ambassadors are due to meet again on Monday to discuss the renewal and will be under pressure to reach a political agreement before the 15 September deadline.

A French official said Paris supported the renewal of sanctions, but declined to comment on the discussions, citing confidentiality.

World.title: UK police ban face coverings at planned anti-migrant protest
World.content:
Police in southern England have banned face coverings at an anti-immigration rally as well as in a counter-protest planned in Portsmouth on Saturday, amid concerns over potential unrest.

 

The demonstration, organised by protesters calling themselves “patriots”, is expected to begin at around noon.

Hampshire Police, which has responsibility for Portsmouth, said the mask ban was to "reduce opportunities for violence, intimidation and criminality".

It said the move followed "recent incidents of violence and intimidation by a minority of those who have been intent on disrupting peaceful protest".

A separate order will allow police to require people to remove masks or other items covering their identity.

Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo, quoted by the BBC, said: "It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially.

"Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest, but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer."

The demonstrations come less than a week after clashes between protesters and police in Portsmouth. Masked protesters attempted to prevent a group of asylum seekers who had crossed the English Channel in a small boat from leaving the area.

Police said official vehicles were damaged and several officers were injured during the unrest, which the government condemned as “thuggish”.

A day earlier, hundreds of masked protesters gathered in Dover and briefly blocked access to the Channel port during a demonstration against migrant crossings.

The unrest in Portsmouth and Dover was condemned by political leaders.

Police were given powers last year to ban face coverings used to conceal identities at protests.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: France: More than 40 injured in train derailment
World.content:
The train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. One of the injured was in a critical state.

A train derailed on Friday evening on the route between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, local authorities said.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement .

One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added.

The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.

What else do we know about the train derailment?

French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.

Local authorities have urged the public to avoid the area.

The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.

"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.

​A police spokesperson said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.

The cause of the accident is being investigated, SNCF said.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2
World.content:
With fighting on the front lines mostly stalled, Russia has been increasingly hitting petrol stations and other civilian targets. Ukraine has also been attacking Russia with drones, killing three people on Friday.

At least two people were killed in Kyiv after Russian jet-powered drones struck a petrol station on Friday.

A 12-year-old boy was among 12 people who were injured by the attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one of the injured was a first responder who was "wounded in a double-tap strike."

Russia has turned to using jet-powered drones in near-constant attacks on Kyiv Image: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia increasingly targeting petrol stations with new, faster drones

Friday's drone strikes come a day after what is thought to be the first Russian attack on a Kyiv gas station during the war.

Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent months, most of which were in or near frontline areas.

The attacks on petrol stations come amid a spike in Russian assaults using new, faster and harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones to strike logistics centers, warehouses and commercial supply chains.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine condemns escalating Russian 'terror'

Zelenskyy said Russia was escalating these strikes on civilian energy infrastructure, calling them "increasingly terrorist in nature."

"Maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones," the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.

The CEO of Ukrainian oil giant Ukrnafta, which owns the gas station and one other that was also struck on Friday morning, condemned Russia for "yet another deliberate strike on civilian facilities."

"There is no military objective in such attacks. This is terror against the civilian population," Bogdan Kukura said.

Russia has not publicly commented on the latest attacks, but has consistently denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine, Russia striking logistics, energy targets

More than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion and with the fighting on the front lines in eastern Ukraine mostly stalled, Russia and Ukraine have been increasingly hitting logistics, energy and other economic targets in a bid to dent the other's war effort.

Ukraine has also stepped up its own drone attacks inside Russia. Overnight, two people were killed in Russia's Tula region, while one person was killed in Kursk on Friday, officials said.

Tula's regional governor Dmitry Milyayev added that three people were injured in the attacks.

Ozon, Russia's second-largest e-commerce platform, said a Ukrainian drone had struck a logistics hub in the city of Saratov, starting a fire.

Kyiv says its strikes against e-comms targets are aimed at disrupting Russia's supply lines Image: REUTERS

More than 20 warehouses belonging to Ozon and Wildberries, Russia's other leading online retailer, have been hit in Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks.

Kyiv says the strikes are justified as part of its campaign to undermine Russia's war effort, which has also seen Ukraine target Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: US commemorates 25 years since 9/11 terror attack
World.content:
A quarter century has passed since Islamists hijacked four commercial jets and turned them into weapons against the US. On Friday, ceremonies in New York, Pennsylvania and Washington DC marked the dark anniversary.

Commemorations are being held across the United States on Friday to mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the deadliest attacks ever carried out on US soil.

Events are taking place at the sites of the attacks — in New York City, Washington DC and Shanksville, Pennsylvania — and elsewhere around the nation to honor the 2,977 people killed that day.

The main ceremony is being held in New York, where Islamists from the terror group al-Qaeda flew two hijacked commercial airliners into the twin towers of the city's famous World Trade Center — a symbol of American economic power.

New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani, Governor Kathy Hochul and former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden are in attendance as well as current Vice President JD Vance.

Friday's event will feature wreath layings and vigils, punctuated by several moments of silence, marking the moments of impact and collapse and honoring the memory of the dead.

Family members will read out the names of the people killed that day, as well as six that were killed in a 1993 al-Qaeda bombing in the building's basement.

The attacks of September 11, 2001, killed nearly 3,000 people, changing New York, the US and the world Image: Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo/picture alliance

This year, the ceremony also acknowledged more than 600 firefighters who died from illness related to the toxic air and dust emanating from the burning structures of the site.

In Washington, President Donald Trump spoke at a ceremony at the Pentagon, the symbol of the US' military might, which was also targeted with a hijacked airliner that day.

In his remarks, Trump referenced his ongoing war in Iran, saying the US will never forget 9/11, adding, "that's why we fight today."

Other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It was there that passengers stormed the cockpit of a hijacked United Airlines jet in midflight, forcing the plane to crash in an empty field and keeping attackers from hitting their final target, the US Capitol.

25 years later: Keeping the memory of 9/11 alive To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU and NATO allies honor victims

European Union and NATO allies also commemorated the event.

European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday expressed admiration for "victims, their families and those who rushed to help others."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen underscored the strength of democracies, pointing out that the attackers had failed to rob democratic nations of their freedom.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte posted on X that allies had, "stood together" that day, "invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in NATO's history."

Rutte added, "America's friends and allies in NATO stood with you then and we stand with you today."

US President Trump has often threatened to attack NATO allies and voiced doubt about alliance members' commitments to helping the US in times of need.

How did the 9/11 terror attacks shape modern America? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The world after 9/11

The audacious attack quite literally changed the world, stunning the US and triggering a chain of events that impact people's everyday lives to this day.

The incident sparked the Bush administration's "War on Terror," which drew the US into its longest-ever military conflict in Afghanistan and shattered trust in the nation when Bush insisted on invading Iraq, which was not involved in 9/11.

America's reputation suffered as a result of extrajudicial policies such as renditioning and "enhanced interrogation" at secret CIA prisons, as well as its creation of a detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where suspected terrorists were held for years in dystopian conditions without trial.

The aftereffects of the wars are still costing the US billions and the debacle of Iraq irreparably damaged the solidarity the US was shown in the immediate aftermath of 9/11.

The attacks changed airport security measures, as well as the US government's ability to surveil citizens — leading to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, one of the biggest agencies in the US government, and passage of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and the USA Patriot Act.

Further, the event dramatically changed attitudes towards Muslims.

There was much controversy this year over whether Mamdani, for instance, should attend the New York ceremony. Republicans argued against it but the mayor insisted he would do so out of love of city and country and respect for those who died that day and in the years after.

US pays tribute to the victims of the 9/11 terror attacks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This year's ceremony honors those who have died in the aftermath of the attack

Mamdani's election as mayor shows just how far parts of the country have come since that day and the young Muslim Democrat this week opened a new chapter in the story of 9/11 by releasing tens of thousands of documents showing that leaders had hidden information about the toxicity of air in the city after the attack.

As asbestos and toxic smoke blanketed the city for months officials told residents and clean-up workers that they had nothing to fear.

In fact, the toxicity of dust, rubble and smoldering plastic and metal has led to at least 9,400 additional deaths according a federal medical monitoring program.

9/11 survivor recalls his escape from WTC To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Iran pursues cautious escalation ahead of US midterms
World.content:
Tehran appears to be boosting pressure on Washington ahead of the crucial midterm vote, but shows little desire to return to a full-scale war.

The war with Iran "is going to end immediately after the [US midterm] election because they can't hold out any longer," US President Donald Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.

Speaking at the Republican midterm convention, the first such event to be held at a massive arena in Dallas, Texas, Trump described the November 3 vote as "one of the most important elections of your lives," and once again defended the war against Iran.

The US president restated his argument that he had launched the attacks to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would fall as soon as the US had won the war.

But even if Trump's promises are taken at face value, rising gas prices are sure to hurt Republicans' electoral prospects in the midterms.

On Wednesday, Brent crude — the global benchmark for prices — jumped to over $100 (€86) per barrel. The fighting escalated again this week, with the US striking Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for Iran's targeting of a US warship.

Iran's tightrope walk

"Iran still appears to see escalation primarily as a controlled instrument of coercive bargaining, rather than as an end in itself," said Mohammad Ghaedi, a Middle East expert and professor at the Department of Political Science at George Washington University.

"Iran is trying to impose costs on the United States without raising those costs so dramatically that Washington feels compelled to return to full-scale war," he explained.

"That helps explain why the number of missiles fired at US naval vessels has remained relatively limited."

The regime wants to demonstrate that it can threaten US forces and disrupt the maritime traffic in the region, the expert said, "but it also wants to keep the confrontation below a threshold that could trigger a much larger American response."

How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A return to the Islamabad truce?

Tehran's preferred outcome would be a return to the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Islamabad in June, Ghaedi said, referring to a preliminary deal that paused the full-scale conflict.

At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in late August, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that, if the United States returns to the memorandum, Iran would return as well.

From Tehran, however, this scenario seems increasingly unlikely.

Ghaedi said the first provision of the memorandum presents a major obstacle, as it requires an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon — "something Tehran sees as unlikely before Israel's elections."

Trump reportedly urged to limit US response

Israel is going to the polls to elect a new parliament on October 27, just days before the US is set to hold its midterm vote. In Tehran, many believe that a decisive turning point in the conflict will not come until after these two elections.

On September 2, the Reuters news agency reported that senior advisers to President Trump were urging him to limit any escalation of the conflict, fearing political repercussions for the Republicans at the midterms.

The White House is reportedly considering expanding the military action after the elections.

Is the lull in fighting between Iran and the US over? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran, Ghaedi said, "has little interest in pushing the conflict into a much higher level of escalation."

"If Democrats gain control of Congress and try to constrain Trump's conduct of the war, Iran would be even more cautious about doing anything that could create a rally-around-the-flag effect or push Democrats closer to Trump."

Will Iran bend to economic pressure?

While military developments are hard to predict, the US will likely continue to boost economic pressure on Iran.

But Ahmad Alavi, an Iranian economics professor based in Sweden, warns that economic pressure alone would not result in political concessions.

"If the leadership of the Islamic Republic concludes that the goal of the pressure is not to change its behavior but to weaken or overthrow it, it might view concessions as a greater threat to its survival and resort instead to escalating military actions," he told DW.

Tehran would be more willing to make concessions if there were a genuine prospect of easing pressure and an established channel for negotiations, he added.

Gulf states search for Hormuz solution

Meanwhile, Oman and several other Gulf states are once again seeking a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

The foreign ministers of the Gulf states are planning to meet with their Iranian counterpart in Salalah, Oman, next week, to try to reach a deal that would temporarily ensure the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported.

However, such an agreement would likely require Washington's approval, given the prolonged US naval blockade against Iran.

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran keeps up hard line in public

Iran's leaders have continued to signal defiance as the conflict drags on.

"We will continue the war until final victory," Ali Nikzad, deputy speaker of parliament, told reporters on September 9.

Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also demanded on September 8 that the US "completely cease hostilities" and refrain from further threats if it wanted to end the current situation.

At the same time, he threatened a more comprehensive Iranian response should the US attacks continue.

On September 10, the IRGC released a video that, according to Iranian sources, shows the capture of a US Anduril Dive-LD unmanned underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz. The vehicle is said to have been deployed on a covert mine-clearing mission.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
World.content:
New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.

India's difficult BRICS chairship To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.

New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition

Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.

Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.

"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.

However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powers Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.

The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.

Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.

"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.

BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow

India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.

Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.

With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.

"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.

Fears of Chinese dominance

The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.

What is BRICS Pay? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"

"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."

India's 'America Plus' strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.

EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.

But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.

"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.

In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
World.content:
Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.

A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.

With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.

In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all of them seem to be profitable Image: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

Africa a difficult market to crack

Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.

However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation: Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.

In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20% — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.

Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers

Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.

He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."

"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.

"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."

Uber makes UK drivers workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.

The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.

"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.

Their pleas and concerns, however, remain largely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.

Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, it comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.

This also makes consumers less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led gas prices to skyrocket Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.

This is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."

The complex economics of ride-hailing

There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.

Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives."

"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.

Spain restricts ride-hailing services To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber:

Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars.

Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?

As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequences Image: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.
