World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: September 28 Holiday in Czechia: What Will Be Open and Closed
World.content:
Czech Statehood Day falls on Monday, September 28, giving people across Czechia a three-day weekend. But anyone planning to shop should be aware that many large stores will be required to close.

The public holiday commemorates Saint Wenceslas, the patron saint of the Czech lands and one of the most important figures in Czech history. September 28 has been observed as Czech Statehood Day since 2000 and is a statutory day off.



For shoppers, however, the key issue is the country’s restrictions on retail opening hours.

Which shops will be closed on September 28

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square metres must close on September 28.

This means most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centres will not be able to operate as normal.

The restriction does not apply to all businesses. Smaller shops with a sales area of up to 200 square metres can remain open, although individual owners decide whether to operate during the holiday.

Some types of businesses are also exempt from the restrictions. These include pharmacies, petrol stations and shops located at airports and major railway stations.

Restaurants, cafés and most other services are not covered by the retail law and can therefore open according to their normal schedules or the decision of their operators.

People planning to use smaller independent shops should still check opening hours in advance. Many owners choose to close during public holidays, particularly when the holiday creates a long weekend.

Why is September 28 a public holiday

Czech Statehood Day is linked to Saint Wenceslas, the medieval ruler who became the patron saint of the Czech lands.

Wenceslas was the son of Duke Vratislav I and Drahomíra. His grandmother, Ludmila, who was later canonised, played a major role in his upbringing and is traditionally credited with influencing his Christian education.

Wenceslas is believed to have been killed in Stará Boleslav on September 28, either in 929 or 935, depending on the historical source.

His death turned him into a martyr and helped establish his lasting importance in Czech religious and national traditions.

World.title: Former state secretary: Former PM Orbán ordered Hungary to pay more for a telecom company than the owners had asked
World.content:
Former state secretary Vilmos Vályi-Nagy has spoken about government meetings held to resolve “problematic cases”, the increase in the purchase price of telecommunications company Antenna Hungária and what he described as massively overpriced state IT procurements in the second part of his interview with Partizán, published on Friday evening.

Vályi-Nagy, who served as a state secretary in the Orbán government between 2010 and 2014, was introduced in the programme as one of the important sources for investigative journalists over the past decade.

He said that meetings were held at Parliament every Monday morning, attended by the then prime minister and state secretaries, where “problematic cases” were dealt with and decisions considered important for the functioning of the economy were made.

According to Vályi-Nagy, the tenders for public lighting in municipalities were among the issues discussed. He said Elios, a company that became closely associated with the business interests of Orbán’s son-in-law, István Tiborcz, regularly won such tenders, while János Lázár was responsible for ensuring that the cases moved forward.

He added that problems arising in connection with the projects were dealt with immediately.

Read more about the interview: How former PM Orbán’s ex-secretary informed media about the shady businesses and was threatened with his kids

‘The proportion of bad projects started to increase’

Vályi-Nagy said that, over time, an increasing number of projects came before the meetings that he considered professionally unsound and financially loss-making for the state.

“More and more cases came up that were totally unprofessional and completely loss-making, and apart from the company implementing the project doing extremely well out of it, they were nothing but a burden and a liability on the back of the Hungarian state,” he said.

He added that the balance had gradually changed, with the proportion of bad projects increasing while the share of good projects declined.

As an example, he cited a government data centre planned for Göd, saying the state had spent HUF 15 billion on the project even though, apart from a concrete structure, nothing was ultimately completed.

Vályi-Nagy described the case as “outright theft”, adding that no one had been held responsible, no investigation had been launched and no criminal complaint had been filed.

Antenna Hungária: ‘I froze’

The former state secretary also recalled negotiations over the state’s repurchase of Antenna Hungária, which had been privatised during the premiership of Ferenc Gyurcsány.

He said that, in the early 2010s, negotiations with the foreign owner had brought the proposed purchase price down from HUF 61–62 billion to HUF 48 billion.

However, when he informed Viktor Orbán about the deal, the prime minister allegedly told him that the lower price was not acceptable and that the purchase price should instead be HUF 53 billion.

“So we had to modify the price backwards,” Vályi-Nagy said. “I froze, because anyone would have frozen in that situation. On the one hand, I did not understand it, but on the other hand, I very much understood what this story might be about,” he added.

State IT procurement became increasingly centralised

Vályi-Nagy also discussed the way the state organised IT procurement, claiming that IT purchases were concentrated among a handful of companies while contract signing was tied to a single ministry. He said the system became so centralised that operational and organisational problems were prevented from reaching the highest levels of government.

According to Vályi-Nagy, a contract for the e-ingatlan system was signed around 2016, but the system has still not worked properly, or has only functioned partially.

He also claimed that the value of active contracts connected to digital citizenship had exceeded HUF 100 billion, despite the system being capable, in his view, of being developed for one-tenth of that amount at a higher professional standard.

The former state secretary said the number of such contracts continued to grow, while in many cases private-sector companies effectively decided what developments the state would carry out.

He described this as “quite incredible”.

From around 2016–2017, he said, there was always someone who effectively took control of the market and decided which companies could enter framework agreements and which could not.

“You can get into this framework agreement, you will be the consortium leader, and you — get out of here,” he recalled the approach as being.

‘Everyone was stealing from everyone’

Vályi-Nagy described the system as a hybrid structure in which even the ultimate owners behind businesses associated with the National Cooperation System (NER) were allegedly sometimes exploited by other NER-linked oligarchs.

He claimed that the oligarchs could also be exploited by their own middle managers.

“So everyone was stealing from everyone,” he said, arguing that this was one reason why the final bill paid by the Hungarian state became so high.

Claims of political interference in investigations

The former state secretary also made allegations concerning investigations by the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV). According to Vályi-Nagy, the NAV had thoroughly investigated and traced the relevant information, collecting extensive data on those involved and carrying out raids.

He then alleged that, several weeks later, political pressure was brought to bear on the leadership of the tax authority.

“The NAV investigated everything very thoroughly and traced everything. It collected all the information about everyone and carried out raids. Then, a few weeks later, politics raided the leadership of the NAV; those who had been working on the case were sidelined, and the case was moved to a provincial investigative office and put into the hands of four to six people.”

He said that the original 100–120 people working on the case were removed from it and replaced by four to six investigators who had to start again from scratch.

“Accordingly, that was how the case continued,” he said.

Vályi-Nagy claimed that there had been hundreds of cases in which the task of people working at the NAV, police or prosecution service had effectively been to put investigations on the back burner.

Calls for scrutiny of state IT contracts

Turning specifically to state IT procurement, Vályi-Nagy alleged that contracts covering various network services and equipment purchases were significantly overpriced. He also said that licensing agreements deserved particular scrutiny, arguing that the issue “cries out for an investigation”.

World.title: Péter Magyar opens World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest alongside Usain Bolt
World.content:
Budapest has welcomed some of the biggest names in athletics as the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship got underway, with Prime Minister Péter Magyar joining athletics legend Usain Bolt and World Athletics president Sebastian Coe for the official opening.

Usain Bolt arrives in Budapest for new athletics spectacle

The three-day competition is being held at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre from 11 to 13 September, bringing together some of the world’s top athletes for a new-style global championship.

Magyar shared a photo on Facebook from the opening ceremony with Bolt, the eight-time Olympic champion, 11-time world champion and world record holder. Bolt is in Hungary as an ambassador for the event and is also attending the competition in person.

The Prime Minister wrote that he had welcomed the athletics legend to Budapest for the first-ever World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

The event is designed to present athletics in a new format, combining elite competition with a more spectacular presentation aimed at attracting audiences beyond the sport’s traditional fan base.

One event at a time, with a USD 10 million prize pool

According to Blikk, one of the biggest changes is the competition format. Rather than several events taking place simultaneously around the stadium, only one event will be held at a time, allowing spectators and viewers to focus entirely on the athletes competing.

The stadium itself has also undergone a striking transformation. The traditional red running track is complemented by a black competition surface, LED strips and extensive lighting effects, creating an atmosphere closer to a concert venue than a conventional athletics meeting.

The stakes are equally eye-catching. A total of USD 10 million will be distributed among the athletes, with each winner set to receive USD 150,000.

There will also be no traditional medals for the podium finishers. Only the winner of each event will receive a trophy, reflecting the organisers’ aim of putting the spotlight firmly on the athlete who reaches the top.

Sebastian Coe said the decision to abandon traditional medals was deliberate, arguing that the new global championship is about determining who is the single best athlete in each event.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

New rules promise a different kind of competition

The Budapest championship also introduces several unusual rules. In the 200-metre final, athletes can choose their lane based on their world ranking. In the high jump and pole vault, ties for first place must be settled through a jump-off, ensuring that every event has a single winner.

The organisers have also introduced changes aimed at making controversial judging decisions more transparent. Appeals must be resolved before the television broadcast window closes, while major decisions will be announced inside the stadium. Spectators will also be able to watch replays of disputed moments on the big screen.

Broadcasts will feature another new element, with viewers able to see the competitors’ chances of winning the overall title based on the results as the competition progresses.

We wrote about the championship in detail earlier: Budapest is about to host an athletics event unlike any before – $10 million in prize money and no medals

Hungarian athletes among the global stars

Hungary is also represented at the championship, including by Olympic sprinter Boglárka Takács, who will compete in the newly introduced mixed 4×100-metre relay. Takács will race alongside Zita Szentgyörgyi, Lili Brucker, Krisztián Kalics, Dominik Pázmándi, Ábel Takács and Apor Jakab in the unusual event.

Meanwhile, the international field includes Swedish pole-vault superstar Mondo Duplantis, who will compete for the Absolute Champion title on the opening night. He is also set to perform the official anthem of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship during Sunday’s closing ceremony.

The event runs from 11 to 13 September at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre.

World.title: Viktor Orbán has returned from his summer vacation: “I’m back”
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán has announced his return to political work following the summer break, posting a short but striking message on Friday evening: “I’m back. Then let’s get cracking!”

Orbán set to speak at “Kötcse picnic”

The Fidesz leader did not provide any details about his plans, but accompanied the message with a fast-paced video featuring highlights from his previous political appearances, including scenes from earlier Fidesz gatherings and Kötcse picnics. The timing of the announcement comes just one day before Orbán is due to address an important Fidesz gathering.

Viktor Orbán is scheduled to deliver a speech at the Kötcse Picnic on Saturday, 12 September, where he is expected to outline his political strategy for the period ahead. The Kötcse meeting is considered one of the most significant events in the Fidesz political calendar.

It traditionally brings together senior party figures, politicians and members of the party’s wider intellectual and political circle. Orbán has typically used the occasion to assess the political situation and discuss the priorities and challenges facing the party, making his speech closely watched for indications of its future direction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A message ahead of an important political gathering

Orbán’s latest video deliberately draws on his political past, combining footage from previous speeches and Fidesz events with music from the 2010 FIFA World Cup era. The post itself offered no indication of the specific issues he intends to address at Kötcse.

The upcoming gathering is also notable because attendance is reportedly no longer compulsory for members of Fidesz’s wider political circle, making this year’s event different from previous meetings. Critics of Viktor Orbán and Fidesz argue that the party is facing political and economic challenges and that the former prime minister needs to deliver a strong message to maintain support.

Whether Saturday’s speech will provide concrete policy announcements or focus primarily on political mobilisation remains to be seen. For now, Orbán’s message is brief but unmistakable: after the summer break, he says he is back in action.

World.title: Hungarian oil giant MOL reacted to the government’s diesel support decision
World.content:
Hungarian oil and gas company MOL has backed the government’s new diesel support scheme but warned that reintroducing a fuel price freeze could lead to petrol and diesel shortages within days.

The company said the monthly HUF 5,000 (EUR 13.76) support announced by the government was a better solution than restoring the previous regulated fuel price, as it provides targeted help to consumer groups most affected by rising diesel costs without discouraging fuel imports.

Price freeze could hit imports

According to MOL, bringing back a protected fuel price would immediately reduce imports because suppliers could no longer operate profitably at the artificially lower domestic prices. The company warned that this could result in petrol and diesel shortages within just a few days. MOL said the international fuel market has also become increasingly fragile. Conflict around the Strait of Hormuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have contributed to tighter global supplies.

Based on July figures, MOL said global diesel exports were 21% lower than a year earlier, while petrol exports had fallen by 14%. Diesel deliveries from India and Turkey to the European Union have also declined, partly because of EU restrictions on products made from Russian crude. Lower water levels on important transport routes are creating an additional challenge, making it more difficult to move imported fuel into the interior of Europe, quotes Blikk.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Diesel demand set to rise

MOL also expects demand for diesel across Europe to increase significantly over the coming weeks, as the continent enters one of its strongest seasonal consumption periods. The company said the next two months are likely to bring particularly high demand at a time when supply is already constrained. The pressure is reflected in international prices. MOL reported that on 8 September, the global oil price was 53% higher, while the European diesel price was 89% higher than before the outbreak of the Iran war.

The company said maintaining a stable domestic fuel supply and ensuring continuous imports are therefore among its main priorities. Despite increasingly limited availability on international markets, Hungary has so far avoided fuel shortages.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

MOL offers temporary premium fuel discount

MOL CEO Zsolt Hernádi and other company executives were recently invited to a government meeting to discuss how fuel prices could be contained without creating shortages or imposing an additional HUF 50–100 billion monthly burden on the state budget. Following the meeting, MOL announced a temporary HUF 35-per-litre discount on its EVO Plus premium fuels for customers using the MOL Move app and an eligible discount coupon.

The promotion is available during three weekends: 10–13 September, 17–20 September and 24–27 September. MOL said Hungarian retail fuel prices remain below the EU average, but argued that domestic prices must remain broadly aligned with those in neighbouring countries. If Hungarian fuel becomes significantly cheaper than the regional market, importers may no longer find it profitable to bring fuel into the country.

World.title: Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors
World.content:
A former school guard and child-care worker has been sentenced to eight years in prison for sexually abusing two minors, the Budapest IV and XV District Court ruled at first instance on Friday.

Court hearing held behind closed doors

The man was found guilty of endangering a minor, repeated sexual violence and exploiting child prostitution. The court also ruled that he will not be eligible for parole. The trial was conducted behind closed doors, meaning only the operative part of the verdict was made public. The court’s reasoning has not been released.

According to the indictment, the man deliberately sought employment in institutions where he could come into contact with vulnerable children, first working as a school guard and later as a child-care worker at a Budapest children’s home.

Prosecutors said he exploited his position to establish sexual relationships with two minors who were in difficult and vulnerable circumstances.

First victim was approached at school

The defendant met the first victim while working as a school guard and gradually established a relationship of trust with the boy. He later invited the child to his home, where he provided alcohol and an intoxicating substance.

According to the indictment, he then exploited the situation and, on some occasions, his physical advantage, to force the boy to engage in sexual acts. The case later involved a second victim after the man began working at a Budapest children’s home.

Second victim was a 14-year-old girl

As a child-care worker, the man was responsible for supervising girls placed in the home, overseeing their work and providing care.

In spring 2023, prosecutors said he abused this position of authority to approach one of the girls, who was aged 14 or older, and subsequently engaged in sexual acts with her. The man then instructed the girl not to tell anyone about what had happened, according to the indictment.

The court found him guilty of the charges brought against him and imposed an eight-year custodial sentence. As the ruling was delivered at first instance, the case is not necessarily concluded.

World.title: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels
World.content:
Hungary could seek financial support from the European Union as it considers gradually reducing its dependence on Russian oil and gas, while analysts warn that replacing Russian energy could significantly increase costs for the Hungarian economy.

Speaking at a V4 summit press conference in Bratislava, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he wanted to see concrete, data-based EU proposals to support Central European businesses, help member states phase out Russian oil and gas, switch to alternative energy sources and develop energy-storage infrastructure.

Péter Magyar calls for EU support over energy transition

The Hungarian government is reportedly considering making compensation payments for countries phasing out Russian energy part of the EU’s next seven-year budget. Péter Magyar said the current global energy situation remained extremely difficult, with fuel shortages being reported in several countries. He also argued that national budgets could not absorb the financial burden indefinitely and that maintaining fuel price caps could ultimately lead to shortages.

The prime minister criticised what he described as a lack of concrete proposals from EU leaders, saying businesses in Central Europe were struggling with rising costs. The Tisza Party’s political programme has previously included a goal of ending Hungary’s dependence on Russian energy by 2035.

Replacing Russian oil would come at a cost

Hungary currently receives most of its Russian crude through the Druzhba pipeline, supplying MOL’s refineries. Around 5–5.5 million tonnes reportedly arrived through the route in 2025, with a similar volume expected in 2026. Analysts say Russian Urals crude has recently been around USD 15–20 per barrel cheaper than Brent, giving Hungary a substantial purchasing advantage.

Alternative supplies could be brought through Croatia, but analysts at Kpler say this would reduce at least part of the current price advantage. More expensive crude could squeeze MOL’s refining margins and raise costs across Hungary’s energy system, reports VG.hu.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Gas dependence presents an even bigger challenge

Hungary is also heavily dependent on Russian natural gas delivered through TurkStream under long-term agreements with Gazprom. A reported 7.8 billion cubic metres arrived through the route in 2025, while daily deliveries in 2026 have reached around 22 million cubic metres.

The precise pricing formula is not public, making the actual cost advantage difficult to calculate. However, previous reports have suggested that Russian gas could be significantly cheaper than prices on Europe’s TTF market.

More on the Hungarian government: Péter Magyar announces monthly diesel support for nearly one million car owners

Russia may also have an incentive to keep supplying Hungary

Analysts disagree over how Moscow might respond to a Hungarian shift away from Russian energy. Some argue that Russia benefits financially from continuing supplies and has an interest in retaining one of its remaining European customers. Others believe changing political relations could lead Moscow to reconsider prices or volumes.

For Hungary, a rapid transition could therefore mean substantially higher energy costs. Despite the reported political shift, the government has not indicated that it plans to abandon existing Russian energy agreements, while cooperation on gas supplies and the Paks II nuclear project is expected to continue.

World.title: Hungary announces monthly diesel support for nearly one million car owners
World.content:
Owners of eligible diesel cars in Hungary will receive HUF 5,000 (approximately EUR 13.75) a month in fuel support through December, with the first payment due in October. The scheme is expected to benefit nearly one million motorists.

Who qualifies for the support?

The payment will cover September, October, November and December, meaning eligible drivers can receive HUF 20,000 (EUR 55) in total. The scheme applies to private individuals who owned a diesel passenger car with a maximum output of 150 horsepower on 1 January 2026. Each person can receive support for one vehicle.

Small-scale farmers and sole proprietors can also qualify if the eligible diesel vehicle is registered in their personal name. People who purchased a diesel car after 1 January 2026 are not yet covered by the main system. A separate procedure is reportedly being prepared, although details and a timetable have not yet been announced.

No application expected for most drivers

Most eligible motorists will not need to submit an application. The National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) will identify qualifying vehicles using its database for vehicle tax.

Payments will be made by the Hungarian State Treasury. The money will first be sent to the bank account used to pay the vehicle tax. If that account is unavailable, another account known to NAV may be used. Those without a suitable bank account may receive the money by post.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Farmers to receive additional diesel relief

Agricultural users will also be able to reclaim the full excise duty included in the price of diesel until the end of the year. The government says the measure is intended to help farmers cope with higher fuel costs during the harvest, autumn ploughing and sowing season, while limiting the impact on production costs and, ultimately, food prices.

Stay up-to-date: Fuel prices soar in Hungary, diesel hits 4-year high, but what does the government say about fuel price caps?

Why has the government chosen targeted support?

The announcement comes as diesel prices have risen sharply. The government says returning to Hungary’s previous regulated fuel price would be difficult, potentially discouraging imports and creating supply problems.

It estimates that restoring the former protected price could cost the state HUF 50–100 billion (EUR 137.5-275 million) per month. Instead, the government has opted for direct support targeted at diesel users. The authorities have attributed recent fuel-price pressures to international market developments, including tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on oil infrastructure linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.

World.title: Tragedy in Budapest: Woman jumps out the window after fire breaks out in 15th-floor flat
World.content:
A woman has died after a fire broke out in a flat on the 15th floor of a tower block in Budapest’s 14th district, Zugló, early on Friday morning.

Another fire broke out in Budapest’s District XIV

The blaze broke out in a flat in the Füredi housing estate in Rákosfalva Park. According to Budapest’s disaster management authorities, one room and a balcony were fully engulfed in flames. Firefighters extinguished the fire using two water jets.

As the report of BudapestKörnyéke claim, ten fire engines, three ambulances and several police units were dispatched to the scene. One firefighter was injured during the operation and was taken to the Honvéd Hospital for treatment. The resident of the flat, a mother of two, died at the scene.

Another case happened only a few hours before, in the same district, on Stefánia Road, where the roof of an apartment complex caught fire, where the flames spread to two neighbouring flats, and was also endangering nearby homes.

Woman fell from the 15th floor

According to local residents, the woman left the burning flat through a window after the fire broke out and died at the scene. However, it has not yet been established whether she deliberately left the building in this way or was attempting to escape the flames.

The Budapest Police Headquarters said an administrative procedure has been launched in connection with the death, while a separate fire investigation is underway to establish the cause and circumstances of the blaze.

Residents heard shouting before the fire

People living in the tower block told local media that residents on lower floors were woken by loud shouting and screaming in the early hours of Friday morning, followed by a loud impact. Neighbours said the woman had lived in the Füredi housing estate since childhood and was known by several people in the area, writes Blikk.

One neighbour said she had normally lived with her mother and two young daughters. The children were reportedly no longer living with her, while her mother was in hospital at the time of the incident. Residents also said the woman had experienced serious personal difficulties and that emergency services had been called to the property on previous occasions.

Investigation continues

The flat was severely damaged by the blaze and is currently uninhabitable. According to the building’s caretaker, the municipality is expected to arrange for the property to be cleared and repaired.

Relatives told reporters that police and ambulance services had previously been called to the property several times because of concerns about the woman’s condition. They said they had repeatedly asked authorities to provide her with appropriate help.

Two days before the tragedy, the woman had published a concerning message on social media in which she claimed that people were impersonating police officers and paramedics and said she was afraid to leave her flat. Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances of the fire and the woman’s death.

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Seven Over Deadly Fire at Tuzla Elderly People’s Care Home
World.content:
Investigators inspect the scene after the fire at the nursing home in Tuzla, November 5, 2025. Photo: EPA/NIDAL SALJIC.

Prosecutors in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tuzla Canton on Friday indicted seven people over the fire at a Tuzla nursing home in November 2025 that killed 15 elderly residents and injured more than 30 others.

The indictment charges former nursing home director Mirsad Bakalovic, service head Zinaida Razic Halilovic and Mustafa Azabagic, who was responsible for fire and occupational safety at the facility.

Three employees of the Tuzla-based company Inproz, which prepared the nursing home’s 2021 fire risk assessment, are also indicted: Nedim Dzambic, Mirsad Zukancic and Jasmin Softic. The seventh defendant is Ibrahim Sarajlic, a fire safety inspector in Tuzla Canton.

The defendants are charged with serious offences against public safety. Bakalovic is also charged with abuse of office and authority, the prosecutor’s office said.

Prosecutors allege that between April 2021 and November 4, 2025, the defendants failed to implement or order legally required fire safety and general safety measures, despite knowing the facility was classified as a high-risk building.

The nursing home run by the city of Tuzla housed 180 elderly residents, 110 of whom were seriously ill, immobile or living with disabilities.

According to the indictment, the failures included inadequate supervision of residents with limited mobility, inappropriate accommodation and allocation of residents according to their health and mobility, and an inadequate fire prevention and protection system.

Prosecutors said these failures prevented the timely detection and containment of the fire, the early detection and reporting of fire and carbon monoxide in residents’ rooms, the evacuation of residents, and the removal of smoke and heat from the building.

“As official and responsible persons, by failing to install prescribed fire protection equipment and by failing to act in accordance with regulations or technical safety rules, they caused a danger to people’s lives, resulting in the deaths of several people,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The fire broke out in a resident’s room on November 4 and quickly spread. Fifteen residents died, with autopsies establishing a direct causal link to carbon monoxide poisoning or other complications related to the fire, prosecutors said. More than 30 people were injured.

The indictment has been submitted to the Tuzla Cantonal Court for confirmation.

Prosecutors have also asked the court to ban all seven defendants from holding public or professional positions or performing certain activities for 10 years.

World.title: North Macedonia Govt Finally Reveals Independence Day Celebrations’ Cost
World.content:
North Macedonia’s government spokesperson, Marija Miteva (R) and State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski (L) at a press conference in Skopje. Photo: BIRN.

The series of celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of North Macedonia’s Independence Day, September 8, cost a total of 5.5 million euros, of which almost 4.9 million euros came from the State Lottery, government spokesperson Marija Miteva told a press conference on Thursday.

The rest of the money, some 650,000 euros, Miteva said, came from “socially responsible” companies.

The financial disclosure followed a BIRN Macedonia report published on Wednesday showing that the government had effectively tasked the State Lottery with taking care of the events, by choosing a production company that would organise them according to the government’s requirements.

Four months ago, the government announced its plan for a series of events marking the anniversary, culminating in a September 8 concert in Skopje by world-famous DJ David Guetta. Since then, officials had repeatedly declined to say how much the events would cost, or who was paying for them.

The government at the press conference focused on its argument that the almost 5 million euros coming from the State Lottery, which is fully owned by the government, was not taxpayers’ money.

State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski told the press conference that the government, as the company’s sole shareholder, had ordered it to allocate the money from its undistributed 2024 profits to the celebrations.

But he insisted it should not be considered budgetary funds because it remained on the company’s account and was therefore “corporate money” until formally transferred to the state budget.

This supported the Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski’s claim on Wednesday, who, confronted by reporters, maintained that the events “cost the budget and the citizens zero denars”.

The funding arrangements raised questions about transparency. In June, BIRN reported that the government was refusing to disclose the financial details of what it described as spectacular celebrations under the slogan “Silno svetnal den” [Brightly shining day], despite repeated requests for information.

On Thursday, Boban Miloseski, the owner of Avalon production, which the State Lottery hired to carry out the celebrations, apologised for an earlier incident on September 7, at a press conference organised by Avalon and the Interior Ministry ahead of Guetta’s September 8 concert in Skopje.

Asked why the cost of Guetta’s contract had not been made public, and whether a clause prevented disclosure, Miloseski had responded: “Do I look like an idiot to you?”, calling the question a provocation. In his apology, he said he uttered these words under a lot of “stress and fatigue”, before he had time to properly think it through.

Besides Guetta, the celebrations in Skopje and across the country featured other world-famous performers and DJs, including José Carreras, Steve Aoki, Paul van Dyk and Paul Oakenfold.

World.title: Week in Review: Tests and Pressures
World.content:
The lavish funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, complete with military honours and attended by senior Serbian and Bosnian Serb officials, drew condemnation from EU states and renewed questions about how deeply the glorification of wartime figures remains embedded in regional politics.

Experts told BIRN that the spectacle in Serbia reflected a state-sponsored politics of memory rather than Serbian society as a whole, while warning that Mladic’s funeral has become entangled with election campaigns and could further damage already strained regional relations.

Writing from Brussels, Gjeraqina Tuhina argued that this is also a test for the EU: after years of accommodating Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, Brussels must decide whether its opposition to war-criminal glorification will have consequences beyond strongly worded statements.

World.title: Concentration Camp to Hotel Catwalk: Montenegrin Fortress’s Makeover Puts History at Risk
World.content:
So the thought of a fashion show being staged on Mamula last month seems grotesque. What is even more worrying is how a place of suffering became a playground for luxury, with the survivors and their families witnessing the quiet obscuring of history.

Eighty years after the concentration camp was dismantled and the Italians fled, an Egyptian investor opened the renovated Mamula fort as a luxury hotel. Under the name Mamula Island Hotel, it was unveiled in 2023 and functioned briefly under this name before the Banyan Group took over and rebranded it as Mamula Island by Banyan Tree, a makeover that went into effect for the 2026 summer season.

When the news about the Montenegrin government decision to lease out the former concentration camp to be turned into a luxury hotel was first announced a decade ago, it caused an outcry, with many former prisoners speaking out against it. Many in the Montenegrin public viewed the commercialisation of this historically significant site of suffering as the loss of an important part of Montenegrin’s history.

The decision triggered international outrage as well, prompting major media outlets to write about the controversy. The government even received a letter from the then UN Secretary general Boutros Boutros-Ghali who expressed concern over the endeavour.

However, the government stood by its decision, citing that they had only two options: either let the fort and the island be abandoned to decay or find an investor who would restore it and open it for visitors. The authorities were very vocal in reassuring the public that the island’s history would be preserved and would become a crucial part of the new development.

Which it was. Sort of.

Mamula Island by Banyan Tree has an accompanying memorial gallery named Historical-Memorial Gallery Mamula, where the details of the island’s dark past along with personal artefact, testimonials and the names of prisoners are laid out on display.

For the fashion show, the invited public came, some of them even visited the memorial gallery. They posted photos, they were or tried to be respectful and then they went on to see the show, ate and slept in the soft beds of their hotel rooms, former prisoners’ holding cells where inmates slept on the hard limestone floors or improvised bunk beds, squeezed in with several dozen other people.

Supporters of the hotel project claim the site needed a curator and that history will not be erased by the renovation or the change in the function of the fortress, and that letting the fortress decay was also a form of erasure.

This last argument is true. Leaving Mamula fortress exposed to the elements and cause it to decay into ruin. But preserving a building does not necessarily preserve memory authentically.

The walls of the fortress hold the truth – bodies crammed against one another, straw mattresses on wooden boards, a gasoline barrel used as a toilet. Luxury hotel rooms do not preserve that memory.

New lives for old buildings?

World.title: Student-Led Movement Launches Election Challenge to Serbian Government
World.content:
Hundreds gathered in Serbia’s second city Novi Sad on Thursday evening for the first pre-election rally held by the student opposition movement ahead of early parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

Their electoral slate – called Student List – Students are Winning – will include 250 candidates chosen by students involved in the long-running protest movement triggered by the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster.

The student movement has become the strongest opposition force in Serbia, and the decision to participate in the elections represents its first direct entry into electoral politics. It hopes to defeat the Serbian Progressive Party led by Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power since 2012.

World.title: This Dalmatian Island is Heavily Visited, But Few Spend the Night There…
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – There’s a beautiful Dalmatian island that attracts around 150,000 visitors each summer, but only 40 or so of them opt to actually spend the night there.

Gorgeous Biševo itself had only 44 registered tourists in 2025, while more than 150,000 people visited the famous Blue Cave. Putni kofer writes that at first glance, Biševo in the middle of summer is anything but a deserted island. Boats full of day-trippers arrive all day long, people wait to board the small boats that transport thousands towards the world-famous Blue Cave. According to currently available data, during the summer, over 150,000 tourists visit the cave, and one of the most famous natural attractions on the Adriatic brings a huge number of people to this small open-sea island every year.

However, most of them board the boat again after visiting the Blue Cave and leave, heading off elsewhere. Few stay to explore the rest of the island. During the whole of 2025, according to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, only 44 people decided to actually spend the night on Biševo.

a contrast unlike any other on the adriatic coast

Day-trippers arrive on Biševo from nearby Komiža, but also from Split, Hvar and the surrounding islands, as well as numerous coastal tourist destinations. The visit to the Blue Cave itself lasts less than half an hour, but on the island it is also possible to visit the Visitor Centre inland, the old military tunnels, and to swim on beautiful beaches such as the one in the place of Porat. It is a real shame to reduce a trip to Biševo only to a visit to the cave. But most people visit it that way, which is confirmed by both statistics and our experience: when we continued exploring the island after viewing the most famous attraction, we met perhaps twenty people during the whole day.

This contrast between the number of visitors and those who stay on the island at least a little longer is unique in Croatia. It is not only a matter of overnight stays: after all, only about thirty beds are registered on Biševo. The island is ideal for a full-day excursion, swimming, getting to know the heritage, which many skip because they concentrate only on the famous cave. This is also confirmed by a study by the Institute for Tourism. Their research showed that only 8.3 percent of guests stay eight hours or longer on the island, and almost half said they came exclusively because of the Blue Cave.

The Blue Cave in Balun bay owes its name to the reflection of the sun’s rays which around noon, in calm seas, penetrate through an underwater opening into the cave, reflecting off the white bottom and creating the blue colour. It is 24 metres long and about 12 metres wide, and its modest depth of 3 to 20 metres and typical karst shape make it an ideal habitat for a diverse ecosystem, while divers discover its mysterious world through hidden underwater cracks. It is said that it is best to visit it between 11:00 and 14:00 on a sunny day.

no shop, no cash machine, and no maritime connections…

The island of Biševo is the most remote inhabited Croatian island. It stands proudly in the middle of the open sea, isolated and a little wild, and a holiday on it is definitely not for everyone. Neither ferries nor catamarans sail to it, and it is connected to neighbouring Vis by the only boat line, Sv. Salvestar, the so-called “pruga”, which departs from Komiža. It spans only 5.8 square kilometres, in the middle of the last century about 300 inhabitants lived on it, and today only about ten remain. Biševo was once known as the home of the Mediterranean monk seal, but that animal disappeared from the island long ago. Besides the most famous Blue Cave, on the southern side of the island, in Trešjavac bay, there is also the beautiful Medvidina Cave. The island also has its own distinctive wine: Biševo plavac.

the home of caves, military tunnels and stunning beaches

In the very centre of the island a few years ago the Visitor Centre was opened, which you can reach from Mezoporat harbour by electric cart. The Centre is really worth visiting; it presents the wonderful world of underwater, terrestrial and geological phenomena, and also showcases the rich past of the island. The surroundings are also interesting: an old village with a beautiful church that was probably once full of life. The military tunnels are located at the other end of the island, on Cape Gatula, and if you are not up for walking, you can specially arrange transport by electric vehicles to them.

A walk that is definitely worth it is the one from the Visitor Centre to the place of Porat, where the regular boat line docks and can take you directly back to Komiža from there. Porat beach is, according to many, one of the most beautiful on the Adriatic. Soft sand, enough shade, a café for refreshment… Although there are day-trippers, the crowds are practically never too big. This island is isolated and certainly not for everyone, but it is a real glimpse of genuine Dalmatian island life that is rapidly being sent to the history books on other islands.

World.title: Meet the Highest Fortress of the Dubrovnik Republic… That Isn’t Even in Dubrovnik
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – The highest fortress of the former Dubrovnik Republic (Ragusa) isn’t even located within the city. It’s a very unusual, irregular fortification that once played a vitally important defensive role.

Nestled against the rock sits one of the most monumental fortification systems in the south of Croatia, and it was once an important cog in the defence of the powerful Republic of Dubrovnik. Putni kofer writes that anyone who looks at Dubrovnik clearly sees that this city is teeming with incredible history. Even without any prior knowledge, the gaze will stop on the monumental walls, fortresses, palaces… Today one of the most beautiful cities on the Mediterranean, it was once a powerful force. The Dubrovnik Republic was small in a territorial sense, but politically, commercially and diplomatically, it was extremely influential.

Lovrijenac, Revelin, Minčeta, Bokar and St. John are fortresses that line up in the defensive ring of the city or next to it, but none of these fortresses was the largest defensive fortification of the powerful republic. It is located about forty kilometres from the city, among the hills of Konavle. Sokol Grad is, according to official sources, the largest single fortress from the time of the Republic of Dubrovnik.

sokol grad towers on a natural 25-metre rock

Sokol Grad was built above the small place of Dunave, on a natural rock that rises more than 25 metres above the surrounding terrain. Its walls so faithfully follow the shape of the rock and blend in colour with the karst that from a distance the fortress looks almost like its extension. The position was not chosen for beauty, although the view today is spectacular. From this point the Konavle field and an important road that led from the hinterland towards Dubrovnik were monitored, and official sources state that from Sokol one of the most complete views of the entire Konavle opens up.

a hillfort existed there all the way back to prehistoric times

The fortress did not originate in the time of the Dubrovnik Dubrovnik. Traces have been found in this area that point to much older fortification of the position, from a prehistoric hillfort through ancient and late antique fortifications. It is mentioned in written documents at the end of the 14th century, and at the beginning of the 15th century its Dubrovnik story begins. The people of Dubrovnik briefly entered the fortress in 1420, and from 1423 it came under their control again and remained part of their defensive system for the next two and a half centuries. Its task was clear: to protect Konavle from enemies who could arrive from the hinterland. Precisely for this reason the Republic of Dubrovnik did not spare on its maintenance. During the 15th century the walls were repaired, expanded and strengthened, and construction works continued in the 16th and 17th centuries. Sokol also protected an area of vital economic importance, including the area of the river Ljuta and the mills that participated in the supply of Dubrovnik.

a three-level fortress

Sokol Grad has an irregular shape and that is no coincidence. The ramparts follow the morphology of the rock, and the entire fortification is organised on three levels. The lowest part, called Kamen (Stone), was arranged as a space into which the surrounding population could take shelter in case of danger. In the outer bailey were the fortified main entrance, kitchen, food stores, rooms for soldiers and crossbowmen, a guard tower and sanitary facilities.

The safest part was at the very top. In the citadel there was a large cistern, stores of food and weapons, grain supplies, the castellan’s residence, a church, a blacksmith’s workshop and a furnace. The system for sheltering the population was precisely determined: children under the age of ten were to be housed in the upper fortress in case of danger, while women and those unfit for combat were housed in the outer bailey.

it survived the devastating 1667 earthquake

Sokol survived the great earthquake of 1667, but after 1672 it is no longer mentioned in the Dubrovnik archival records, so it is considered that it was abandoned at that time. For centuries it decayed, and the surrounding population used its stone as building material. The Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities took it over in 1966, after which decades of conservation and restoration followed. Intensive works lasted from 2007 to 2013, when Sokol Grad was reopened to visitors. Today, instead of guards on its walls, there are day-trippers, and the former military position has become one of the best viewpoints in Konavle. Sokol Grad is open to visitors, and in the current period the official website lists opening hours from 08:00 to 19:00; tickets can also be purchased online and the price is 10 euros for adults and 5 euros for children.

World.title: Croatia is the Only EU Country Without a Waste Incinerator
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – After the hazardous waste scandal in Lika comes the news that Croatia is actually the only EU country without a proper waste incinerator.

Croatia is facing an enormous waste management problem with nowhere left to dispose of it, and at the same time it is the only EU Member State without a single waste incinerator. Index reports that all across the rest of Europe, more than 500 of them are currently operating. Switzerland, Norway, the UK and others also have numerous incinerators. After the scandal involving improperly disposed waste in Gospić, the question of building energy plants, facilities for the thermal treatment of waste, is being raised once again.

After the horrific case in Gospić, it seems the question is no longer whether Croatia can avoid thermal treatment of waste, but where it will even carry it out. Landfills have limited capacity, and European rules require less and less landfilling of waste that can be treated differently.

croatian ministers are confused

Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar points out that Croatian companies are building such facilities across Europe. “If all EU Member States have them, only Malta does not but is building them, and if there are 500 of them, is Croatia the smartest or is there some other issue here? When it comes to building incinerators, Croatian companies today are building them across Europe, in Iceland, Belgium, Scotland and Germany. If we can do that for the whole world, I think we should also do it here,” said Šušnjar, as reported by N1.

Energy plants burn waste and use the resulting energy to produce electricity and heating. They are not a replacement for recycling, but a solution for the remaining part of the waste. Their construction in Croatia has for years been opposed by part of the public due to concerns about emissions, impacts on health and the environment, and the disposal of residues after incineration.

Minister of Environmental Protection Marija Vučković believes that the set waste management targets cannot be achieved without energy plants. “Would I accept an energy plant in my neighbourhood? If the environmental impact assessment has shown that it is acceptable, if the conditions from the permits are regularly controlled and, of course, if the supervision system is fully functional, there is no reason not to have an energy plant in one’s neighbourhood,” said Vučković.

is the system the problem?

Nikola Grmoja from Most sees the problem in the system, not in the disposal model itself. “If we do not have a control system, if hazardous waste could be imported into Croatia without anyone noticing or doing anything about it, how will we know what is being burned there, where it is being brought from, what the by-product is and where that by-product ends up?” asks Grmoja. He believes this is a question of a non-functioning system and corrupt people in key positions. “If we talk about the model, I am not sure how incinerators fit into all the goals that the European Commission has set for us regarding waste separation,” he said.

the zagreb project and interest from other cities

Interest in building energy plants has been shown by Šibenik, Osijek and Rijeka, and Zagreb is also considering it. A feasibility projection for Zagreb was made back in 2024 and showed that such facilities pay off. President of the Zagreb City Assembly Matej Mišić confirmed the position of the city SDP to N1. “The city SDP continues to advocate the construction of an energy plant that would burn refuse-derived fuel and thereby generate thermal energy. In fact, the City Assembly already in 2024 adopted a conclusion launching the preparation of documentation for the construction of an energy plant,” said Mišić. Although the project was started, it has not been realised. If energy plants become part of the solution for waste in Croatia, the open question remains whether the need for waste disposal will ultimately outweigh the resistance to such facilities.
