World.title: Peñafrancia traslacion in Naga City peaceful amid tight security
World.content:
Thousands of devotees join the annual Traslacion procession of Our Lady of Peñafrancia in Naga City on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. The religious event remained peaceful and orderly amid heightened security measures, with police personnel and partner agencies deployed along the procession route. (Photo courtesy of Archdiocese of Caceres)

LEGAZPI CITY — The annual Traslacion procession of Our Lady of Peñafrancia in Naga City remained peaceful and orderly on Friday (Sept. 11), with 820,000 devotees joining the religious event.

Heightened security measures included the deployment of police personnel along the procession route, with officers using placards, megaphones and Oplan Bandillo to remind devotees to secure their belongings.

CCTV cameras, drones and Starlink devices were also used to monitor the crowd and improve communication among police units.

Article continues after this 

READ: Thousands join Peñafrancia Traslacion in Naga City

Police Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio, Bicol police director, personally monitored security operations in strategic areas and reminded police personnel to remain alert, courteous and responsive to devotees.

“The peaceful and orderly conduct of the Traslacion is a shared accomplishment, with the cooperation of devotees, police, local government units, government agencies, volunteers and force multipliers,” Silvio said.

He also commended police personnel and partner agencies for their professionalism and dedication, adding that security operations would continue until the end of the Peñafrancia Festival. INQ

World.title: 2 wounded in Basilan drive-by shooting
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

LAMITAN CITY, Basilan — An intended target was shot while another man was hit by a stray bullet Friday night when gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire, police said.

Efren Salahuddin Custodio, a resident of Barangay Maganda, was hit in the leg at around 7:20 p.m. in Sitio Riverside, Barangay Matibay.

The intended target, Halid Dompol Mujanil, 32, a businessman and resident of Barangay Matibay, was shot in the stomach, according to Police Lt. Col. Janz Vladimir Hilarion, chief of the Lamitan City Police Station.

Article continues after this 

READ: Martin Romualdez transferred to PGH for medical examination

Police said two unidentified suspects riding a Yamaha Aerox motorcycle arrived at the area and opened fire at Mujanil. Custodio, who happened to be passing through the area, was hit by stray gunfire.

The suspects fled toward an unknown direction after the shooting.

Responding police officers led by Hilarion brought the two victims to the nearest hospital for treatment.

Police launched hot pursuit and dragnet operations in coordination with neighboring law enforcement units to locate the suspects. Scene of the Crime Operatives also processed the shooting scene for evidence.

Article continues after this 

Hilarion said investigators were still determining the motive and had not ruled out the possibility that the shooting was politically motivated.

“This is just an isolated incident, and we are still verifying if this is an election-related incident. We are still conducting a validation for that,” Hilarion said.

Article continues after this 

He assured residents that security forces were stepping up efforts to maintain peace and order, particularly with the elections approaching.

“The citizens of Lamitan have nothing to worry about because we in the PNP and AFP are doubling our efforts to ensure a safe and secure election here in Lamitan City. We do this not only for the elections, but as part of our daily commitment to prevent this kind of incident in Lamitan,” he said.

World.title: Overcast skies, rains expected in Luzon on Saturday — Pagasa
World.content:
(Satellite image from Pagasa)

MANILA, Philippines — Gloomy skies with rains may affect some areas in Luzon due to the trough of the low-pressure area (LPA) off Southwestern Luzon and the southwest monsoon, or habagat, the state weather bureau said.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) reported in the 5 a.m. weather advisory that the extension of the LPA outside the Philippine area of responsibility may bring scattered rains over Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Isabela, Quirino, and Nueva Vizcaya.

READ: Rains to persist over Luzon; fair weather in Visayas, Mindanao

Article continues after this 

As of 2 a.m., the LPA was located 970 kilometers west of Southwestern Luzon. It has a high chance of developing into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours.

“Gayunpaman, hindi naman natin inaasahan yung pagpasok na ito sa ating Philippine Area of Responsibility. Wala din naman itong direct effects sa anumang parte ng ating bansa,” Pagasa weather specialist Veronica Torres said.

(“However, we did not expect it to enter our Philippine Area of Responsibility. It also has no direct effects on any part of the country,”)

Meanwhile, Metro Manila, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, and Bicol Region may experience cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the continued effects of the southwest monsoon.

“Sa nalalabing bahagi ng Cagayan Valley, aasahan nga natin yung mas magandang panahon, partly cloudy to cloudy skies. Gayon pa man, may mga tsansa ng mga localized thunderstorms, lalo na tuwing hapon at gabi yung kailangan nating bantayan,” she added.

(“For the rest of Cagayan Valley, we can expect better weather, with skies ranging from partly cloudy to cloudy. However, there is a chance of localized thunderstorms—particularly in the afternoon and evening that we need to watch out for.”) /mr

World.title: Gatchalian seeks localized class suspensions amid widespread disruptions
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian. FILE PHOTO / Senate

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday sought to push for more localized learning measures amid prolonged in-person class suspensions due to recent weather disturbances.

Gatchalian raised concern over possible learning loss among students because of repeated widespread face-to-face class disruptions.

READ: WALANG PASOK: Class suspensions on Friday, Sept. 11 amid habagat rains

Article continues after this 

“This is concerning. While we know that class suspensions seek to ensure the safety of learners and teachers, widespread disruption to classes can aggravate learning loss,” he expressed in a statement.

Through Senate Bill No. 53, also known as the 21st Century School Boards, the senator seeks to make the local school board establish and decide on “timely, organized, and localized interventions” in delivering basic education amid calamities and other emergencies.

He noted that for this month, at least 20 weekdays of in-person classes in several areas across the country were disrupted due to the severe effects of the southwest monsoon, or habagat and recent tropical cyclones.

Even areas unaffected by inclement weather were affected because of the system-wide implementation of suspensions, according to him.

“Bagama’t tinitiyak natin ang kapakanan ng ating mga mag-aaral tuwing may kalamidad, kailangan din nating tiyaking magpapatuloy ang edukasyon sa mga ligtas na lugar,” he said.

Article continues after this 

(“While we ensure the welfare of our students during calamities, we must also ensure that education continues in safe locations.”)

Within the last two years, an average of 30 to 50 class days out of the 180-day school calendar suffered because of suspensions, he cited in a study by the Second Congressional Commission on Education. /mr

World.title: Baguio wins gold in Asean Smoke-Free Awards
World.content:
Baguio City has been named a Gold Award recipient in the 2nd Asean Smoke-Free Awards, recognizing its efforts to implement and enforce smoke-free policies that protect residents and visitors from tobacco smoke. The award was presented on Sept. 10 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Maureen Matayew)

BAGUIO CITY — This city has been named the Gold Award recipient in the second Asean Smoke-Free Awards, recognizing its efforts to implement and enforce smoke-free policies to protect residents and visitors from tobacco smoke.

The award was presented on Sept. 10 during the opening ceremony of the Asean Health Ministers Meeting in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The awards are led by the government of Lao PDR under Asean Health Cluster 1, in cooperation with the Southeast Asia Tobacco Control Alliance (Seatca) and the Asean Secretariat.

READ: Baguio, Benguet landslide death toll rises to 13

Article continues after this 

Seatca said Baguio received the Gold Award following a rigorous screening process. The awards recognize sub-national governments for achievements in developing and implementing smoke-free policies and are aligned with the Asean Post-2015 Health Development Agenda and the 2017 Asean Declaration on Culture of Prevention.

George Town in Penang, Malaysia received the Silver Award, while five local governments from Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines and Thailand received Bronze awards. Singapore was given a special recognition for its consistent and outstanding smoke-free enforcement.

Seaca Executive Director Dr. Ulysses Dorotheo said the awardees demonstrated that strict and firmly enforced smoke-free policies can be implemented at the local level. He said local governments could serve as examples for other governments in Southeast Asia by placing public health first and resisting challenges from the tobacco industry.

The recognition marks the second time a Philippine city has received the top Asean Smoke-Free Award. Iloilo City won the inaugural Gold Award in 2024 after obtaining the highest evaluation score. This year, Baguio was the Philippine Gold awardee, while Pasig City received a Bronze Award.—Maureen Matayew/ contributor /mr

World.title: Almaty Museum of Arts Opens Exhibition Tracing Seven Decades of Kazakh Sculpture
World.content:
ASTANA – The Almaty Museum of Arts has opened a major exhibition exploring the development of Kazakh sculpture over seven decades.

The exhibition, titled “Müsinder: Sculpture in Kazakhstan from the 1950s to the Present Day,” opened on Sept. 8 in the museum’s Saryarka Hall and brings together more than 50 works by several generations of Kazakh artists, reported the museum’s press office. The project is curated by art historian Aliya Tiesenhausen and is part of the museum’s first-anniversary programme.

Among the artists represented are Kha­kimzhan Nauryzbayev, Isaac Itkind, Erkin Mergenov, Madina Zholdybek, Rysbek Akhmetov, Moldaqul Narymbetov, Yerbossyn Meldibekov and Aruzhan Zhumabek.

Rather than presenting a strictly chronological history, the exhibition examines how the language of sculpture has changed from the Soviet period to contemporary Kazakhstan. The works explore themes including the human body, memory, family, identity and social change.

The title refers to the Kazakh word “musin,” which can mean both “sculpture” and “human figure.” The human body therefore becomes a central element of the exhibition, allowing artists from different periods to reflect on society and personal experience.

The exhibition is divided into four thematic sections. One of them, “Game of Opposites?”, focuses on sculpture from the late 1950s through the early 1990s and examines the tension between officially accepted artistic practices and more individual approaches developed by artists in their studios. Works by Isaac Itkind and Erkin Mergenov demonstrate the emergence of more personal forms of sculptural expression during the Soviet period.

Later sections turn to contemporary approaches to the human body and its relationship with politics, culture, gender and personal experience. The exhibition thus connects works created under very different historical circumstances, highlighting changes in artistic materials, techniques and interpretations of the human figure.

According to curator Aliya Tiesenhausen, the exhibition presents sculpture as a “living artistic process” rather than simply a historical record. Soviet-era academic works are placed in dialogue with contemporary pieces to show how both artistic language and perceptions of sculpture have evolved.

“The history of sculpture is at the same time a history of society, memory, and the human being,” said Tiesenhausen.

The exhibition will run from Sept. 8 through May 2027. An illustrated catalogue accompanying the exhibition will be published in Kazakh, Russian and English, featuring scholarly texts by Tiesenhausen and art historians Valeria Ibrayeva and Alexandra Tsai.

The exhibition is also part of the Almaty Museum of Arts’ broader effort to study and present Kazakhstan’s artistic heritage. The museum, which opened in September 2025, was established as a major platform for Kazakh, Central Asian and international contemporary art.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, the museum’s artistic director Meruert Kaliyeva described its mission as combining the study and preservation of regional art with greater public access to international contemporary art. The museum was featured in an episode of The Astana Times exploring Almaty’s major cultural landmarks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Out Priorities Ahead of BRICS Summit in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI – Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is expected to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12-13, with Kazakhstan seeking to advance cooperation in energy, critical minerals, transport connectivity and global water security.

India is hosting the summit under the theme Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. BRICS is a group of eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. They include Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, representing almost half of the world’s population and 40% of the global GDP.

Priorities of Kazakhstan, which joined the group as a partner country in 2025, were presented by Kazakh Ambassador to India Azamat Eskarayev at the BRICS Energy Partnerships for Progress and Prosperity diplomatic dialogue in New Delhi on Sept. 3.

Energy security was among the central topics of the meeting. Participants discussed traditional and renewable energy, new technologies, infrastructure, investment and critical minerals. Particular attention was given to resilient supply chains and emerging energy and transport corridors.

For Kazakhstan, the agenda closely aligns with its efforts to strengthen its role in Eurasian transport and energy connectivity. Eskarayev emphasized the country’s potential in traditional energy, renewable energy and critical minerals.

The discussion was not focused on a single project or agreement but on areas Kazakhstan intends to promote through the BRICS partnership.

Water initiative adds another dimension

Separately, Yeskarayev highlighted Tokayev’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

The initiative calls for stronger international coordination on water resources and seeks to bring greater political attention to global water security. Kazakhstan has previously presented the proposal in other international forums, including the United Nations.

According to Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan (KazISS), the initiative could gain practical value if it is accompanied by cooperation on water technologies and management.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could develop pilot projects for arid regions involving satellite monitoring of water resources, digital irrigation management, wastewater reuse and specialist training.

“Kazakhstan could offer its territory for pilot projects involving Indian, Chinese and Emirati companies. Then the idea of an international water organization will gain a practical dimension, and potential partners will see specific facilities, technology needs and a possible financing model,” Kurmashev told The Astana Times.

From critical minerals to concrete projects

Kurmashev noted that in critical minerals, Kazakhstan should promote projects focused on domestic processing, component manufacturing and modern exploration technologies, Kurmashev said.

He emphasized that projects should have a clearly defined resource base, site, energy and water requirements, technology partner, potential buyer and financing model. The same approach should apply to transport and digital projects.

“Tokayev’s participation in the summit could help present Kazakhstan as an independent Eurasian participant with a practical agenda covering transport, energy, water and food security and technology,” Kurmashev said.

“The Indian context is also important. India’s chairmanship makes South Asia, sustainable supply chains and technological cooperation issues more prominent,” he added.

However, he noted that the value of Kazakhstan’s participation should ultimately be measured by what follows the summit.

“Political presence should be assessed by the continuation: whether there are bilateral agreements, responsible operators and projects with certain deadlines after the summit,” Kurmashev said.

BRICS as a tool for economic diversification

For Kazakhstan, BRICS can provide an additional platform for expanding economic ties beyond its traditional partners, particularly with major economies in Asia, the Middle East, Africa and South America.

The grouping was established in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have since joined as members.

Kazakhstan is not a BRICS member but became one of the group’s partner countries in 2025. It participated in the 2025 BRICS Summit in Brazil as a partner country.

According to Kurmashev, the partner-country format gives Kazakhstan flexibility to advance its interests without making BRICS an exclusive foreign policy platform.

“Kazakhstan has a dense network of bilateral and multilateral channels with Russia and China. These are the Eurasian Economic Union and the the Commonwealth of Independent States with Russia, the the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, the Central Asia-China format and regular high-level meetings,” Kurmashev said.

“Therefore, the additional value of BRICS lies primarily in reaching a wider audience. On the same platform, Kazakhstan gets access to the leadership and business circles of India, Brazil, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Egypt and other countries with which the intensity of economic contacts still varies,” he said.

Kurmashev emphasized that BRICS membership or partnership does not automatically increase trade. The grouping is not a customs union and does not create a common market or uniform tariffs.

Its practical value lies in bringing governments, companies and development institutions closer together, helping them identify partners and address barriers.

For Kazakhstan, the success of economic diversification should therefore be measured not simply by total trade with BRICS countries, but by increased trade with countries such as India, Brazil, Indonesia, the UAE, Egypt and South Africa, the emergence of new export categories and a broader investor base.

Kurmashev suggested that government agencies along with QazTrade, a state-owned agency aimed at promoting trade, develop individual country strategies, organize trade missions and support companies through the contracting process.

Can BRICS strengthen transport links with India?

Transport connectivity is another area where Kazakhstan sees potential for BRICS cooperation, although the grouping itself does not manage transport corridors.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route links Kazakhstan through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye with European markets. For connections with India, the International North-South Transport Corridor, Iranian ports such as Chabahar, and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway offer potential links.

According to Kurmashev, a possible long-term route could connect India, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, with onward access through the Kazakh ports of Aktau and Kuryk to the Trans-Caspian route.

However, he noted that political declarations alone would not make such a route commercially viable. Stable cargo volumes would be needed to support regular container trains and shipping services, reduce empty runs and distribute fixed costs.

“At the BRICS Summit, Kazakhstan could propose preparing a pilot container shipment involving Indian, Iranian, Turkmen and Kazakh operators. Such a project could help identify actual transit times, tariffs and bottlenecks at each stage of the route,” he said.

At the same time, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye remain essential to the Trans-Caspian route, meaning key decisions on its operation would need to be coordinated outside the BRICS framework.

“Payments, insurance, sanctions risks around Iran and the number of transshipment points will remain important constraints. Therefore, BRICS can bring together interested parties, but the commercial viability of the route must ultimately be confirmed by carriers and shippers,” Kurmashev said.

World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s economic and financial development, sovereign wealth strategy and global ambitions, alongside Elena Rybakina’s historic rise to world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen

Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1. Elena Rybakina took the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis, reported The New York Times on Sept. 9.

“It’s a great achievement, and I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career,” Rybakina said in a news conference, when asked about the milestone.

Kazakhstan’s AIFC says other countries are seeking to replicate its model

Kazakhstan’s financial hub says its model is attracting interest abroad as competition between financial centres intensifies, while limited market liquidity remains a key challenge, reported Euronews on Sept. 9.

For two days, Astana Finance Days 2026 brought together representatives of global financial institutions that collectively manage more than $26 trillion in assets, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position in the global competition for capital.

How Kazakhstan’s economic reforms have turned the tenge into the best-performing currency in Europe and Asia

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 7 examining the tenge’s strong performance in 2026 and highlights Kazakhstan’s accelerating economic transformation, driven by foreign investment, diversification, digitalization, infrastructure development, and the expansion of its financial and technology sectors.

“The Kazakhstani tenge has become the best-performing currency in Asia and Europe in 2026, according to the Financial Times. Since the beginning of the year, it has appreciated by nearly 10% against the US dollar, outperforming all other currencies worldwide except for several currencies of Latin American and African countries. This performance has been underpinned by economic growth driven by the transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic model. The country is rapidly evolving from a commodity-based economy into a financial and technology hub for Central Asia, amid growing inflows of foreign capital,” reads the article.

Erlan Karin’s appointment links reform and national identity

The Times of Central Asia published an article on Sept. 1 about Erlan Karin’s appointment as Vice President of Kazakhstan.

“When President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put forward Erlan Karin for vice president on Aug. 31, he called him ‘a genuine patriot’ with long experience in government. He also stressed Karin’s part in implementing major reforms, his grasp of long-term state strategy and his understanding of Kazakhstan’s prospects for socioeconomic development.

Karin has spent seven years in senior posts under Tokayev. He also has a sustained interest in a question that runs through the president’s agenda — how Kazakhstan can modernize while remaining connected to its own history and national identity,” reads the article.

From oil reserves to infrastructure: How Kazakhstan invests in future generations

EU Reporter released an article on Sept. 8 examining how Kazakhstan can transform part of its sovereign wealth from financial savings into long-term national capital by investing in infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other assets that can generate lasting economic and social benefits for future generations.

“Savings from the National Fund are already being utilized directly in the interests of future generations. Since 2024, Kazakhstan has operated the National Fund for Children program: every young citizen of Kazakhstan is annually allocated a portion of the fund’s investment income, and upon reaching 18 years of age, the accumulated funds can be used for education or housing improvement. This program has already entered the phase of practical asset utilization. Between February 2024 and Aug. 1, payouts were received by more than 338,000 young Kazakhstanis, totaling approximately $67.8 million. Meanwhile, the funds belonging to minors remain within the National Fund’s assets and continue to be invested until they reach adulthood,” reads the article.

Almaty and Astana set to retain Central Asia’s economic lead

Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia on Sept. 7.

“Almaty and Astana benefit from an economic scale unmatched elsewhere in Central Asia. Kazakhstan alone accounts for more than half of the region’s GDP and roughly two-thirds of its inward FDI stock, according to TCA’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That scale helps generate the fiscal resources needed to build and maintain the municipal infrastructure that supports business activity,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks to New Players and Products to Drive Next Phase of Digital Finance, NBK Governor Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built the core digital infrastructure for its financial sector and is now entering a new stage focused on developing new products, attracting new market participants and creating innovative business models, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in Almaty on Sept. 11.

Speaking at the opening of the third annual summit, Suleimenov said Kazakhstan’s financial sector has already reached a high level of digitalization, with more than 90% of payments made without cash and most basic banking and government services available through digital platforms.

The summit, held on Sept. 11, brings together regulators, financial institutions, technology companies and experts to discuss the future of financial markets, digital currencies, artificial intelligence, digital assets, cybersecurity and other areas of fintech.

Suleimenov said the National Bank’s approach has evolved from simply digitizing its own operations to actively encouraging innovation across the financial market.

“We decided to change the approach altogether – instead of being the one who is pushed, to become the one who pushes the market,” he said, describing the regulator’s role as creating a “push” for the market and encouraging participants to move faster.

Kazakhstan builds digital financial infrastructure

Kazakhstan has established a national digital financial infrastructure. It includes biometric identification, interbank payments, the digital tenge and mechanisms designed to protect citizens and businesses from financial fraud.

The infrastructure has been expanded through successive stages, with the digital tenge entering industrial use in 2023, the National Anti-Fraud Center launched in 2024 and new interbank and QR payment infrastructure introduced subsequently.

The digital tenge is gradually being integrated into government financial processes, including public procurement, budget planning and the management of state funds. Suleimenov said the National Bank, together with the government, intends to increase the volume of digital-tenge operations to 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion) over the next 12 months.

Suleimenov pointed to the interbank mobile payment system launched this year as one of the latest developments. The system includes transfers by phone number and a unified QR code. Since its launch on July 19, it has processed more than 20 million transactions worth around 400 billion tenge (US$888 million), according to the National Bank.

He described the high level of digitalization as a major achievement, noting that in many countries reaching 50–60% of non-cash turnover remains a challenge.

From infrastructure to products

The next challenge, Suleimenov said, is no longer primarily about building the technological “rails” of the financial system but about using them to create products that meet the needs of businesses and consumers.

During the opening plenary, moderator Vitaliy Volyanyuk, co-founder and CEO of Digital Business, asked Suleimenov to assess what the measures introduced by the NBK and other regulators had actually delivered and how Kazakhstan’s financial sector looks today.

Suleimenov described the sector as bank-centered but increasingly diverse, with the domestic financial system, the Astana International Financial Center and emerging digital-finance initiatives creating complementary opportunities.

“Briefly, the system is strong, highly capitalized and digitalized, and it has a huge future,” he said.

But Suleimenov stressed that infrastructure alone would not be enough.

“The second step is, of course, financial infrastructure, on which these solutions have to run. We are also creating that. But now, probably, the main step is creating products,” he said.

“We cannot and will not create the products ourselves,” he added, calling on banks, traditional financial institutions and new financial companies to work both together and in competition to develop new products and business models. The objective, he said, is to make access to financing, payments and cross-border transactions easier for both businesses and individuals.

Digital maturity remains uneven

The transformation, however, is not taking place at the same pace across the entire financial sector, Chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market Madina Abylkassymova said during the summit.

Volyanyuk also asked about the readiness of smaller banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions for digital and AI transformation, rather than focusing only on the largest banks with significant technological and financial resources.

Abylkassymova said the agency had assessed the digital readiness of 94 financial organizations this year, examining process digitalization, data quality, infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI use and employee competencies.

“Banks remain the leaders, with almost 75% already using artificial intelligence. However, a gap remains between banks and other parts of the financial sector, particularly insurance and microfinance,” she said, stressing that digital transformation is not simply about introducing technology.

“It is also about the competencies of employees,” Abylkassymova added, arguing that digital and AI tools need to be embedded into the actual processes of financial organizations.

According to her, the agency is now developing a strategy for large-scale digitalization and further AI adoption across the financial sector. It has identified 1,200 specific measures and prepared individual development plans for the 94 organizations assessed.

Kazakhstan looks to export financial services

Suleimenov identified exporting Kazakhstan’s financial industry as another strategic priority. This includes helping domestic financial companies enter foreign markets and attracting international players that can serve global customers through Kazakhstan’s jurisdiction and financial infrastructure.

He said the country has a strong domestic financial jurisdiction alongside the Astana International Financial Center, which he described as an additional driver of competition and investment.

The next stage, however, will depend on whether market participants can turn the established infrastructure and regulatory framework into products that can compete both domestically and internationally.

“We have a strong foundation, but now we need the market to become more active – with new products, partnerships and business models that will allow us to fully use these opportunities,” Suleimenov said.

The Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 brings together more than 120 speakers and experts. It focuses on the development of digital finance, including payments, digital assets, AI, cybersecurity, tokenization and anti-fraud technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights Middle Corridor Growth and Digitalization at Batumi Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan highlighted the rapid growth of the Middle Corridor and the need to accelerate its digitalization at the Georgian International Maritime Forum in Batumi on Sept. 7-8.

Kazakhstan Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) rose 22% in January-August, while East-West transit increased 55%.

Digitalization drives seamless transit

Speaking at the panel session From Seas to Corridors: The New Geography of Global Trade, Taizhanov stressed the importance of integrating maritime, rail and port infrastructure to make international supply chains more efficient and resilient, the ministry’s press service reported.

He also presented President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to develop a digital map of transport routes, providing an integrated view of transport infrastructure, logistics chains and cargo flows along international corridors.

The Middle Corridor currently has a capacity of 6 million tons, including 182,000 TEUs. Measures to streamline logistics have reduced cargo delivery times from 38 days to 13-17 days, with a target of 10-12 days from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Kazakhstan is also advancing the Digital Trade Corridor, which enables online cargo tracking and single-window contracting. Its Tez Customs module has reduced transit customs processing from eight hours to 30 minutes, the ministry told The Astana Times.

Infrastructure expansion

The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.
