World.title: TOYO identifies gas chemicals, fertilizers as key areas in Turkmenistan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. TOYO Engineering sees gas processing, gas chemicals, and fertilizer production as key areas for industrial cooperation with Turkmenistan.

The Japanese company made this statement in an exclusive interview in response to a request from Trend about which types of industrial projects in Turkmenistan best align with its current expertise.

"Areas most closely aligned with TOYO’s current expertise are natural-gas processing and gas chemicals, petrochemicals, and ammonia and urea fertilizer plants," the company said.

According to TOYO, plant modernization, major overhauls, and ongoing operation and maintenance support also represent strong areas for potential cooperation.

"TOYO has experience in Turkmenistan through the Kiyanly Polymer Plant, which includes gas-separation, ethylene, polypropylene and high-density polyethylene facilities," the company added.

In 2025, TOYO and its consortium partner were awarded the first phase of a major overhaul of the Kiyanly complex. The company said this experience, combined with its broader international track record in gas chemicals and fertilizers, provides a strong foundation for further cooperation with Turkmenistan.

"Power and GX-related infrastructure could also be considered where TOYO’s capabilities match the specific needs of the Turkmen side," TOYO added.

TOYO Engineering Corporation is one of Japan's leading engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies, founded in 1961 and positioning itself globally under the concept of "Engineering for Sustainable Growth of the Global Community." The company specializes in gas processing, petrochemicals, fertilizers, power infrastructure, hydrogen, carbon management, and other industrial projects, while also expanding digital engineering and sustainability-oriented solutions across its international operations.

Turkmenistan has become one of TOYO's longest-standing markets in Central Asia. In 2018, the company completed the Kiyanly Polymer Plant for Turkmengaz, delivering a gas separation unit, a 400,000-ton-per-year ethylene plant and an 80,000-ton-per-year polypropylene plant using its proprietary COREFLUX technology. Since 2025, TOYO has been carrying out a major overhaul of the Kiyanly complex together with Türkiye's Rönesans Endüstri Tesisleri, while in February 2026 the partners signed a second-phase cooperation memorandum with Turkmenhimiya. Earlier this year, TOYO President and CEO Eiji Hosoi described Turkmenistan as one of the company's main partners during talks with President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

World.title: IMF assesses Kyrgyzstan’s public sector wage system
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Government employee compensation in Kyrgyzstan accounts for around 9.5% of GDP, according to a technical assistance report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

According to the report, the Kyrgyz government is considering a significant adjustment to public sector wages in 2026. The IMF assessed wage levels, staffing needs and options for improving public compensation management as part of its technical assistance.

"About 9.5% of GDP is spent on compensation of government employees, which is above regional peers," the report said.

The IMF notes that approximately 7.4% of the working-age population is employed in general government. Meanwhile, data from the National Statistical Committee showed that employment in public administration accounted for about 3.9% of the working-age population in 2024. The difference reflects the broader coverage of the general government measure, which also includes sectors such as education and healthcare.

The report also noted an increase in doctors’ remuneration following healthcare sector reforms in 2024. According to the IMF’s assessment, doctors’ remuneration is now estimated at approximately 1.3–1.5 times that of administrative personnel.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) approved its new Strategic and Capital Framework (SCF) for 2026–2030, outlining key priorities for the Bank’s activities in Central Asia and other regions.

According to Huseyin Ozhan, EBRD Managing Director for Central Asia and Mongolia, the framework is focused on three main areas: accelerating the green transition, strengthening economic governance, and developing human capital while promoting equal opportunities.

He noted that these priorities serve as the main guidelines for the EBRD’s operations in Central Asia. The Bank also develops individual country strategies for each state in the region in close cooperation with national authorities, with a focus on strengthening private sector competitiveness, creating jobs, improving skills, promoting inclusion, and supporting digital transformation.

World.title: Turkish gold returns vary across investment horizons in 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Gold generated the highest monthly and annual real returns among major financial instruments tracked in Türkiye in August 2026, while its performance differed across investment periods.

This is according to data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).

"Maximum monthly real profit rate was realized in gold (ingot)," TÜİK said in its report on the rates of real profits created by means of financial investment.

According to TÜİK, gold ingots recorded the highest monthly real return in August, at 7.17% when adjusted by the domestic producer price index (D-PPI) and 7.93% by the consumer price index (CPI). Government domestic debt instruments (GDDI) followed with returns of 0.66% and 1.38%, respectively. The U.S. dollar and stock exchange instruments recorded negative monthly real returns under both inflation measures.

Gold also recorded the highest annual real returns, at 19.73% by D-PPI and 16.49% by CPI, exceeding GDDI returns of 4.21% and 1.39%, respectively. Trend calculations show that the difference between gold's annual real return and the euro's annual real return of -8.68% by D-PPI amounted to 28.4%age points, representing the widest gap between two instruments tracked in the report over a 12-month period.

Over a six-month period, gold recorded a lower real return performance, with a decrease of 19.35% by D-PPI and 18.01% by CPI. During the same period, deposit interest generated the highest semi-annual real returns among tracked instruments, at 1.19% by D-PPI and 2.87% by CPI.

Trend's calculations show that the difference between gold's six-month D-PPI-adjusted performance and its one-month return of 7.17% reflects significant changes in gold prices during the period, highlighting fluctuations in investment returns across different timeframes.

For reference, TÜİK's real profit report compares nominal returns on major financial instruments against inflation indicators to assess changes in investors' purchasing power, using both producer and consumer price indices as separate benchmarks.

World.title: Georgia’s manufacturing, construction show high output-to-employment ratios
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Manufacturing and construction accounted for a higher share of production value than their respective shares of the workforce in Georgia's business sector in the second quarter of 2026.

This was reported in data published by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

According to Geostat, manufacturing employed 11.3% of the business sector's workforce in the second quarter and accounted for 20.5% of total production value, while construction employed 7.6% of workers and generated 14.4% of production value. Trade employed 29.5% of the workforce and accounted for 18.0% of output, while transportation and storage employed 8.1% and generated 9.8% of output.

Trend's calculations, dividing each sector's production-value share by its employment share, show manufacturing's ratio at 1.8 and construction's at 1.9 — the highest among the sectors reported — compared with 0.61 for trade and 1.21 for transportation and storage. The ratios indicate that the shares of production value generated by manufacturing and construction were substantially higher than their respective shares of employment, while trade's production-value share was lower than its employment share.

"Information and communication also recorded a production-value share above its employment share, employing 6.4% of the workforce while accounting for 8.9% of production value, with a ratio of 1.39," Trend's calculations show.

For reference, total business sector production value in the second quarter of 2026 stood at 25.7 billion lari ($9.8 billion), according to Geostat. The comparison uses production value rather than turnover as a proxy for economic contribution, as turnover figures can be influenced by resale activity and gambling-related transactions. Currency conversions are based on the National Bank of Georgia's exchange rate of 1 lari to $0.3813 as of early August 2026.

World.title: Service Tasmania contact centre cuts will fuel digital divide, MP says
World.content:
A proposal to cut the operating hours of multiple Service Tasmania service centres by up to half has prompted concern for older residents.

The state government is proposing to reduce the opening hours of five Service Tasmania centres, due to a "reduction in foot traffic".

The changes would affect centres in the regional communities of Queenstown on the state's west coast; Oatlands and Campbell Town in the Midlands; and at Currie and Whitemark on the Bass Strait islands — all of which already operate at reduced office hours.

The earmarked Service Tasmania centres are in regional locations, such as Queenstown. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The government has said no jobs will be lost, with "existing Service Tasmania staff in those regions to contribute remotely".

Some residents 'really impacted', mayor says

Flinders Island mayor Rachel Summers, who previously worked in customer service for Service Tasmania, said the proposal was concerning — particularly in an isolated region such as hers.

"We have a number of older people, a number of people who aren't able to access reliable internet services, and they're going to be really impacted by this decision," Cr Summers said.

The Flinders Island Service Tasmania service centre at Whitemark, the only one on the Bass Strait island, currently operates two days a week.

Rachel Summers says some residents in her community would be negatively impacted by the changes. (ABC News: Lucie Cutting)

Under the proposed changes, its face-to-face operating hours would drop from 20 to 10 a week.

Cr Summers said additional restrictions on days and times would "further hamper" access, for a trip that is already a long distance for some residents.

She said while accessing services digitally could "absolutely work for some people", it would exclude others.

"Government talk on forms and information sheets can be quite difficult to understand," Cr Summers said.

"If you're trying to get help with filling in a form, sometimes you actually need to be there in front of the person to see what they're writing, where they're writing.

" If you're checking that something's been filled in completely and accurately, you can't do that over the phone. "

Whitemark is the main administrative centre on Flinders Island. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Cr Summers said she expected the proposed changes would be discussed by the council.

The proposal was also criticised by the state opposition, which said contact hours would be "difficult to restore" once hours were cut.

"It's not like there's another shop that's just 10 minutes down the road for people that live on Flinders Island or King Island, for example," Bass MP Jess Greene said.

"We know that we have a digital divide in Tasmania.

'We know that these service cuts will have a negative impact on regional and our island communities.

"We're asking Premier Rockliff to reconsider these cuts."

Under the proposal, the reduced weekly opening hours would see Oatlands go from 25 hours to 20 hours; Queenstown, 32.5 hours to 16 hours; Campbell Town, 25 hours to 16.5 hours; Whitemark, 20 hours to 10 hours; and Currie, 20 hours to 10 hours.

Usage behind decision, government says

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the centres in question had been chosen following analysis of two years of customer visitation data, which found demand was much lower than the hours currently offered.

Where are the cuts coming from in Tasmania's state budget? Treasurer Eric Abetz wants to find $1.47 billion in "efficiencies" in Tasmania's state budget. This is what's on the chopping block.

"The way people access government services has changed significantly over recent years," Mr Rockliff said.

"As these customer preferences continue to evolve, it is important that we regularly review how services are delivered.

"We know many Tasmanians still rely on in-person services and that's why these changes have been proposed based on current customers' usage."

Consultation on the proposed changes, including which times and days would best meet local needs, will open on Monday and run until October 2.

World.title: World-first trial finds floating wetlands can cut greenhouse gas emissions
World.content:
Researchers believe a floating garden of native plants on a wastewater lagoon in VIctoria's east could help tackle greenhouse gas emissions, after it cut the lagoon's emissions by about 30 per cent.

The floating wetland is part of a world-first study conducted by RMIT University, Westernport Water and the CSIRO on Phillip Island over two years.

The 330-square-metre platform, roughly the size of one-and-a-half tennis courts, was planted with native reeds and sedges, with their roots hanging into the wastewater below.

RMIT's Centre for Nature Positive Solutions research fellow Lukas Schuster said the plants' roots created habitat for microbes that could help break down organic matter and absorb nutrients and pollutants.

"Floating wetlands are, you can imagine, like buoyant platforms that basically have the wetland plants planted onto them and the roots are hanging down into the water," Dr Schuster said.

Lukas Schuster says the trial's scale was important in testing whether floating wetlands could work in a real-world wastewater treatment setting. (Supplied: RMIT)

"So they're made to clean the water basically."

Researchers found the floating wetland reduced carbon dioxide emissions by up to 36 per cent, methane by up to 66 per cent and nitrogen by 18 per cent compared with a control lagoon without a wetland.

Dr Schuster said wastewater treatment was a significant source of emissions globally.

"On a global scale, they produce roughly 700 million tonnes of greenhouse gases every year," he said.

The world-first trial by RMIT University, Westernport Water and CSIRO has found a floating wetland cuts emissions from a wastewater lagoon by about 30 per cent on average. (Supplied: RMIT)

"Now we think about Victoria alone, for example, that is roughly one million tonnes of greenhouse gases every year.

"And so reducing those emissions is very tricky, but it's a very important step that we show basically that we can reduce emissions in open lagoons."'

The lagoon contained about 14 million litres of wastewater, with emissions monitored continuously over two years using solar-powered sensors.

Lukas Schuster says floating wetlands are like "buoyant platforms", with roots hanging down into the lagoons. (Supplied: RMIT)

Years of research

Dr Schuster said the trial's scale was important in testing whether floating wetlands could work in a real-world wastewater treatment setting.

"We were basically measuring the greenhouse gas emissions continuously; we were there every month deploying sensors and measuring the emissions continuously across the two years," he said.

Researchers say the technology could be useful because floating wetlands could potentially be retrofitted into existing lagoons without major infrastructure changes.

The floating wetlands hold a number of plants that assist in cutting greenhouse gas emissions from the lagoons. (Supplied: RMIT)

Dr Schuster said water companies had already expressed interest in further trials.

"It's also not only emission reduction, but also pollutant removal," he said.

"We're talking about perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) removal or other pollutants in the wastewater and also maybe provide habitat for biodiversity."

Dams to be trialled next

Researchers are now trialling similar floating wetlands in farm dams across the Bass Coast, investigating their potential to improve water quality, biodiversity and emissions.

An aerial view of a floating wetland in a Bass Coast farm dam as part of another ongoing trial, where researchers are exploring the potential benefits. (Supplied: RMIT)

Dr Schuster said future research would also look at making the floating platforms more sustainable, including through recycled or plant-based materials.

"It will also be super interesting to see whether we can make them a bit more sustainable," he said.

"For example, like with recycled materials or plant-based materials rather than having actually plastic-based baskets, for the floating wetland."

Benefits for farmers

Kernot farmer Camilla Graves has floating wetlands in two of her 26 farm dams as part of the trial.

"Dams are essential, and one thing we have been concerned about is actually the quality of the water in our dams," Ms Graves said.

She said the floating wetlands also provide protection to ducks, which use dams for habitat, from predators.

Camilla Graves has two dams that are being used to test floating wetlands. (Supplied: RMIT)

"The floating wetlands have actually provided an opportunity for them to take some shelter where the foxes can't get to them because the floating wetland literally is in the middle of the dam," Ms Graves said.

She said people who were not from regional Victoria may not realise how dependent nearby agricultural communities are on water collected and stored on farms.

"Water quality is really prime to agriculture," Ms Graves said.

She said the floating wetlands could be easily adopted by other farmers.

"Its simplicity is amazing; this concept can definitely be rolled out Australia-wide to farmers that are interested in giving it a go," Ms Grave said.

World.title: Live: Finals heavyweights clash, NRL backs bunker after Bennett call out
World.content:
— reporting by AAP

The NRL has backed its bunker over two contentious calls in South Sydney's finals exit, after Wayne Bennett unloaded on the game's video review system.

An irate Bennett declared on Friday night that "the quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I'll be", questioning who was actually refereeing the game.

The veteran coach's main issue in the 20-10 loss to Newcastle came when Jayden Sullivan had a try chalked off midway through the second half.

Ashley Klein sent the decision up as a try but bunker official Chris Butler overruled the referee's call, believing there was a knock-on by Souths winger Alex Johnston in the build-up.

And to add to Bennett's frustration, Newcastle winger Dominic Young had a try awarded 10 minutes later.

Klein gave a try, and though Young's foot appeared to have potentially grazed the touchline at the SFS, Butler backed up the call made by the on-field referee.

A long-time critic of the bunker, Bennett claimed that highlighted an inconsistency in what video officials required to overturn a decision.

But AAP understands the NRL thoroughly reviewed both calls on Saturday, and are comfortable with the decisions made.

The league also moved to clarify that the on-field call only stood if the bunker had inconclusive or insufficient evidence to go upon.

Otherwise, video officials were required to make their own impartial call regardless of how tight the decision was.

"I want to know who's refereeing the game. That's the first thing I want to know. Is it the bunker, or is it the referee?", Bennett asked on Friday night.

"It's not where I want the game to be, personally.

"I've been in it a long time and seen a lot of things and I don't think the bunker enhances our game to the amount of what we believe it does.

"I'm happy to live with the referee's call. Always have been. Always will be. None of us are getting it right. The bunker doesn't get it right either every time."

Bennett, who warned the issue would continue to rumble on through the finals series, said he had no qualms with try decisions simply being determined by one on-field referee.

World.title: London tourist tax on accommodation will be capped at 5pc, mayor says
World.content:
A new tax on overnight stays in London will be capped at 5 per cent of the cost of accommodation, the BBC has reported.

Under the legislation, local authorities will be able to charge a flat fee or a percentage of the cost of an overnight stay for domestic and international guests in London accommodations.

London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan told BBC London that he welcomed plans by the government and promised it would not be above 5 per cent per night.

The exact amount has not yet been determined.

"I fully support the government's decision, after years of lobbying, to give us the same powers that other cities, from New York to Los Angeles, from Chicago to Paris … have, which is the ability to raise a levy on those who come to our great city," he said.

"We've got to invest in making sure that [our] city continues to be attractive."

There are concerns the costs could put visitors off heading to London, an extremely popular destination for Australians heading abroad.

How will the tax work?

Between November of last year and February of 2026, the UK government consulted on the design of a new power for English councils to introduce overnight visitor levies or a "tourist tax".

London 'tourist tax' proposed for international travellers Australians heading to England could soon pay a new "tourist tax" on accommodation.

The legal framework to do so will be introduced in the Overnight Visitor Levy bill, which has not yet been tabled in parliament.

A visitor levy set by English mayors would apply to hotels, guesthouses, bed and breakfasts, hostels, campsites, self-catering properties, and short-term lets, and university and religious accommodation when let commercially.

The levy would be set as a percentage of the price of the accommodation.

Mayors would be able to set local exemptions.

They would also be able to choose to set a visitor levy in some of their local authority areas but not others.

Members of the combined authority would be able to reject a levy by a two-thirds majority.

It will bring England in line with Scotland and Wales, which have already introduced powers for local authorities to raise a visitor levy.

Why is it being implemented?

The bill proposes that English mayors can spend revenue from the levy for "broader initiatives which have a positive impact on the region's economic health."

"Mayors will be empowered to deliver more long-term, locally led investment in transport, regeneration and cultural assets that can unlock growth and make places more attractive for residents, businesses and visitors," the bill said.

"The government will not compel any mayor to introduce this levy, nor will central government reduce funding for mayors if they decide to do so."

The levy could raise up to £240 million ($450 million) annually, according to Central London Forward, which represents 12 London local authorities and is based on a 3 per cent levy on the cost of a room.

Where else has it been applied?

Similar schemes have been implemented around the world.

In Europe, a city tax is the norm for many popular locations, including Venice, Rome, Amsterdam, Barcelona and Berlin and is used to fund local infrastructure and manage over-tourism.

In Paris, travellers pay from $2 to $15 per night depending on how the hotel is rated.

In New York, several taxes are applied to an overnight stay, which total about 14 per cent per night.

Japan also charges an overnight stay tax for foreign visitors per night.

How has Australia responded?

According to the most recent data from Visit Britain, 1.2 million Australians travelled to the UK in 2024.

During the travellers' visits, their total expenditure was a record £1.7 billion, with an average spend of £1,358 ($2,561) per visit.

Australians have criticised the proposed changes amid the growing expenses of overseas travel.

Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long previously told the ABC the decision to tax travellers would add to an already expensive long-haul destination at the top of many Aussies' bucket lists.

"We're entering a new era where governments are increasingly targeting travellers with taxes," he said.

"It's a never-ending battle that ultimately means less money spent in the economy and less revenue for the small businesses employing the people who deliver the experiences."

World.title: Mother's search for help before son's suicide sparks call for change
World.content:
Warning: This story contains references to suicide and self-harm.

In the years between her son Felix's first attempt at taking his own life at the age of 12 and his suicide last year, Darwin mother Gertrude Jane-Knight says she tried everything to help him.

"I was reaching out to everyone — 'Help me, what do I do?' — and constantly I was being told, 'you don't know what you're talking about, there is nothing wrong with your son'," Ms Jane-Knight said.

But, tragically, she was right.

Gertrude Jane-Knight and her son Felix who took his own life last year. (Supplied: Gertrude Jane-Knight)

"My son passed away on the 3rd of November," she said.

"This year would've been Felix's 17th birthday."

This week, Felix's friends and family walked together in his memory, describing him as a "beautiful, energetic, lively, creative, hilarious human being".

"[His friends] have suffered terribly from what's happened and they all say to me, 'We miss him so much'," Ms Jane-Knight said.

Ms Jane-Knight was one of around 40 speakers at a suicide prevention forum in Darwin this week, where she relayed her experience trying to get her son help within the NT's mental health system.

Gertrude Jane-Knight says her late son Felix's friends, who participated in a Suicide Prevention Day walk this year, "miss him dearly". (Supplied: Gertrude Jane-Knight)

"I had tried desperately to get appointments for my son with psychologists, I was constantly having the door shut, or appointments weren't ready," she said.

"At a time where I was spending 24 hours a day trying to keep my son safe, I was madly also trying to find out who could help me.

"Wherever I ended up I was constantly being told that there was nothing wrong with my son."

The NT has the nation's highest rates of suicide, acute mental illness and hospital presentations for self-harm.

Felix's loved ones say he was a "beautiful, energetic, lively, creative, hilarious human being". (Supplied: Gertrude Jane-Knight)

At the same time, the Royal Darwin Hospital youth mental health facility was found to have posed serious risks to staff and patients in 2024 and mental health workers say other services aimed at prevention and early intervention are struggling to keep up with high demand.

Now Ms Jane-Knight is calling on NT health practitioners to listen and act on the experiences of those reaching out for help on behalf of a loved one, and also to be better equipped to make referrals to appropriate services.

"We have all of those different elements here that could've worked for my son, but I didn't know about them and no-one was telling me about them," she said.

"This is a hard conversation for me to have, but I know so well that I have to keep on having these conversations."

Remote mental health impacted by poverty, trauma

Karyn Moyle is an Eastern Arrernte, Warlpiri and Djaru woman whose family was part of the Stolen Generations.

Ms Moyle was a co-host of this week's suicide prevention forum.

She is a founder of Waterlily Healing Indigenous Corporation, which runs programs in remote communities throughout the NT around mental health and wellbeing, suicide prevention and bereavement.

She said many Aboriginal people in remote areas experienced the compounding grief of premature deaths, intergenerational trauma and poverty.

"What I have learnt is that when I meet people and they tell me about their story, I know there's always a bigger picture," she said.

Karyn Moyle says too often mental health services in remote regions are "box-ticking" exercises. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Moyle said too often, mental health services in remote regions were "box-ticking" exercises, with fly-in-fly-out staff who had not gained the trust of the people who needed help.

"Relationship building is really important, you need to prove yourself that you're actually in their community for the right reasons," she said.

Ms Moyle called on the government to invest in training and educating more remote mental health workers in remote communities.

"Because they're the ones that are going to stay in that community," she said.

Challenge to have 'courageous' conversations

Lidia and Michael Di Lembo founded not-for-profit Sabrina's Reach4Life after the death by suicide of their 19-year-old daughter in 2017.

In his 2018 report, former NT Coroner Greg Cavanagh found there were serious failings by GPs and other medical professionals in the weeks leading up to Sabrina's death.

Lidia Di Lembo says GPs should have the skills and training to deal with patients who are suicidal. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Lidia Di Lembo was one of the organisers of this week's forum, which explored barriers in the Territory's health system that prevented tough conversations being had.

"The first thing thing that people get told when they do reach out to a help line is, 'Go to a GP'," she said.

"How do we change that so that people that go to a GP have more time to be listened to, but making sure that GPs have the skills and the training to deal with people that are suicidal?"

Sabrina Di Lembo's parents founded Sabrina's Reach4Life in her honour after her death. (Supplied: Lidia Di Lembo)

Ms Di Lembo said there were many people outside the health profession who could be called on to help implement change.

World.title: Zak Butters fixes sights on Western Bulldogs move
World.content:
Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has nominated Western Bulldogs as his preferred club, weeks after announcing his decision to head home to Victoria.

In a statement on Saturday morning, the Western Bulldogs confirmed Butters had informed the club of his desire to join.



"The club will work with Port Adelaide to facilitate a suitable outcome during the upcoming player movement period," the Bulldogs said.

The 26-year-old's future had dominated headlines during the season with reports of offers over eight years from Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs.

Butters had narrowed his choice to the Bulldogs and Geelong before settling on the club he supported as a child.

He has reportedly been offered a nine-year deal worth up to $2 million per season to join Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in a high-powered Dogs engine room.

But Port Adelaide has the right to match the bid for restricted free agent Butters and force the Bulldogs into a trade for the three-time All-Australian.

On August 24, Butters announced his decision to "head home", saying it was a "tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly".

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them," he said at the time.

Three-time All-Australian Butters won three best-and-fairest awards with Port and stood in as captain this year with regular skipper Connor Rozee sidelined by a serious hamstring injury.

Butters' last game in Power colours was a defeat to St Kilda in round 18, when he suffered an ankle syndesmosis injury that ended his season early.

Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge has long been an admirer of Butters and irked Port counterpart Josh Carr this season when openly addressing his club's desire to lure the star midfielder.

"Marcus [Bontempelli], and some of Marcus's teammates, are quite naturally drawn to Zak," Beveridge said in June.

"They played in the state team together [in February], so he's developed some relationships with some of the other boys who played in that game."

ABC / AAP

World.title: These girls fear new child protection laws will lead to 'lost generations'
World.content:
Surrounded by the ocean, where eucalypt forest stretches from the sand to meet the sky, the Tiwi Islands are a living library for the young people who call it home.

Etched into the landscape are guides on how to live off the land and language that describes their way of life, all of which has taught kids their traditional customs over generations.

The island and its community hold the knowledge that tells the story of each family and how they're connected.

But there are fears these connections to kin and culture are under threat.

Tahni and Shanina fear changes to NT laws could result in more young people losing vital kinship connections. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

These fears are acutely felt by 17-year-old Tiwi Island girls Shanina Kantilla and Tahni Thompson, who are cousins on their mother's side.

Even when they're hundreds of kilometres from home, the islands are never far from their minds.

Shanina recalls a happy childhood spent camping, hunting, swimming and fishing.

"It's very important, especially starting from a young age, learning about our culture, skin groups and also our country … where we inherit our tribes, the sacred sites, ceremony," she said.

Tahni also feels a deep connection to being Tiwi, having returned after spending part of her childhood in Darwin.

"It's like my safe place. Whenever I go to other places, I always feel homesick," she said.

Life on the Tiwi Islands

Hundreds of fans gathered for the 2026 senior men's grand final clash on the islands. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The Tiwi Islands is known for many things — vibrant artwork, secluded fishing spots and die-hard footy fans — with some of Australia's most renowned AFL players coming out of the region.

"We have a local league of AFL and it gets really hectic around those times," Tahni said.

Melville Island's Imalu Tigers took home the premiership this year. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Tiwi culture is also embedded in the girls' schooling, with weekly lessons on country.

But the real tutoring starts young and comes from within families — grandparents, parents, aunties and uncles.

Shanina's mother and grandmother taught her cultural practices from a young age. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Shanina's pride in her family traditions shines through as she explains how she's been taught to take wood from the local paper bark trees to weave into baskets.

"We scrape all the wood out and when we're done, we have to boil it and then we fold it, and let it sit for about two, three hours," she said.

"Once it dries up, we come back and start doing our traditional paintings."

Shanina describes weaving baskets using wood collected from the paper bark trees. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Both girls are well aware past government policies prevented this cultural knowledge from being passed down.

"Since the missionaries came, they just changed everything," Tahni said.

"Some of the kids on the other island, [due to] the [Stolen] Generations, don't really speak Tiwi."

From the early 1900s, Catholic missions on the Tiwi Islands controlled much of daily life, influencing where people lived, who they married and the upbringing of their children.

For many families, the policies disrupted the transmission of language, cultural practices and traditional knowledge.

Today, cultural disconnection can take different forms.

Tahni has fond memories of growing up on the islands and learning from her elders. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Tahni knows this firsthand. Growing up away from her homelands, she felt as though a part of her identity was missing until she returned to the Tiwi Islands.

"I wouldn't want to be taken away from my family," she said.

"I would want to stay with them forever."

Deflating the 'political football'

People gather for Garma each year from across the nation and the world. (ABC News: Erin Byrne)

On the other side of the territory's coastline, as thousands gathered for the Garma festival, First Nations people voiced fears of a renewed threat to kinship systems and culture.

Culture is celebrated as children show off their skills at the nightly Bunggul (dance). (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For almost 30 years, Yolŋu people have opened their ceremonial grounds to visitors. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Political leaders have been urged to engage with the young people most affected by their policies. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Just weeks before, the Northern Territory government announced changes to child protection laws which critics said weakened the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle.

National Indigenous children's commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter was among those fearing it would lead to more children removed from their communities.

"I'm not here in a battle, I'm here to protect our children and make sure they're safe," she said.

"I feel like it's a bit of political football for everybody, and that's not what our kids should be."

The child placement principle aims to keep Aboriginal children connected to family, community and culture when they enter care.

It prioritises placing children with family in the first instance, then the child's own First Nations community and then other First Nations carers.

Sue-Anne Hunter has spent just over a year in the role. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

But under the NT changes, introduced after the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the government no longer needs to try to place a child with their community or a First Nations carer if they can't be placed with family.

Sue-Anne Hunter sees devastating echoes of the past.

"No-one is saying that our children need to be unsafe. If a child needs to be removed, then that's the fact. The thing is that culture is part of safety. It's their identity," she said.

"Maybe they [the NT government] need to have a discussion with some Stolen Generation people about how being disconnected affected their lives."

Legal experts say the CLP has taken an increasingly punitive approach to youth crime. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Hunter spent much of her time at Garma hearing directly from young people, many of whom told her they were anxious about the changes.

"It's front of mind for youth as well," she said.

"We need to be investing in the front end. Family support, getting into families early, not waiting until we're ready to remove them."

Hundreds of young people attend Garma and take part in the youth forum. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

A spokesperson for the NT government denied the changes were weakening protections for Aboriginal children.

"These reforms — designed after extensive consultation — created a Universal Child Placement Principle so the same strong provisions apply to every child," they said.

"Additional provisions have been retained for Aboriginal children that reflect their cultural needs and connection to family, community and country."

Child protection isn't the only policy change adding to Ms Hunter's workload.

Sue-Anne Hunter told attendees she would "tell you the truth about how this nation is treating your children". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In recent years the NT lowered the age of criminal responsibility and reintroduced spit hoods, the NT, Victoria and Queensland removed the principle of detention as a last resort for children, Victoria and Queensland brought in "adult crime, adult time" laws and nearly all jurisdictions tightened youth bail.

Ms Hunter said she wished the politicians who attended Garma, including NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, had asked the next generation what they thought of the changes.

"There are a whole lot of people here ready to give some solutions, have some discussions, but it just doesn't seem to be happening," she said.

"It would have been nice if [Ms Finocchiaro] was able to stay, maybe go into the youth forum and listen to the kids."

The NT government spokesperson said lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 10 was about "early intervention and community safety".

"Strong families, cultural connection and early intervention are the best way to break the cycle of youth crime, alongside clear consequences when offending occurs," they said.

'They are just little kids'

Shanina and Tahni are cousins who love spending time together. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Inside the youth forum, Tahni and Shanina reflected on family and friends who had been caught up in the justice system or removed from their families.

"Those ones that are under Territory Families [in out-of-home-care], they don't know our culture much because they only come once a year for a visit around the community," Shanina said.

"It's hard for them to know who their family is, who they are, and their culture … I feel for them."

The girls say they're worried about the impact of new laws on their family and peers. (ABC News Billy Cooper)

They were also worried about children as young as 10 being held responsible for crimes.

"Ten years old, they're not really teenagers yet, they are just little kids. They aren't mature enough [to understand]," Tahni said.

The cousins share a strong connection with their culture. (ABC News Billy Cooper)

"Instead of sending them away, just discipline them on the island and that way they can learn from their mistakes instead of getting them sent off somewhere else.

"[Juvenile detention is] pretty traumatic, and they'll have to carry that trauma for the rest of their lives."

The cousins say there are deeper issues affecting young people and punishment isn't the solution.

"I think younger children have to do counselling, talk about their feelings … instead of getting frustrated. That causes a lot of problems," Shanina said.

Tahni's message to government is that "our voice matters". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

As the youth forum began to wind up, Tahni shared her message for the NT government.

"Our voice matters," she said.

"We don't want [Stolen Generations] to happen again.

"If we didn't have culture, we wouldn't know our identity. That's why it's important for us to learn at a young age.

"[Otherwise] there might not be any Tiwi people left. There will just be lost generations."

World.title: 'Look out': The inside story of 9/11, told by an advisor on Air Force One
World.content:
On September 11, 2001, the White House daily intelligence briefer was standing not far from where George W Bush was entertaining a classroom of children when he watched a plane collide into the World Trade Center live on television.

Up until that moment, Michael Morell had been following the US president on an otherwise normal day as he prepared to discuss education initiatives in Florida. He was joined by White House political adviser Karl Rove, press secretary Ari Fleischer and chief of staff Andrew Card.

But after watching the second jet crash in New York, everyone realised this was no ordinary event: America was under attack.

"I was 100 per cent sure that this was terrorism," Mr Morell told the ABC.

Within minutes, Mr Card was making his way to the president to whisper in his ear the news of what had happened.

The moment, captured on camera and later broadcast around the world, became a defining photograph of the day that shook the United States.

Behind the scenes, there was a flurry of activity at Emma E Booker Elementary as phone calls were made, directives issued and a statement prepared for Mr Bush.

By the time the president addressed the nation with the news that "today, we've had a national tragedy", Mr Morell said everybody in the staff room had been told to pack up and go.

With few details of what other attacks might be planned, the Secret Service's priority was getting the president far from the school and somewhere safe.

President George W Bush and White House staff watch news coverage of the plane striking the south tower of the World Trade Centre while at Emma E Booker Elementary school in Florida. (Supplied: George W Bush Library)

"The Secret Service was really worried … because this [visit to the Booker Elementary] had been on the president's schedule for a while," Mr Morell said.

A decision was made to get the president to the airport and into the sky.

"We got in a plane and we took off at a steeper angle than I've ever been on a plane in my life," Mr Morell said.

"At that point, I didn't know what was going to happen. I didn't know whether I was going to get kicked off. And I remember the president's military aide came back and he said: 'The president said you're staying with us.'"

A normal day until it wasn't

As Mr Bush's briefer, Mr Morell was required to provide daily intelligence assessments to the president wherever he was in the world, whether it be the Oval Office, Camp David or his ranch in Texas.

On September 11, Mr Morell had woken at his usual time, just before 4am, and gone straight to work preparing for a busy morning of reading reports.

Michael Morell was the intelligence briefer to George Bush on 9/11 and was a former deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency. (Getty: David Hume Kennerly)

About 8am, Mr Morell delivered his briefing inside the president's suite at the Colony Resort Hotel. He distinctly remembers terrorism did not come up, disputing accounts given in the years since that it had been discussed.

About 40 minutes later, he was inside the senior staff van on the way to Booker Elementary when a phone rang.

"Ari Fleischer [answered and then] turned around and said, 'Michael, do you know anything about a plane hitting the World Trade Center?'" Mr Morell said.

Mr Morell started ringing around, thinking a small plane might have crashed in bad weather in New York. A call to the CIA operations centre revealed little more than the scant information he already had, except for one specific detail.

"They did say one thing that changed my thinking immediately … it wasn't a small plane, it was a large commercial jet," he said.

"[Then] a second [plane] hit."

Face to face with the president

At some point after leaving the school and before arriving at the airport, the news reached Mr Morell and other members of the Bush entourage that a third plane had crashed at the Pentagon.

The symbolic and physical headquarters of the US military sits just outside Washington DC, significantly shifting the scale of the attacks beyond New York.

Mr Morell remembers arriving to an intense security presence at the airport and uncertainty about where to go once they were in the sky.

The Secret Service eventually chose an air force base in Louisiana, where Mr Bush delivered another statement before they took off again to another base in Nebraska.

Mr Morell says he was surprised when he was told mid-flight to go and see the president in his office on Air Force One.

President George W Bush talks on the telephone as senior staff huddle aboard Air Force One. (Supplied: George Bush Library)

"[That] day was a mixture of the intensity of doing my job and the surreal. And there were different moments of the intensity of doing my job, but one of the biggest was [when] the president asked to see me," he said.

After he entered the room, he remembers Mr Bush turning to him and looking him straight in the eye.

'I think [it's] bin Laden and Al Qaeda'

It was somewhere over a stretch of land in North America that Mr Morell was asked a question he will never forget.

"[Mr Bush] said, 'Michael, who did this?'" he recalled.

President George W Bush watches television coverage of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, from his office on Air Force One, on September 11, 2001. (Supplied: George W Bush Library)

"So I said, 'Mr President, one's mind might go to a nation state like Iran or Iraq. And both of them have the capability to do something like this,'" he added, noting he had not seen any 9/11 intelligence prior to the meeting.

"'But doing it is in no way in their interest, right? They have no reason to do this. They're going to get caught. They're going to go to war, right? They're not going to do this.'

" So I said, 'I think when we get to the end of the trail, we are going to find [Osama] bin Laden and Al Qaeda.' "

Mr Morell said the terrorist group and its notorious leader had been a topic of discussion "more than any other" in the previous nine months. The subject was certainly not a new one to the US president.

Al Qaeda, a designated terrorist group founded by Osama bin Laden, was quickly blamed for the attacks. (Reuters: Hamid Mir/Editor/Ausaf Newspaper for Daily Dawn)

Mr Bush's next question of "when will we know?" wasn't a surprise to Mr Morell either.

"[It's] just the kind of question the president asks you, for which there's no answer, right? So I fell back on the training and the experience of being an analyst," he added.

"And one of the things you get taught as an analyst … is that context is everything … so I gave him some context."

He laid out how long it took to identify the perpetrators behind previous terror attacks and concluded they could know who was responsible in as little as two or three days, or it "may take quite some time".

"After I said that, he didn't say anything. He just sat there … And I remember starting to feel a little awkward because Andy Card [who was also in the room] didn't say anything either. I mean, it wasn't the moment, right?" Mr Morell said.

"And so finally I said, 'Mr President, is there anything else?' And he said, 'No, Michael, thank you very much.'"

Mr Morell said he later found out the CIA had the same view on the perpetrator of the 9/11 attacks and had shared it directly with Mr Bush.

George W Bush on the phone on September 11. (Supplied: George W Bush Library)

"When I told the president that I hadn't seen any intelligence, the CIA had already figured out that it was Al Qaeda. They just hadn't told me yet," he said.

"They ran the flight manifests … against our terrorist databases and there were hits … to Al Qaeda. So they came to the conclusion pretty quickly. It was pretty clear who did it."

The jets guarding Air Force One

After touching down at the Air Force Base in Nebraska, Mr Morell recalled being invited into the room with the president as they called advisors back in Washington, DC.

"At the end of that, the director of the Secret Service was saying, 'We think you should still stay away from Washington. We don't know it's safe,'" Mr Morell said.

"And [the president] said, 'The American people want to know where their president is. I'm coming home.'"

President George W Bush delivers remarks on the terrorist attacks from Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, before departing for Offutt Air Force in Nebraska. (Supplied: George W Bush Library)

The Bush team were on a plane bound for Washington when Mr Morell said he had "the most surreal moment".

"I was in the staff compartment of Air Force One in its old, business class seats, [near] the president's military aide, the guy that carries the nuclear codes, [who] had become [a] friend the previous nine months," he said.

"I saw him looking out the window on the left side of the aircraft and we caught eyes. The lights were dimmed, and he waved me over, so I went over to him and he said, 'Look out.'

Mr Morrell remembered looking out the window to a clear, blue sky and seeing an F-16 fighter on the wingtip of Air Force One.

An F-16 escorts Air Force One from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska to Andrews Air Force Base on September 11, 2001. (Supplied: George W Bush Library)

"He said: 'That's an F-16. It's from the DC National Guard. There's another one on the other wingtip,'" he said, noting it was "so close that you could see the pilot."

"In the distance you could see the still smouldering Pentagon. And the military aide said to me, 'Do you know why they're there?' And I had no idea. I'm not a military guy. And every commercial flight had been grounded … so nobody was going to fly a plane into us.

" And he said: 'They're there in case someone fires a surface-to-air missile at Air Force One on final approach. Their job would be to put themselves between that missile and the president of the United States. "

The pilots in those fighter jets were not required to lay down their lives that day. Thousands of others, however, were not so lucky.

"People say to me, 'Did you know at that moment that history would change?' And I said, 'No, I was doing my job'. I was intensely focused on my job, but that's when it really started [to hit me] the magnitude of this," Mr Morell said.

How will history view 9/11?

Decades after the tragedy of 9/11, the wake-up call it delivered to America's biggest institutions has not been forgotten, according to Mr Morell.

Flowers and flags on the south pool commemorate the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. (AP: Julia Nikhinson)

"I always have seen 9/11 as a national failure [of] intelligence, policy, congressional oversight, congressional lawmaking, and public attitudes," he said.

Mr Morell added the overwhelming sentiment inside the nation's intelligence agencies afterwards was that an attack of 9/11's scale could not be allowed to happen again.

"That sense flowed from two things. It flowed from guilt that [the CIA] didn't penetrate this organisation enough to learn in advance about what they were doing so it could have been prevented," he said.

"And the other was anger that … the FBI were being blamed for this when we were the only two organisations in the entire US government who were focused on this guy … our warnings over a long period of time, people didn't act on them."

Mr Morell served as the intelligence briefer for Mr Bush until January 4, 2002. He went on to become the deputy director for the CIA and is now co-founder at Aardwolf Global Solutions.

There were many big moments throughout his 33-year CIA career, but he said he would never forget 9/11.

"It's quite possible that in 100 years, historians look back at 2001 and 9/11 is not the most important thing that happened [that year]," he said.

"I think it's going to be really interesting to see how our long-term history judges all of this."

World.title: AFLW round five: Top Hawk suffers serious knee injury
World.content:
Aine McDonagh has fired Hawthorn to an 11-point AFLW win over the Western Bulldogs that was soured by captain Emily Bates’ serious leg injury.

Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher at the Kennedy Community Centre on Saturday after her right leg twisted underneath her in a tackle late in the third quarter.

The decorated 30-year-old, who played her 100th AFLW match a week earlier, was expected to be taken to hospital for further assessment.

Hawthorn’s Emily Bates goes to ground and suffers a knee injury. AFL Photos

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at half-time.

But Daniel Webster’s side piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter – four of those before Bates’ injury – to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

AAP, more to come

World.title: NRL finals LIVE: Warriors host Dolphins before Sharks face Cowboys
World.content:
The Warriors sold 26,000 tickets for Saturday’s final against the Dolphins in around 17 minutes. Win, and they’ll shift almost twice as many for a grand final qualifier at Eden Park in a fortnight. The smart money says they’ll do it in half the time.

Thirty-one years since they were born out of rugby league’s last great rush to expand and conquer, the Warriors are better placed than ever before to assume the true powerhouse status that has seemingly always been theirs for the taking, if only they could ever get their house in order long enough to do it.

In their most recent rise, pivotal figures in the club’s history abound. From coach Andrew Webster and foundation halfback Stacey Jones to current owner Mark Robinson and retired attacking phenom Shaun Johnson.

Roger Tuivasa-Sheck looms as influential as any.

World.title: Rescue operation under way after woman falls down Blue Mountains cliff
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A major rescue operation is under way to help a woman who fell 30 metres down a cliff face in the Blue Mountains.

Emergency services rushed to the Blue Mountains National Park at 11am on Saturday after a woman plunged down a slope in Leura.

A woman has fallen down a Blue Mountains cliff face. Destination NSW

The woman, aged in her 30s, fell down the Ben Trovato Wall at Sublime Point, a popular spot for climbers, a spokesperson for NSW Ambulance said. She remains in a stable condition and is being treated at the scene by four paramedics and a doctor for arm injuries, abrasions and back pain.

A spokesperson for NSW Police said they were called to a walking track in Leura, following reports of a hiker falling from a cliff.

World.title: Look who is back running: Huge finals boost for Roosters
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Look who is back running: Huge finals boost for Roosters Adrian Warren September 12, 2026 — 2:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson is convinced rookie utility Hugo Savala can handle the heat of NRL finals action, but it could be a temporary solution with star halfback Sam Walker back running. Walker had ankle surgery on August 30 after suffering a syndesmosis injury in the round 26 clash with the Dolphins a day earlier, and has made a remarkable recovery. Sam Walker is trying to get back on the field for the Roosters. Sydney Roosters Robinson wouldn’t be drawn on whether Walker could feature in a preliminary final should the Roosters beat Penrith in Sunday’s qualifying final at Commbank Stadium, but neither did he rule out the possibility. “He’s recovered probably quicker than I’ve seen most syndesmosis injuries and he’s back moving in a straight line in a pretty good way which is really pleasing,” Robinson said.



“He’s on a good track to progress over the next couple of weeks.” Utility Savala has appeared in 19 games this season, lining up in the centres for the vast majority, though Robinson stressed the 24-year-old was well-equipped to wear the No.6 jersey. Savala played in the halves as a junior while he started there in all but three of his 21 matches in 2025. “You lose a player in that position, you’ve got to bring someone up from reserve grade, or they haven’t been playing, whereas Hugo has been able to play in other positions, that means he’s already in tune with the energy of the group and the combinations there,” Robinson said.



Another perspective NRL 2026 Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt “He’s only moved in one position from where he has been playing, obviously a pretty critical link role there, but he’s also played over a decade of that position growing up. “It was just about re-establishing those connections in a slightly different position, but he brings intensity and an energy to our group as well, that we’ve seen at centre, but looking forward to it at six. Penrith prevailed in four of the last five finals clashes against the Roosters, though the latter won a 12-6 defensive slugfest in their most recent meeting last month. Robinson declared his side “ready to go” for the finals despite losing their last three games, with plenty of big names returning after being rested from last week’s clash with South Sydney.



“It doesn’t matter whether you’ve won or lost the last three weeks, all that matters is tomorrow,” Robinson said. “You’ve got to handle whatever emotions or technical or tactical things that you’ve got to improve, you’ve got to put that in to a place early on in the week and then you have the belief about how you’re going to play tomorrow.” Forward Angus Crichton was named on the interchange bench earlier in the week after missing 11 games with a foot injury, but Robinson said he wasn’t ready to play. AAP

World.title: Teen drone operator charged with murder arrested while allegedly conducting surveillance
World.content:
An 18-year-old drone operator charged over his alleged involvement in the fatal shooting of Joshua Macdonald in western Sydney earlier this month was allegedly conducting another criminal surveillance operation when he was arrested on Friday. An emerging Cronulla Sharks player, 19-year-old Ratu Viliame Koroitamana, was driving a car in which the alleged drone operator was arrested on Friday. He was arrested and charged with driving while disqualified and participating in a criminal group to contribute to criminal activity. He has not been charged in relation to the Macdonald murder. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News Macdonald was shot at a Merrylands West home on the afternoon of September 2, in a case that police believe was mistaken identity. The 40-year-old died at the scene. Macdonald was not known to police and had no links to organised crime.



About 5.30am on Friday, Raptor Squad detectives arrested the 18-year-old and Koroitamana in West Hoxton and took them to Liverpool police station. Police allege the younger man is a drone operator. Ratu Viliame Koroitamana. A member of the public had reported unusual drone activity over West Hoxton, near Liverpool, and police arrested the pair shortly afterwards.
