World.title: ‘Trump got the headlines he wanted’: Inside the Republican midterm convention
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterm elections ‘Trump got the headlines he wanted’: Inside the Republican midterm convention Michael Koziol September 12, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dallas: At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, 17 supersized photographs lined the walls outside the main arena. Sixteen of them were of Donald Trump (the other was a crowd shot from the previous convention). This might have been a Republican Party event, but there’s no doubt who it was for. Donald Trump on stage for night two of the Republican midterm convention, where attendees recited a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States”. AP Photo/Julio Cortez “I’m not on the ticket,” Trump said during his closing appearance on night two. “You’ve got to pretend. You’ve got to do me the biggest favour you’ve ever done me. You’ve got to do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket. He’s on the ticket. Pretend I’m on the ticket.” On the face of it, it’s an odd strategy. Trump’s approval rating nationally is in the 30s: 33 per cent, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1167 Americans at the end of August. It has never been lower throughout this second term.



Making the election a referendum on an unpopular president seems like a recipe for disaster. But Republicans’ strategy relies on convincing Trump’s base to show up on November 3 and vote for the Republican candidate in their district, and for the Senate. “A lot of people that came out for President Trump don’t come out unless his name is physically on the ballot,” says Aaron Del Mar, a Republican Party operative from Illinois who is running to become the state’s lieutenant governor. Trump was everywhere in Dallas – whether on stage, on the walls or in the outfits worn by loyal supporters. Bloomberg “So, this whole program is an effort to try to drive those Trump supporters that only vote for him to come out and vote for all Republicans up and down the ticket.” Del Mar points out that in Illinois – a blue state – Trump received 700,000 more votes than the Republican candidate for governor did in 2022, and 200,000 more votes than the successful Democratic candidate for governor, JB Pritzker.



“The whole point and the whole reason [for this convention] is to engage what we call low propensity voters. Those are voters that traditionally will vote in presidential elections, but won’t vote in midterms. By our math, if we drive out about 40 to 45 per cent of those unreliable voters, we can flip our state.” Hence, the two days here in Dallas with dozens of speakers singing Trump’s praises, an onslaught of Trump imagery, and pleas from the man himself – including leading the crowd in reciting a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States”. Merchandise on sale at the convention. Bloomberg The stakes are high for Trump because if Republicans lose control of one or both chambers, not only will he lose the power to legislate, but he will likely be subject to impeachment proceedings, as in his first term. It will make for a trying final two years, even though he will retain the executive power he has wielded so emphatically. Both sides are not so much appealing to independent or swing voters as they are trying to motivate their own bases to show up to the polls. Such is the reality in a country that is so harshly divided, and where the two big parties stand so far apart.



“Trump’s popularity is the same as it’s always been – high among his supporters, low among his opponents,” Allyn Meyers, chairman of the Rhode Island Republican Party, tells this masthead on the sidelines at Dallas. “Look who we’re running against. We’re running against people who want to sell communism.” Loading Loyal Trump supporters, including the “Front Row Joes” who regularly attend his rallies. Bloomberg Meyers says voters will likely divide even further. “In the blue states, it could get darker [for Republicans], and in the red states, it could get better.”



As speaker after speaker thanked Trump, or railed against communism and Islamism, the real party was happening up on the second level inside the suites belonging to the pro-Trump right-wing media outlets – particularly Real America’s Voice, the channel that is home to activists Steve Bannon and Jack Posobiec. A throng of conservative pundits, social media influencers and Republican personalities mingled inside and outside the suite all evening, with chips, dips and drinks provided. Politicians and their staff came and went. Some carry takeaway cups of 7-Eleven filter coffee, which costs $US7.85 (that’s $10.95, plus tip) from an arena store. Attendees cheer Trump’s arrival on night two. Bloomberg Among the crowd was John Solomon, a conservative media entrepreneur who founded digital news organisation Just the News and recently became a special government employee chairing the White House’s so-called “Government Transparency Task Force”. Solomon’s temporary job with Trump was to find, release and promote documents that purportedly showed widespread plotting to undermine US election integrity. Other people in the ultra-MAGA orbit, including Trump’s former strategist Bannon, said it was a precursor to declaring a national security emergency ahead of the midterms.



But Solomon told this masthead there was no indication Trump was planning such a thing, and little need for it. Speaking as a journalist rather than a government employee, he conceded the economy was “in a weird state” – with job indicators strong, but the price of petrol inflated due to the Iran war. Related Article Exclusive

US midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide Solomon pointed to four factors he said could avert the usual outcome of a midterm election, which is that the party in power suffers. The first was the convention itself, which aimed to “get people excited”. Second, “the Democrats don’t have any answer for it”. Third, Republicans had successfully redrawn the electoral maps to their advantage in several key states – what most people would call gerrymandering. “That makes the margin grab by the Democrats much harder to complete,” Solomon said. But the fourth factor is the biggest: money. The Republicans have a $US1 billion-plus war chest, housed across various super PACs including Trump’s MAGA Inc, which had $US403 million cash on hand at the end of July.



Federal Election Commission returns show the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund had $US239 million at the end of June, the Congressional Leadership Fund had $US142 million and the Republican National Committee $US130 million at the end of July. By contrast, the Democrats’ had just over $US241 million across their two super PACs, the Senate Majority and House Majority funds, while the Democratic National Committee had a cash deficit of $US2 million. It was recently revealed the DNC used its Washington office and other assets as collateral to secure a $US15 million loan last year. Republicans need to motivate Trump’s base as if his name were on the ballot. Bloomberg “The DNC is mortgaging their headquarters for money,” Solomon said. “Those are factors that go against the countervailing forces that normally would be against an incumbent president.” Still, those forces are significant. The president is unpopular, the Iran war is dragging on, the price of petrol is consequently high – as is the cost of living generally. Government debt is at a record $US40 trillion, and the Trump administration is trying to avert a bond market sell-off.



Republicans who gathered in Dallas were not blind to these problems, publicly or privately. But in both cases they expressed optimism that – with Trump leading the charge – they could still sell a positive story to the American public. “Here’s the reality,” said Mike Markey, a Republican from Michigan who recently lost a primary for the state Senate. “When people are upset about affordability and where everything is in this country right now, let’s remember that this isn’t a problem that we created. This is the problem that the Biden administration and Democrats really celebrated, letting in 20 million illegals.” Trump announced a $US5000 “dividend” for every adult American if Republicans retail control of both chambers. Bloomberg But Joe Biden did not start the war with Iran that has sent Brent crude, the international oil price benchmark, above $US100 for the second time this year. Markey says it’s a dose of medicine; he tries to explain using an analogy from Mrs Doubtfire. “Right at the beginning, what separates Sally Field and Robin Williams: she comes home, their son had struggled in school, she feels bad about not doing a birthday party. And she comes home and Robin Williams is on the table dancing, they’ve got a petting zoo. She had to be the un-fun parent. And Republicans, we’re the un-fun parent right now. We are fixing the mess that they made.”

World.title: The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final Jonathan Drennan September 12, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After completing an intense week of training on Friday afternoon, Swans players were divided on what to do that evening. Some wanted to watch the semi-final between Fremantle and Geelong, which would determine their opponent in next weekend’s preliminary final. Others were happy to tune out of footy for the night and wait until they reconvened to begin the forensic analysis of their next match. The Swans who did tune in to the Dockers’ tense 14-point victory at Optus Stadium were treated to an exceptional performance from ruckman Luke Jackson, with the onus now shifting to how to stop him at the SCG. Loading Swans coach Dean Cox, one of the AFL’s greatest ever ruckmen, will be aware that if Sydney can nullify Jackson, another grand final is possible. Jackson was a key man in Fremantle’s minor premiership, but the Dockers are by no means a one-man band. Jackson was joined on this year’s All-Australian team by four teammates: Shai Bolton, Jordan Clark, Murphy Reid and Josh Treacy. Against the Cats, Bolton was outstanding, kicking two goals and finishing with 26 disposals. But it was Jackson who flipped the game.



With five minutes left of the third quarter, Fremantle had conceded three successive goals and their home crowd was tense. Jackson, a former Australian under-17 basketball star, finished the quarter with eight disposals, two goals, four score involvements and 12 hitouts. In their previous meeting this season, in Perth in July, the Swans held a two-point lead at the end of the third quarter before Fremantle kicked nine goals in the final term to win by 38 points and underline their premiership credentials. Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos In that game, Swans ruckman Brodie Grundy had 29 hitouts to Jackson’s 26, with Fremantle also able to utilise Mason Cox, who had 10 hitouts. The Swans do not have a deputy with the experience of Cox, having recently used forward Hayden McLean to relieve the veteran Grundy at stoppages. Grundy’s dominance has been a foundation of Sydney’s finals run, but against Jackson in the preliminary final he will face one of the biggest tests of his career. Grundy cannot match Jackson’s scoring threat, with the Fremantle ruck averaging a goal a game and finishing the season with 27 majors, a rarity for his position.



But in the core skill of hitouts, Grundy averages 34.3 a game compared with Jackson’s 25.7. Grundy also possesses an ability to act as an auxiliary midfielder when needed and will need to do so to curb Jackson’s influence. The Swans’ midfield trio of James Rowbottom, Jai Serong and Errol Gulden combined beautifully in their qualifying win against Brisbane to help dominate clearances, but a lot of their success came through Grundy’s dominance at stoppages. Brodie Grundy tussles with Luke Jackson in the last meeting between the sides, in Perth in July. AFL Photos via Getty Images Grundy’s presence in the Swans side has transformed their ability to score from clearances. According to Champion Data, no player has averaged more hitouts-to-advantage at centre bounces than Grundy (3.9) since 2024. This season, the Swans rank No.1 for scores from clearance, and they have 14 wins and 0 losses when they outscore the opposition from clearance, highlighting the importance of Grundy’s ability to outwork Jackson.



Fremantle will travel to face a heavily depleted Swans team, missing the suspended Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey. Captain Callum Mills is also missing from the backline after suffering an ACL injury against Brisbane, depriving them of vital on-field leadership. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘You just have a lot more to lose’: How fatherhood has centred Swans star Grundy History is not on Fremantle’s side at the SCG. Fremantle have won six times at the stadium and lost 14 times. However, more recently, Fremantle have won two out the last three games at the SCG dating back to 2023. The AFL will on Sunday confirm the date and time of the preliminary final. In his post-match press conference on Friday, Geelong coach Chris Scott was full of praise for the impact of Jackson. “I always hesitate to say unique, but he’s as close as there is to unique in that position as there is in the competition,” Scott said. The Swans also have their own unique ruckman. The contest between them will go a long way to deciding which side progresses to the grand final.

World.title: Jiu-jitsu coach, stand-up comic, apiarist: Inside the surprise day jobs of Sydney’s councillors
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For 40 years, Victor Macri has spent five days a week cutting hair at Fernando’s Hair, the business his father started in Marrickville in 1960. A dispute with local councillors over a building matter prompted Macri to run as an independent for the former Marrickville Council – which was later merged to form the Inner West Council – in 2004. Victor Macri has been a part of the Marrickville community for four decades. Sam Mooy But the veteran councillor still spends Tuesday to Saturday giving haircuts with an ear to the ground. “That’s how I keep in contact with the community,” Macri says. “I get all the complaints.” He is among hundreds of local councillors in NSW for whom public office is not their primary source of income. From retail workers and Uber Eats drivers to martial arts masters and cosmetic surgeons, Sydney’s council chambers are filled with elected officials juggling a range of jobs.



Mayors and councillors at the state’s 128 local councils are not paid full-time wages but receive fees determined by the Local Government Remuneration Tribunal. Those payments are determined by the size and type of council on which they serve. For example, a City of Sydney councillor is paid between $32,810 and $48,140. In Strathfield, it’s between $10,920 and $24,080. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams is a trade lane gatekeeper three days a week at Bunnings, where he loads cars and checks receipts – and the community’s pulse. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams keeps an eye on the local economy by working at Bunnings. Janie Barrett He replies to emails during his lunch breaks, and Saturdays to Tuesdays are booked with council commitments, community events and citizenship ceremonies. Williams, a member of the Your Northern Beaches Independent Team, estimates he spends about two hours a day reading council documents, but says it’s worthwhile. “When you’re of service to other people, you forget about your own problems ... It’s about dopamine, and doing nice things for people,” he says.



Lane Cove Labor councillor David Roenfeldt drives buses from Sydney Airport to Yass and Canberra, while Bayside Council’s Chris Saravinovski, also Labor, works as an airport ramp agent and is a jack-of-all-trades, from baggage handling to health and safety. Saravinovski says council work is flexible and rewarding. Related Article Sydney councils This Sydney council was meant to pick a new deputy mayor. A jaunt to the UK got in the way “It’s not for the money,” he says. “You can’t survive on it ... I don’t blame any other councillor having another job and picking this up as a side thing.” Wollondilly Mayor Matt Gould, an independent, once juggled council with drone piloting. Since becoming mayor, he resolved he could do “both poorly or one properly”. Bayside Liberal councillor Dr Ron Bezic is a cosmetic surgeon, while the Hills Shire’s Dr Mila Kasby is a Greens councillor who stepped away from her veterinary practice to focus on volunteer work. She says the system favours financially comfortable candidates. “We need a whole range of different people from different backgrounds … because councillors aren’t paid a living wage, I think that excludes a lot of people,” Kasby said.



Hawkesbury councillor Shane Djuric, who is a Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party member, was a beekeeper but retired following a 2023 injury. Trade-offs between full-time work and council push some to rely on side hustles. Katie Little once spent her spare time on the DJ circuit. Now, she picks up odd jobs such as dog boarding. James Brickwood Lane Cove Labor councillor Katie Little, a former DJ and stand-up comedian, manages a retirement village but also boards dogs at her home. Striking the balance between single motherhood, having a day job and being a councillor made side hustles necessary. “When I started dog boarding, the dogs sent to me came with food better than my kids and I were surviving on,” Little says. Ethan Hrnjak, a Greens councillor from the Northern Beaches, studies law at Macquarie University. His odd jobs have included test kitchen assistant at KFC headquarters and Uber Eats driving.



Ryde’s Felix Lo is a notary public and a Brazilian jiu-jitsu coach taking up to 15 classes a week. The Labor councillor says the similarities between governance and BJJ run deeper than it might seem. “Jiu-jitsu is very much physical, but it’s also like playing chess. Every move, you have to be very careful ... This analogy can apply to local politics and in running the city, right?” Dr Felix Lo studied law at university and teaches regular jiu-jitsu classes. Wolter Peeters Blacktown has a retired NSW police chief inspector, Robert Fitzgerald, a Labor councillor, and police prosecutor Mohit Kumar, a Liberal, on council. Kumar, who spends his days at Blacktown Court House, says his capacity is constrained by the fact that his council role isn’t full-time. “There are a lot of sacrifices you got to make, especially with family.” Some professions feature repeatedly. Ryde’s Daniel Han, a Liberal, and Strathfield Labor councillor Rory Nosworthy both teach high school chemistry.

World.title: AFLW round five: Top Hawk suffers serious knee injury
World.content:
Aine McDonagh has fired Hawthorn to an 11-point AFLW win over the Western Bulldogs that was soured by captain Emily Bates’ serious leg injury.

Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher at the Kennedy Community Centre on Saturday after her right leg twisted underneath her in a tackle late in the third quarter.

The decorated 30-year-old, who played her 100th AFLW match a week earlier, was expected to be taken to hospital for further assessment.

Hawthorn’s Emily Bates goes to ground and suffers a knee injury. AFL Photos

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at half-time.

But Daniel Webster’s side piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter – four of those before Bates’ injury – to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

World.title: NRL finals LIVE: Warriors host Dolphins before Sharks face Cowboys
World.content:
The Warriors sold 26,000 tickets for Saturday’s final against the Dolphins in around 17 minutes. Win, and they’ll shift almost twice as many for a grand final qualifier at Eden Park in a fortnight. The smart money says they’ll do it in half the time.

Thirty-one years since they were born out of rugby league’s last great rush to expand and conquer, the Warriors are better placed than ever before to assume the true powerhouse status that has seemingly always been theirs for the taking, if only they could ever get their house in order long enough to do it.

In their most recent rise, pivotal figures in the club’s history abound. From coach Andrew Webster and foundation halfback Stacey Jones to current owner Mark Robinson and retired attacking phenom Shaun Johnson.

Roger Tuivasa-Sheck looms as influential as any.

A major rescue operation is under way to help a woman who fell 30 metres down a cliff face in the Blue Mountains.

Emergency services rushed to the Blue Mountains National Park at 11am on Saturday after a woman plunged down a slope in Leura.

A woman has fallen down a Blue Mountains cliff face. Destination NSW

The woman, aged in her 30s, fell down the Ben Trovato Wall at Sublime Point, a popular spot for climbers, a spokesperson for NSW Ambulance said. She remains in a stable condition and is being treated at the scene by four paramedics and a doctor for arm injuries, abrasions and back pain.

A spokesperson for NSW Police said they were called to a walking track in Leura, following reports of a hiker falling from a cliff.

World.title: Look who is back running: Huge finals boost for Roosters
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Look who is back running: Huge finals boost for Roosters Adrian Warren September 12, 2026 — 2:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson is convinced rookie utility Hugo Savala can handle the heat of NRL finals action, but it could be a temporary solution with star halfback Sam Walker back running. Walker had ankle surgery on August 30 after suffering a syndesmosis injury in the round 26 clash with the Dolphins a day earlier, and has made a remarkable recovery. Sam Walker is trying to get back on the field for the Roosters. Sydney Roosters Robinson wouldn’t be drawn on whether Walker could feature in a preliminary final should the Roosters beat Penrith in Sunday’s qualifying final at Commbank Stadium, but neither did he rule out the possibility. “He’s recovered probably quicker than I’ve seen most syndesmosis injuries and he’s back moving in a straight line in a pretty good way which is really pleasing,” Robinson said.



“He’s on a good track to progress over the next couple of weeks.” Utility Savala has appeared in 19 games this season, lining up in the centres for the vast majority, though Robinson stressed the 24-year-old was well-equipped to wear the No.6 jersey. Savala played in the halves as a junior while he started there in all but three of his 21 matches in 2025. “You lose a player in that position, you’ve got to bring someone up from reserve grade, or they haven’t been playing, whereas Hugo has been able to play in other positions, that means he’s already in tune with the energy of the group and the combinations there,” Robinson said.



Another perspective NRL 2026 Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt “He’s only moved in one position from where he has been playing, obviously a pretty critical link role there, but he’s also played over a decade of that position growing up. “It was just about re-establishing those connections in a slightly different position, but he brings intensity and an energy to our group as well, that we’ve seen at centre, but looking forward to it at six. Penrith prevailed in four of the last five finals clashes against the Roosters, though the latter won a 12-6 defensive slugfest in their most recent meeting last month. Robinson declared his side “ready to go” for the finals despite losing their last three games, with plenty of big names returning after being rested from last week’s clash with South Sydney.



“It doesn’t matter whether you’ve won or lost the last three weeks, all that matters is tomorrow,” Robinson said. “You’ve got to handle whatever emotions or technical or tactical things that you’ve got to improve, you’ve got to put that in to a place early on in the week and then you have the belief about how you’re going to play tomorrow.” Forward Angus Crichton was named on the interchange bench earlier in the week after missing 11 games with a foot injury, but Robinson said he wasn’t ready to play. “The whole point and the whole reason [for this convention] is to engage what we call low propensity voters. Those are voters that traditionally will vote in presidential elections, but won’t vote in midterms. By our math, if we drive out about 40 to 45 per cent of those unreliable voters, we can flip our state.” Hence, the two days here in Dallas with dozens of speakers singing Trump’s praises, an onslaught of Trump imagery, and pleas from the man himself – including leading the crowd in reciting a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States”. Merchandise on sale at the convention. Bloomberg The stakes are high for Trump because if Republicans lose control of one or both chambers, not only will he lose the power to legislate, but he will likely be subject to impeachment proceedings, as in his first term. It will make for a trying final two years, even though he will retain the executive power he has wielded so emphatically. Both sides are not so much appealing to independent or swing voters as they are trying to motivate their own bases to show up to the polls. Such is the reality in a country that is so harshly divided, and where the two big parties stand so far apart.



“Trump’s popularity is the same as it’s always been – high among his supporters, low among his opponents,” Allyn Meyers, chairman of the Rhode Island Republican Party, tells this masthead on the sidelines at Dallas. “Look who we’re running against. We’re running against people who want to sell communism.” Loading Loyal Trump supporters, including the “Front Row Joes” who regularly attend his rallies. Bloomberg Meyers says voters will likely divide even further. “In the blue states, it could get darker [for Republicans], and in the red states, it could get better.”



As speaker after speaker thanked Trump, or railed against communism and Islamism, the real party was happening up on the second level inside the suites belonging to the pro-Trump right-wing media outlets – particularly Real America’s Voice, the channel that is home to activists Steve Bannon and Jack Posobiec. A throng of conservative pundits, social media influencers and Republican personalities mingled inside and outside the suite all evening, with chips, dips and drinks provided. Politicians and their staff came and went. Some carry takeaway cups of 7-Eleven filter coffee, which costs $US7.85 (that’s $10.95, plus tip) from an arena store. Attendees cheer Trump’s arrival on night two. Bloomberg Among the crowd was John Solomon, a conservative media entrepreneur who founded digital news organisation Just the News and recently became a special government employee chairing the White House’s so-called “Government Transparency Task Force”. Solomon’s temporary job with Trump was to find, release and promote documents that purportedly showed widespread plotting to undermine US election integrity. Other people in the ultra-MAGA orbit, including Trump’s former strategist Bannon, said it was a precursor to declaring a national security emergency ahead of the midterms.



But Solomon told this masthead there was no indication Trump was planning such a thing, and little need for it. Speaking as a journalist rather than a government employee, he conceded the economy was “in a weird state” – with job indicators strong, but the price of petrol inflated due to the Iran war. Related Article Exclusive

US midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide Solomon pointed to four factors he said could avert the usual outcome of a midterm election, which is that the party in power suffers. The first was the convention itself, which aimed to “get people excited”. Second, “the Democrats don’t have any answer for it”. Third, Republicans had successfully redrawn the electoral maps to their advantage in several key states – what most people would call gerrymandering. “That makes the margin grab by the Democrats much harder to complete,” Solomon said. But the fourth factor is the biggest: money. The Republicans have a $US1 billion-plus war chest, housed across various super PACs including Trump’s MAGA Inc, which had $US403 million cash on hand at the end of July.



Federal Election Commission returns show the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund had $US239 million at the end of June, the Congressional Leadership Fund had $US142 million and the Republican National Committee $US130 million at the end of July. By contrast, the Democrats’ had just over $US241 million across their two super PACs, the Senate Majority and House Majority funds, while the Democratic National Committee had a cash deficit of $US2 million. It was recently revealed the DNC used its Washington office and other assets as collateral to secure a $US15 million loan last year. Republicans need to motivate Trump’s base as if his name were on the ballot. Bloomberg “The DNC is mortgaging their headquarters for money,” Solomon said. “Those are factors that go against the countervailing forces that normally would be against an incumbent president.” Still, those forces are significant. The president is unpopular, the Iran war is dragging on, the price of petrol is consequently high – as is the cost of living generally. Government debt is at a record $US40 trillion, and the Trump administration is trying to avert a bond market sell-off.



Republicans who gathered in Dallas were not blind to these problems, publicly or privately. But in both cases they expressed optimism that – with Trump leading the charge – they could still sell a positive story to the American public. “Here’s the reality,” said Mike Markey, a Republican from Michigan who recently lost a primary for the state Senate. “When people are upset about affordability and where everything is in this country right now, let’s remember that this isn’t a problem that we created. This is the problem that the Biden administration and Democrats really celebrated, letting in 20 million illegals.” Trump announced a $US5000 “dividend” for every adult American if Republicans retail control of both chambers. Bloomberg But Joe Biden did not start the war with Iran that has sent Brent crude, the international oil price benchmark, above $US100 for the second time this year. Markey says it’s a dose of medicine; he tries to explain using an analogy from Mrs Doubtfire. “Right at the beginning, what separates Sally Field and Robin Williams: she comes home, their son had struggled in school, she feels bad about not doing a birthday party. And she comes home and Robin Williams is on the table dancing, they’ve got a petting zoo. She had to be the un-fun parent. And Republicans, we’re the un-fun parent right now. We are fixing the mess that they made.”

World.title: The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final Jonathan Drennan September 12, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After completing an intense week of training on Friday afternoon, Swans players were divided on what to do that evening. Some wanted to watch the semi-final between Fremantle and Geelong, which would determine their opponent in next weekend’s preliminary final. Others were happy to tune out of footy for the night and wait until they reconvened to begin the forensic analysis of their next match. The Swans who did tune in to the Dockers’ tense 14-point victory at Optus Stadium were treated to an exceptional performance from ruckman Luke Jackson, with the onus now shifting to how to stop him at the SCG. Loading Swans coach Dean Cox, one of the AFL’s greatest ever ruckmen, will be aware that if Sydney can nullify Jackson, another grand final is possible. Jackson was a key man in Fremantle’s minor premiership, but the Dockers are by no means a one-man band. Jackson was joined on this year’s All-Australian team by four teammates: Shai Bolton, Jordan Clark, Murphy Reid and Josh Treacy. Against the Cats, Bolton was outstanding, kicking two goals and finishing with 26 disposals. But it was Jackson who flipped the game.



With five minutes left of the third quarter, Fremantle had conceded three successive goals and their home crowd was tense. Jackson, a former Australian under-17 basketball star, finished the quarter with eight disposals, two goals, four score involvements and 12 hitouts. In their previous meeting this season, in Perth in July, the Swans held a two-point lead at the end of the third quarter before Fremantle kicked nine goals in the final term to win by 38 points and underline their premiership credentials. Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos In that game, Swans ruckman Brodie Grundy had 29 hitouts to Jackson’s 26, with Fremantle also able to utilise Mason Cox, who had 10 hitouts. The Swans do not have a deputy with the experience of Cox, having recently used forward Hayden McLean to relieve the veteran Grundy at stoppages. Grundy’s dominance has been a foundation of Sydney’s finals run, but against Jackson in the preliminary final he will face one of the biggest tests of his career. Grundy cannot match Jackson’s scoring threat, with the Fremantle ruck averaging a goal a game and finishing the season with 27 majors, a rarity for his position.



But in the core skill of hitouts, Grundy averages 34.3 a game compared with Jackson’s 25.7. Grundy also possesses an ability to act as an auxiliary midfielder when needed and will need to do so to curb Jackson’s influence. The Swans’ midfield trio of James Rowbottom, Jai Serong and Errol Gulden combined beautifully in their qualifying win against Brisbane to help dominate clearances, but a lot of their success came through Grundy’s dominance at stoppages. Brodie Grundy tussles with Luke Jackson in the last meeting between the sides, in Perth in July. AFL Photos via Getty Images Grundy’s presence in the Swans side has transformed their ability to score from clearances. According to Champion Data, no player has averaged more hitouts-to-advantage at centre bounces than Grundy (3.9) since 2024. This season, the Swans rank No.1 for scores from clearance, and they have 14 wins and 0 losses when they outscore the opposition from clearance, highlighting the importance of Grundy’s ability to outwork Jackson.



Fremantle will travel to face a heavily depleted Swans team, missing the suspended Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey. Captain Callum Mills is also missing from the backline after suffering an ACL injury against Brisbane, depriving them of vital on-field leadership. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘You just have a lot more to lose’: How fatherhood has centred Swans star Grundy History is not on Fremantle’s side at the SCG. Fremantle have won six times at the stadium and lost 14 times. However, more recently, Fremantle have won two out the last three games at the SCG dating back to 2023. The AFL will on Sunday confirm the date and time of the preliminary final. In his post-match press conference on Friday, Geelong coach Chris Scott was full of praise for the impact of Jackson. “I always hesitate to say unique, but he’s as close as there is to unique in that position as there is in the competition,” Scott said. The Swans also have their own unique ruckman. The contest between them will go a long way to deciding which side progresses to the grand final.

World.title: Jiu-jitsu coach, stand-up comic, apiarist: Inside the surprise day jobs of Sydney’s councillors
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For 40 years, Victor Macri has spent five days a week cutting hair at Fernando’s Hair, the business his father started in Marrickville in 1960. A dispute with local councillors over a building matter prompted Macri to run as an independent for the former Marrickville Council – which was later merged to form the Inner West Council – in 2004. Victor Macri has been a part of the Marrickville community for four decades. Sam Mooy But the veteran councillor still spends Tuesday to Saturday giving haircuts with an ear to the ground. “That’s how I keep in contact with the community,” Macri says. “I get all the complaints.” He is among hundreds of local councillors in NSW for whom public office is not their primary source of income. From retail workers and Uber Eats drivers to martial arts masters and cosmetic surgeons, Sydney’s council chambers are filled with elected officials juggling a range of jobs.



Mayors and councillors at the state’s 128 local councils are not paid full-time wages but receive fees determined by the Local Government Remuneration Tribunal. Those payments are determined by the size and type of council on which they serve. For example, a City of Sydney councillor is paid between $32,810 and $48,140. In Strathfield, it’s between $10,920 and $24,080. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams is a trade lane gatekeeper three days a week at Bunnings, where he loads cars and checks receipts – and the community’s pulse. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams keeps an eye on the local economy by working at Bunnings. Janie Barrett He replies to emails during his lunch breaks, and Saturdays to Tuesdays are booked with council commitments, community events and citizenship ceremonies. Williams, a member of the Your Northern Beaches Independent Team, estimates he spends about two hours a day reading council documents, but says it’s worthwhile. “When you’re of service to other people, you forget about your own problems ... It’s about dopamine, and doing nice things for people,” he says.



Lane Cove Labor councillor David Roenfeldt drives buses from Sydney Airport to Yass and Canberra, while Bayside Council’s Chris Saravinovski, also Labor, works as an airport ramp agent and is a jack-of-all-trades, from baggage handling to health and safety. Saravinovski says council work is flexible and rewarding. Related Article Sydney councils This Sydney council was meant to pick a new deputy mayor. A jaunt to the UK got in the way “It’s not for the money,” he says. “You can’t survive on it ... I don’t blame any other councillor having another job and picking this up as a side thing.” Wollondilly Mayor Matt Gould, an independent, once juggled council with drone piloting. Since becoming mayor, he resolved he could do “both poorly or one properly”. Bayside Liberal councillor Dr Ron Bezic is a cosmetic surgeon, while the Hills Shire’s Dr Mila Kasby is a Greens councillor who stepped away from her veterinary practice to focus on volunteer work. She says the system favours financially comfortable candidates. “We need a whole range of different people from different backgrounds … because councillors aren’t paid a living wage, I think that excludes a lot of people,” Kasby said.



Hawkesbury councillor Shane Djuric, who is a Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party member, was a beekeeper but retired following a 2023 injury. Trade-offs between full-time work and council push some to rely on side hustles. Katie Little once spent her spare time on the DJ circuit. Now, she picks up odd jobs such as dog boarding. James Brickwood Lane Cove Labor councillor Katie Little, a former DJ and stand-up comedian, manages a retirement village but also boards dogs at her home. Striking the balance between single motherhood, having a day job and being a councillor made side hustles necessary. “When I started dog boarding, the dogs sent to me came with food better than my kids and I were surviving on,” Little says. Ethan Hrnjak, a Greens councillor from the Northern Beaches, studies law at Macquarie University. His odd jobs have included test kitchen assistant at KFC headquarters and Uber Eats driving.



Ryde’s Felix Lo is a notary public and a Brazilian jiu-jitsu coach taking up to 15 classes a week. The Labor councillor says the similarities between governance and BJJ run deeper than it might seem. “Jiu-jitsu is very much physical, but it’s also like playing chess. Every move, you have to be very careful ... This analogy can apply to local politics and in running the city, right?” Dr Felix Lo studied law at university and teaches regular jiu-jitsu classes. Wolter Peeters Blacktown has a retired NSW police chief inspector, Robert Fitzgerald, a Labor councillor, and police prosecutor Mohit Kumar, a Liberal, on council. Kumar, who spends his days at Blacktown Court House, says his capacity is constrained by the fact that his council role isn’t full-time. “There are a lot of sacrifices you got to make, especially with family.” Some professions feature repeatedly. Ryde’s Daniel Han, a Liberal, and Strathfield Labor councillor Rory Nosworthy both teach high school chemistry.

World.title: Medicine company bids to get pseudoephedrine out from behind pharmacy counters
World.content:
A pharmaceutical company wants the cold and flu drug pseudoephedrine out from behind the counter and back on pharmacy shelves.

Reckitt Benckiser has put in an application with drug regulator Medsafe to make the medicine easier to purchase.

The medicine - a precursor for manufacturing methamphetamine or P - was no longer a threat in its retail form because criminal gangs imported their raw ingredients in bulk, Reckitt said in its application.

Currently, pseudoephedrine was available as a restricted medicine from pharmacies, meaning it was not stocked on open shelves.

People who wanted to buy it must instead ask a pharmacist who would decide if it was suitable for them before providing it.

Under the new proposal, small packets of the pill form, effectively one day's worth, would be available for people to select themselves, alongside medicines like panadol and ibuprofen.

It would still only be sold in pharmacies.

Pseudoephedrine was made a prescription-only drug in 2011 because of its use in the manufacture of P.

But in 2024, it was reclassified to its current status after ACT's David Seymour pushed for the change on the back of an election campaign promise.

ACT's David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Reckitt's application said the proposed change would give New Zealanders better access to a very effective nasal decongestant and lessen the workload of stretched pharmacists.

Heavily restricting pseudoephedrine in 2011 did not effectively control the supply and use of meth in New Zealand, it said.

"The supply and manufacture of methamphetamine use in New Zealand has shifted from small scale production, where pharmacy sourced pseudoephedrine was the main precursor used," it said.

Instead it there was "large scale clandestine manufacture" with ingredients brought in from overseas or bulk importation of methamphetamine, the application said.

When pseudoephedrine was banned from shelves in 2011, many cold and flu remedies changed to the drug phenylephrine.

That was now the subject of a class action lawsuit after evidence it was ineffective.

Medsafe's Medicines Classification Committee would discuss Reckitt's application at its meeting next month.

World.title: Wellington Airport evacuated after burnt cooking triggers smoke alarm
World.content:
Wellington Airport has been evacuated after a smoke alarm went off.

Fire and Emergency responded with one crew from Kilbirnie, and another from Newtown, at 4.19pm on Saturday.

It found the alarm had been triggered by burnt cooking.

Wellington Airport said the southwest pier had been briefly evacuated, with the area quickly cleared for re-entry.

World.title: Why officials are 'reasonably confident' of avoiding fuel supply shocks
World.content:
Regardless of the uncertainties surrounding the Iran war and the US administration, New Zealand officials six months on are hopeful - confident, even - that supply chains will hold. In the first of this two-part series RNZ political reporter Russell Palmer sits down with MBIE's Iain Cossar.

"Reasonably confident" is how New Zealand's top fuel official rates the country's chances of avoiding fuel shortages.

It's a remarkable shift considering the level of exposure for New Zealand which Iain Cossar says is among the highest in the world.

"As far as markets go, we couldn't be probably more. We were probably one of the most exposed to a Hormuz closure and were rightly quite worried about what that might mean for actual supply."

After the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran in February, resulting in the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet set up an all-of-government response group including 11 agencies.

Treasury leads the price response, and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) leads the supply response. At the height of the crisis they were meeting daily at 7.30am.

At the time, the world was producing about 106 million barrels of oil a day, and consumed about 104 million a day in 2025. Nearly 20 percent transits the Hormuz Strait - mostly from Middle-East states to Asia.

A fine line between too much and not enough

Cossar took over in early April as the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's deputy secretary for the fuel supply response, which has drawn on expertise from 180 ministry staff and secondees.

He says with New Zealand no longer refining onshore, it is largely reliant on Asian markets with Korea, Singapore, Malaysia and Japan supplying more than 90 percent of the fuel Kiwis used in 2025.

"We are highly dependent on them getting the raw product to refine and then send to us. We're about three weeks shipping away, give or take," he says.

New Zealand runs on a "just-in-time" model where about 50 days of fuel - with about 20 days' of that being offshore - are booked on shipments up to three months in advance.

So far, only one shipment has been delayed, because the ship diverted to another destination.

"It's literally the equivalent of you driving to one petrol station and then deciding you can get a better price at another one," Cossar says.

"The fuel that was on that consignment ... was sought and bought from another supplier to come to New Zealand within six hours," Cossar says.

New Zealand's top fuel official Iain Cossar. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

New Zealand also needed to worry about the opposite problem: ullage, a term from the wine industry meaning the space left in the tank. With the just-in-time model relying on stable fuel consumption, people buying less to save money could disrupt things.

"We can only hold so much fuel in the country and if people reduce their consumption of that fuel, what could happen is that a ship arrives with ... jet or petrol and it can't offload," Cossar says.

"They are then waiting in harbour and because you've got a large tanker sitting at dock doing nothing, you're actually paying quite a price for that."

Cossar says the Strait's closure had an impact on the world economy "consistent with, and I think slightly higher maybe, than the supply shock of the '70s", but several factors helped:

markets adjusted very quickly, with oil and refined product flows around the globe going to those countries that could afford it

more product was coming out of the Middle East than anticipated, including through other channels and some through the "closed" strait

Southeast Asian markets and poorer countries were affected and responded by reducing consumption

China reduced its demand considerably, easing global demand (about 5 million barrels per day)

more oil production came online in other countries, particularly the US, Kazakhstan and Brazil (about 1.2 million barrels per day)

the International Energy Agency ordered 400 million barrels of global oil reserves to be released to market over the course of the crisis (about 300 million were released by early August).

Going dark, or over land

Cossar says markets have always been optimistic the conflict in Iran would be resolved eventually "so they priced that in, but you do see continuing variability with the ever-changing geopolitics".

Oil continued to leave the Middle East through various methods: dark transits, ship-to-ship transfers, US military night corridors and alternative land pipelines.

In August, the pre-conflict rate of 55 ships a day had dropped to about 10, largely through dark transits where ships "go dark" by shutting off their identification transponders to avoid detection.

Sometimes these were small ships that could run the Strait, then transfer oil to larger tankers in the open Arabian sea. Other times, the US military would run convoys at night in coordinated groups.

Ways oil was leaving the Strait of Hormuz. Supplied / International Energy Agency

Overland pipelines also played a part, with the East-West pipline across Saudi Arabia and the UAE taking up to 7 million barrels a day; the Habshan-Fujairah Pipeline carrying up to 1.8 million barrels a day from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah; and Saudi Arabia increasingly diverting Yanbu exports via the SUMED pipeline and the Suez Canal.

China a big player in supply and demand

China - as one of the world's biggest importers of crude - "played and continues to play quite a critical role" by cutting imports by a third to half.

"They solved a third of our problem right there, globally. Now, we don't know exactly why they've done that - the price would have been an impact and perhaps they just chose to not import, as they had quite extensive reserves."

Beijing did impose export controls on refined fuel for a time but released those again in July, and Cossar says a return would not necessarily mean a shortage.

The size of China's reserves is a mystery - particularly below ground - but Cossar says they are believed to be "significant" and demand remains below pre-conflict levels.

He says despite the uncertainty, and although New Zealand is prepared in case a supply shock should emerge, he is not expecting that to happen.

"We're reasonably optimistic we won't face a supply shock because we have seen world markets adjust, new supply has become available, and there is supply getting out of the Middle East that we weren't actually aware of.

"Some countries will continue to buy for those who can afford it, and those who can't, won't. Put bluntly, New Zealand is in the countries who could probably afford it. We won't like it [when prices are higher] and it will have impacts on us, but we'll still be able to afford fuel."

A graph of global fuel reserves. Supplied / International Energy Agency

Further reassurances come from New Zealand's "robust" regulatory system, the additional reserves loaded up at Marsden Point, continued shipments finding ways out of the Hormuz Strait and out of the Red Sea.

By the end of May, the number of staff dedicated to the response had dropped to 110, and today fewer than 12 people remain involved, many splitting their time with other work.

In the long term, although global reserves have fallen below 7.9 billion barrels, they are still above 2022 levels "so it's not like we are in uncharted territory", Cossar says.

World.title: Hundreds turn up to see Dunedin Hospital's new outpatient building
World.content:
A hospital is not usually a place people want to spend a lot of time in, let alone give up some of their Saturday to go to.

But about 1300 people jumped at the chance to explore the new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building as part of a free community open day on 12 September.

The new build - which was one of the country's biggest health infrastructure projects - was expected to allow for thousands of more scans, day surgeries and specialist appointments each year.

Retired GP Sharleen was relieved to walk through the new building, saying it was beautiful and fit for purpose, unlike the old hospital, which has not been for a long time.

"It feels like a bit of a rabbit warren at the moment but I think that's just a question of getting the signage and things sorted out and outfitted," she said.

"But I think it's going to be a wonderful building and it's really going to speed up outpatients and also have an impact on inpatients services by diverting some of the services over here - radiology and minor theatre."

Part of the foyer at the new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building, September 2026. Tess Brunton / RNZ

She was not entirely sold on the check-in kiosks, but said staff had assured her that there would be plenty of people to support as well as a face-to-face option.

It was an excellent step up for staff, she said.

"I think there's been a lot of mucking around over the whole build and we've taken a paired down service with reduced beds and we haven't been promised a PET scanner yet and I think really people have to step up and make this a top-level facility and not hold back."

Dunedin resident Elena Calvert was excited to explore the new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building. Tess Brunton / RNZ

Dunedin resident Elena Calvert was eager to check it out.

"We've been waiting for this building to open for probably a decade now so as soon as they announced there's going to be tours, we signed up because we'd love to see it on the inside and all the exciting things that we've heard about for such a long time," she said.

"You'll never be able to see into those rooms unless you use them and ideally you don't want to use them for as long as possible."

The excitement from staff was contagious and she believed the new build would greatly benefit the region, Calvert said.

"It's a lovely space. It's so sunny, it's so bright, it's colourful, it's new. The colours are inviting, there's a story, there is great artwork."

Ian Ross joined a morning tour of the new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building. Tess Brunton / RNZ

Ian Ross used outpatient services regularly and also wanted to see where his taxpayers dollars went.

"The existing outpatient facilities are old, they're tired. You really get the sense that the staff there are putting up with a lot and that a space like this will give them all the solutions that they've always wanted," he said.

GP Kevin said it was great to see a future-proofed hospital.

"It's very welcoming and friendly. All the rooms are very light and there's lovely natural light and there's great spaces for the staff to work in. It's comfortable for both staff and patients."

Dunedin resident Robbie said the guides were lovely.

"You sort of get that sense of pride and relief that it's getting just about there and that it will take some pressure off the system, which is good to hear," she said.

Dunedin resident Russell was impressed by the size and the quality of the build as well as the artwork spread throughout the building.

He and his wife have spent time at the eye clinic, and he said it could be quite cluttered but the new building had a great sense of space.

But it would take a bit of time to get used to seeing high-rise buildings after growing up in Dunedin.

"When I see the crane and the top storey [of the inpatient building] is about where the cab is. It will be a very high building," he said.

"The fire station, as a child, was a big building. Well, it's quite dwarfed by that."

Warren and Mahoney Architects principal David Mahon was involved in designing the outpatient building. Tess Brunton / RNZ

Warren and Mahoney Architects principal David Mahon was involved in designing the outpatient building.

He believed it was important to design it in a way that gave back to the community and was well integrated, including a landscape buffer along Cumberland Street and large windows overlooking historic buildings.

"Some those patients may only be in a room for say 15 or 20 minutes and it needs to be a nice environment for them," he said.

"But at the same time, you've got staff that will be in this building for eight or nine hours a day. So access to daylight is a huge part of a working environment.

"So it gives back to them, as you say, just that those views out across the harbour, across the city, just really utilising them. They're a great natural sort of aspect for the project."

They worked with mana whenua and cultural advisors, Aukaha, for the aesthetic and functionality of the build, which included a dedicated space for iwi.

"The two buildings, actually one sits in the water, one sits on the land, along the historic, now reclaimed foreshore. So the two colours of the buildings reflect their sort of different locations," he said.

"The inpatients which comes in the future will be blue and greens, whereas just the yellow is more reflective of the sands and the foreshore colouring ... it's just deeply, deeply embedded.

"It's not just a pattern making at the end. It was very much a co-design process throughout."

New Dunedin Hospital programme director Bridget Dickson. Tess Brunton / RNZ

New Dunedin Hospital programme director Bridget Dickson was delighted to be able to welcome the community into the new building, saying it was a significant milestone and a long time coming.

"We know that people have been waiting for this opportunity to be able to come inside," she said.

"They've been watching the building come out of the ground over the last couple of years and it's fabulous to be able to give this opportunity for people to see inside, see the modern fit for purpose facilities that will be beginning to deliver clinical care in the coming weeks."

One of the differences people might notice were the four full-sized operating theatres and four procedure rooms that boosted their ability for day surgeries, Dickson said.

It had been built with the patient in mind.

"We are aiming for the first year of the operation of this facility to be able to deliver 1700 more day surgery procedures.

"We are also aiming to be able to deliver 13,000 more imaging scans, and this includes being able to deliver MRI scans, CT scans and X-rays in our new facility here in the outpatient building."

There had already been tours for staff and their families and for people who needed a lower sensory tour.

A new X-ray machine at the new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building, September 2026. Tess Brunton / RNZ

The outpatient building was expected to be opened to patients next month but an official date has yet to be announced.

As for the inpatient building, Dickson said it was on time and on budget.

World.title: Why am I paying to withdraw my KiwiSaver? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

I recently found out that it can cost $300 per person in lawyer fees to withdraw KiwiSaver funds for a deposit on a house. The funds we deposit are taxed before they go in the fund, we pay fees to the fund manager, and tax on the interest, then fees to withdraw. I guess you can say we get a government contribution and employer contribution but even so it is not as good a deal for worker as the original scheme was, and it is locked in.

First, I do have sympathy for the argument that we don't have enough incentives to get people investing in KiwiSaver in New Zealand. Lots of other countries offer tax breaks that can make saving for the future a lot more appealing.

But that aside, on your point about first-home withdrawals from KiwiSaver, lawyers usually handle a lot of the process of the application, and receive the money in their trust account before it's paid out to the vendor.

They charge for their time in doing this. Sometimes, they bundle the cost of this into the overall cost of conveyancing for the purchase. The first-home withdrawal bit is usually quite small in comparison to the rest of the bill. I asked my lawyers about this and was told that they charge $325 including GST for an application.

This is specific to a first-home withdrawal, you wouldn't be paying fees for taking your money out when you are 65, for instance.

When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

I am retired since 2024 and IRD has recalculated my PIR at 10.5 percent. I was on 28 percent prior to the update. My partner is still working and on a 28 percent PIR. All our investments are held jointly. What will happen at tax time with the two different PIR?

It seems that this will depend on the type of investment you have. For things like term deposits and direct shares, you'll have an ownership split, usually 50/50, and you'll be each taxed on your proportion of the income, interest, gains and so on, at your own PIR.

But if you have a jointly held portfolio investment entity (PIE) investment, you'll be taxed on that one at the higher of your two PIR rates.

In 15 months' time I would like to retire. I am presently with an active manager KiwiSaver provider, paying high fees. However, having looked into fees and availability I'm seriously considering transferring to a passive index provider. Is it advisable, given looming retirement, to change to passive investment with overall lower fees or stay with an active manager with higher fees and moderate funds? I have a substantial amount in my KiwiSaver account and presently not making substantial gains given past down turns.

I was at an event this week where someone asked me the same question - is it better to be in a cheaper KiwiSaver fund, when you're retired and potentially not making contributions to KiwiSaver any more?

I can't give personalised financial advice, but here are some general thoughts. I would tend to say that people should not move provider simply for the fees, although they are one of the few things that are actually in our control as investors.

I can understand why, if your balance, isn't growing as much through contributions, you might be particularly keen to make sure that it's not being eroded by higher fees.

If it were me, I would compare after-fee returns over a number of years from a range of providers to get a sense of whether there are better options elsewhere.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub recently conducted some research that showed what made the difference to outcomes was really the type of fund people were in, not the provider they chose or, overall, the fees they were paying.

On that basis, I would suggest the most important thing to do is to make sure that you have a good understanding of your risk profile and time horizon, and that your invsetment fund choices align with that. A year or so before retirement is a good time to get some personalised advice, if possible, to come up with a strategy to make your money last through retirement.

World.title: Mistakes and lack of clear guidance led to millions being misspent, pokie trust says
World.content:
A pokie trust believes mistakes and a lack of clear guidance from regulators led to millions of dollars being misspent.

The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) has found up to $28 million that should have been available for community grants has been used to cover other expenses instead.

Pub Charity chief executive Martin Cheer said some trusts may have misunderstood the rules, but ignorance of the law was no excuse.

"There's an element of hand in glove really; the industry is regulated and we need guidance from the regulator.

"But also these are sovereign entities with governance structures and management. They should have done better."

Cheer said the trusts were working to rectify the situation, with $11.5 million recovered so far.

Gaming Machine Association chair Peter Dengate Thrush told RNZ that while mistakes were made in the accounts, it looked worse than it was because of the review's timeframe.

"If the total figure that the department is now saying needs accounting for is $28m, while that's a lot of money, spread out over the 10 years that the department has now gone back ... it's only a very small proportion of the total flow."

He said it was the regulator's job to keep the industry clean.

Most trusts tried to comply with the rules, work closely with officials and operate transparently, he said.

Millions of dollars spent by pokie orgs, instead of grants Nine To Noon Download MP3 18m

However, he believed there should be consequences for any trusts that did engage in creative accounting.

"There will be some societies who are in deep trouble, for which this is not just an accounting readjustment.

"The department occasionally finds some people breaking the law. If there are any at that end of the scale, then they should be prosecuted," he told RNZ.

On Friday, DIA director of gambling Vicki Scott said about three-quarters of the 32 trusts were non-compliant with the rules to some degree.

"We've been investigating for two to three years now.

"Many were essentially prioritising their own growth and their own competitive advantage over the interests of the community.

"They were spending beyond their means on things like gaming machines."

She believed about $20m could be recovered. Repayment plans have been devised with some trusts.

"Our role isn't to put a significant section of the industry out of business but we are really firm that the money needs to be back in the community's hands in a reasonable period of time."

World.title: Trump welcomed to Ireland with trash-covered double
World.content:
Donald Trump's satirical double has beaten him to Dublin, as Ireland prepares to welcome the US president.

'The Trash Talker' by Wexford artist TinKicker depicts Trump emerging from a wheelie rubbish bin, covered in trash. He is posing with his post-assassination campaign fist-pump.

Images of the artwork went viral when it first appeared at CAN-AL Fest in St Mullins last month. It is now on display at the Teal House Gallery in Dublin.

The US president's visit this weekend has sparked one of the biggest security and policing operations ever undertaken by the Republic of Ireland.

He is expected to touch down on Air Force One at Dublin Airport on Saturday night (NZ time). During his two-day visit, he will visit Ireland's President Catherine Connolly at her official residence and Irish Prime Minister (Taoiseach) Michael Martin at Farmleigh House, the republic's official state guest house located inside Dublin's Phoenix Park.

World.title: One dead after house fire on Matakana Island in Bay of Plenty
World.content:
One person has died in a house fire on Matakana Island in the Bay of Plenty.

Fire and Emergency Northern Shift Manager Garreth Lewis said crews from Matakana Island, Omokoroa, Greerton, and Te Puke were called to the fire at about 4am on Saturday morning.

He said the fire was well involved upon arrival, about 10 metres by 15 metres in size.

A police spokesperson confirmed they were at the scene on Saturday morning

They said one person was being treated for burns, but wouldn't confirm if there had been any fatalities.

World.title: Newcastle's finals win is proof the future has come
World.content:
If Newcastle were going to pull off a classic finals ambush on South Sydney they were going to need some new heroes to be born under the bright lights of the Sydney Football Stadium.

The Knights went into the game light up front, not in size, strength or willingness, but certainly in experience and definitely in recognition. After their 20-10 win over South Sydney, however, they will never have the luxury of being underestimated again.

Across 80 minutes of a classic blood-and-thunder final, fresh faces and young legs won the day as the star-studded Rabbitohs outfit fought on despite being busted until they were finally beaten.

NRL Finals live Newcastle holds on for a 20-10 victory over South Sydney to kick-off the 2026 finals series, but Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett fumes at more Bunker confusion after a contentious call.

Perhaps it could have all been different were it not for Cody Walker falling to a sniper's shot early in the second half, suffering a calf injury that ended his night early.

The ageless Walker is what binds the Rabbitohs left edge together and takes it from a series of talented individuals to the closest thing rugby league has to a hammer of the gods.

But you'll find little sympathy for an injury up Newcastle way. They were without Dylan Brown, Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti heading into this and while plenty expected them to fight few expected them to win.

After their first finals win away from home in 13 years, expectations be damned. They defied them all over the park, perhaps no more than down their right, where backrower Jermaine McEwan had the game of his young life.

It was always going to be a big night for the 21-year old, one way or the other. It was he who would be tasked with setting up Newcastle's defences against the Rabbitohs knockout left.

He did that with aplomb, even before Walker went down, from setting the tone with driving hits from the inside to holding his width and his nerve when Souths gave their chainsaw a rip.

Throw in two tries and it's the last time McEwan will catch anybody by surprise.

Together that Knights edge put together some of the best defensive plays of the night, but it wasn't the biggest — that honour must belong to McEwan's backrow partner, Francis Manuleleua.

They call him "Big Frisco" and people were put in Alcatraz for the type of violence he dropped on Cameron Murray late in the first half as he raced out of the line to dish out one of the hits of the season.

Technically it was illegal — the shot was clean, but Manuleleua was half a metre offside. The red and blue hordes at the southern end of the ground didn't seem to care, even though Souths scored off the field position, because sometimes it's worth it.

Paying the blood price for a little bit of rough stuff is something Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell know well.

The two centres fought like demons after a scuffle midway through the first half and while both won their share of battles it was Gagai who won the war.

Gagai is one of the few older heads in this side — you can call him older but don't call him old, whatever you do — and only a player as sure as himself as the 35-year old would risk poking a bear like Mitchell.

It's something few have done while surviving to tell the tale but Gagai didn't just weather the might and power, he fought like a far younger man, with nothing held back and no regard for his own safety.

His try in the 25th minute was a snapshot the endless love of competition that keeps him young even as the years keep passing and his roar of triumph after he was first to a Sandon Smith kick was among the first harbingers of what was unfolding.

There were other fine battles and contributors — Bradman Best and Jack Wighton, who was close to his side's best, went hell for leather on the other side of the field to Gagai and Mitchell.

Tyson Frizell had a game up front that puts the war back into warhorse and Keaon Koloamatangi left everything out there in his final game as a Rabbitoh.

Kalyn Ponga, once the sun around which everything in Newcastle orbited, was prominent throughout but the class of Smith and Fletcher Sharpe meant the whole game was not on his shoulders and the Knights fullback thrived as a result.

It meant he was able to access the best parts of his game, something the Rabbitohs found difficult throughout even as a torrid defensive effort and several last gasp saves by Campbell Graham kept their heads above water.

They will be haunted by the hypothetical over the summer after their first trip to the finals in four years fell at the first hurdle.

Walker cut a forlorn figure on the South Sydney bench. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If only Walker didn't get injured, or at least had made it through more of the game.

If only Bud Sullivan's circus act of a try wasn't chalked off for a knock on from Alex Johnston that could have easily been called a strip, just as Dom Young's try could have easily been rubbed off the board.

If only Brandon Smith's last desperate effort with three minutes left — which would have forced a big finish at the very least — didn't come up a blade of grass short.

If only, on a night where they played something resembling their top side for one of the first times all season, they were able to tap into the tried and true talent that lurks somewhere within and rises to the surface enough to tantalise and tease.

They are a team built for the present with stars who made their reputation on tearing down what came before them. That's the law of the jungle and the nature of the game.

The Rabbitohs will fancy their chances of returning to the mix next year but this time around were served a reminder there comes a time when the young feed on the old.

This night was such a time and with nothing to lose and everything to prove, Newcastle was ravenous.

World.title: Shelton through to US Open final as he looks to end 23-year drought
World.content:
American eighth seed Ben Shelton has the chance to end his country's long wait for another men's US Open champion after beating compatriot Frances Tiafoe to reach the final.

Shelton posted a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory over Tiafoe in the second semi-final and will play top seed Alexander Zverev in the final on Monday morning, AEST.

He showed plenty of energy after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended at 3:33 am Wednesday, local time.

It was the latest finish to a match in US Open history.

Andy Roddick was the most recent American to win the men's US Open title, in 2003.

Zverev will play for his second major title this year after beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) in the first semi.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men's player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, which he lost to Jannik Sinner, and is 24-2 in grand slam matches this season.

"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I've had a lot of struggles at the major level. I was so close so many times and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.

Alexander Zverev on his way to a straight-sets win against Karen Khachanov. (Getty Images: Manuela Davies/USTA)

Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the US Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.

Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first number one-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third grand slam semifinal, including second at the US Open.

He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev's serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.

Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.
